Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verses 1–2:

Surat al-Rum

It is Meccan, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them. Indeed, Ibn 'Atiyyah and others said: there is no disagreement regarding its being Meccan, and they did not except anything from it. Al-Hasan said: it is Meccan except the words of Allah Most High: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening﴾ [al-Rum: 17], and the verse [that follows]. This is contrary to the position of the majority, and to the interpretation that is accepted, as its explanation will come, Allah willing. Its number of verses is sixty, and according to some fifty-nine. The connection of this surah with the preceding one, according to what al-Jalal al-Suyuti said, is that the preceding surah ended with the words of Allah Most High: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 69], and this surah opens with the promise of the victory of those among the People of the Book who were overcome, with triumph and support, and with the joy of the believers at that, and that the dominion belongs to the people of striving in it, and that what befell them before that of defeat does not harm them. This is in addition to their correspondence with what precedes it in the opening letters, (Alif-Lam-Mim). It is not hidden that fighting the People of the Book is not part of striving in the cause of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and by this the connection becomes weak. Whoever considers the reports of the occasion of revelation will see that what this surah opens with includes the support of the believers by repelling the gloating of their enemies, the polytheists, and they had never ceased striving in the cause of Allah Most High, for His sake, and for His face, the Mighty and Majestic; and the fact that they did not strive with the sword at the time of revelation does not harm this. In my view, this is a better connection than the one mentioned by al-Jalal.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ The discussion of it is as has passed regarding its like among the noble openings. ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾. Al-Rum is a great tribe, from the descendants of Rumi ibn Yunan ibn 'Iljan ibn Yafith ibn Nuh, peace be upon him. It was also said: from the descendants of Yafan ibn Yafith. It was also said: from the descendants of Ra'wil ibn 'Is ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Al-Jawhari said: from the descendants of Rum ibn 'Is, the one mentioned. They had an encounter with Persia in the time of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and Persia overcame them and subdued them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 3:

﴿in the nearest part of the land﴾ i.e., the nearest of it.

By "the land" is meant the land of the Romans, with "al-" (the definite article) standing in place of the pronoun added to it, and the nearness is considered with respect to the people of Makkah, since the discourse is addressed to them. Or it is meant the land of Makkah and its surroundings, since that is the land known to them, and the nearness is considered with respect to the Romans. Or the land is the land of the Romans, because they have been mentioned, and the nearness is considered with respect to their enemy, namely Persia, in accordance with the hadith of the defeat. It has come through many chains that the battle took place between Adhri'at and Busra. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: in al-Urdunn and Filastin. Mujahid said: in al-Jazirah, meaning al-Jazirah al-'Umariyyah, not the Arabian Peninsula. Each opinion has been matched to one of the three aspects, in order. Ibn Hajar preferred the first opinion.

Al-Kalbi read "fi adani al-ardi" (in the nearest parts of the land). ﴿And they﴾, i.e., the Romans, ﴿after their defeat﴾, i.e., after Persia defeated them. This is a verbal noun (masdar) in the genitive, governed by its object, or by its deputy of the agent if it is a verbal noun of the passive voice. Some scholars preferred this reading because it agrees with the sublime arrangement of the verse.

Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah read "ghalbihim" with a sukun on the lam. From Abu 'Amr it is narrated that he read "ghilabihim" on the pattern of "kitab". All of them are verbal nouns of "ghalaba". The prepositional phrase is connected to the statement of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿they will be overcome﴾. In this there is emphasis on what is understood from the sin (the future particle), and on the fact that their vanquisher was the one who had been victorious over them. In constructing the sentence upon the pronoun there is reinforcement of the ruling, i.e., they will certainly overcome Persia.

And His saying, ﴿in a few years﴾, is also connected to ﴿they will be overcome﴾.

Al-Bid' (a few) is, according to al-Asma'i, what lies between three and ten. In al-Mujmal (a lexicon), it is what lies between one and nine. It is also said to be "what is above five and below ten." Al-Mubarrad said it is what lies between two decades in all numbers.

It is related that "the Persians attacked the Romans, and they met them at Adhri'at and Busra, and the Persians prevailed over them. This reached the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, who were in Makkah, and it grieved them. The Prophet ﷺ disliked that the unlettered (Majus) Magians should prevail over the People of the Book, the Romans. The disbelievers in Makkah rejoiced and gloated. They met the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'You are People of the Book, and the Christians are People of the Book. Our brothers, the people of Persia, have prevailed over your brothers, the People of the Book. If you fight us, we will surely prevail over you.' So God, exalted is He, revealed ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. The Romans have been overcome﴾ and the verses that follow. Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, went out to the disbelievers and said: 'Have you rejoiced at the victory of your brothers over our brothers? Do not rejoice. May God not gladden your eyes. By God, the Romans will surely prevail over the Persians. Our Prophet ﷺ informed us of this.' Then Ubayy ibn Khalaf stood up to him and said: 'You have lied.' Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, said to him: 'You are the liar, O enemy of God. Come, let us make a wager (munahaba): ten she-camels from me and ten she-camels from you. If the Romans prevail over the Persians, you pay; and if the Persians prevail, I pay, within three years.' So he made the wager with him. Then Abu Bakr came to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him. He ﷺ said: 'That is not what I mentioned. Al-bid' is what lies between three and nine. So increase the stake and extend the term.' Abu Bakr went out and met Ubayy and said: 'Perhaps you have regretted?' He said: 'No. Come, I will increase the stake for you and extend the term for you. Make it one hundred she-camels for nine years.' He said: 'I have agreed.' When Abu Bakr intended to emigrate (hijrah), Ubayy demanded from him a guarantor for the stake, in case he (Abu Bakr) lost. His son Abd al-Rahman stood surety for it. When Ubayy intended to go out to Uhud, Abd al-Rahman asked him for a guarantor, and he gave him one. Ubayy died from a wound that the Prophet ﷺ had inflicted on him. The Romans prevailed over the Persians when the seventh year began."

It is reported in the narrations that they prevailed over them on the day of Hudaybiyah.

Al-Tirmidhi related, and graded it as good (hasan), that "when the Day of Badr came, the Romans prevailed over the Persians. Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, took the stake from the heirs of Ubayy and brought it to the Prophet ﷺ. He ﷺ said: 'Give it in charity (tasaddaq).'"

In a narration of Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn Asakir, from al-Bara' ibn Azib, that he ﷺ said: "This is suht (ill-gotten gain); give it in charity."

It is raised as an objection: if that happened before the prohibition of gambling (qimar), as Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi related from Qatadah, and al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, related from Niyar ibn Mukram al-Aslami, and this is the apparent view, because the surah is Makkan and the prohibition of wine and gambling is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, then what is the sense of calling it suht? And if it happened after the prohibition, how can he be commanded to give in charity something unlawful that is not mixed with anything else, while its owner is known, and in such a case it is obligatory to return the property to him? If it is said that it is property of the enemy (harbi), and the incident took place in Makkah, which before the Conquest was Dar al-Harb (abode of war), and that invalid contracts ('uqud fasidah) are permitted in it according to Abu Hanifa and Muhammad, may God have mercy on them both, then the word suht does not apply. You, however, may object to the authenticity of this narration. If its authenticity is not established, then the command to give in charity remains, and in that case it may be for a benefit that the Messenger of God ﷺ saw, and it is charity from what is lawful. As for if it happened before the prohibition of gambling, as is relied upon, then it is clear. As for if it happened after the prohibition, then it is because Abu Hanifa and Muhammad said that invalid contracts are permitted in Dar al-Harb between Muslims and disbelievers, and they argued for the validity of this by what Abu Bakr did in this story. It is well established in the narrations that he ﷺ did not object to the wager itself, but he objected to the postponement for three years, and directed him to increase the stakes for them. It may perhaps be said, if the report is authentic, that suht does not mean unlawful, but rather what becomes a cause of shame and deficiency in manliness (muruwwah), to the point that it is as if it uproots it (yushhituha), i.e., destroys it, as in his ﷺ saying: "The earnings of the cupper (kasb al-hajjam) are suht." Al-Raghib said: this is because it destroys manliness, not religion. So it is as if he ﷺ saw that acquiring wealth from this, even if lawful, damages the manliness of Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, so he called it suht. His permission for the wager does not contradict this, since it does not harm manliness at all. And in it is a manifestation of certainty in the truth of what the Prophet ﷺ brought, and the Prophet ﷺ was confident of the righteousness of the Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, and that if he commanded him to give away what he took and forbade him to make it his property, he would not disobey him. It is also said that suht here means that for which there is no liability on the one who consumes it, which is one of its meanings, as in al-Nihayah (a lexicon). The meaning is: this is what there is no liability upon you for if you consume it and dispose of it as you wish; give it in charity. It is as if the Prophet ﷺ, after informing the Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, that there was no obstacle to his disposing of it as he wished, guided him to what is better and more fitting, saying: "Give it in charity." This is, as you see, [a weak view]. It is also said that suht, as in al-Nihayah, occurs in speech sometimes with the meaning of unlawful and sometimes with the meaning of disliked (makruh), and this is determined by context. So it is possible that in the report, if it is authentic, it means disliked, since the command to give charity precludes its being unlawful, so it is necessarily the meaning of disliked. There is room for consideration in this. As for interpreting suht as unlawful, and committing to the view that it is permissible to give unlawful property in charity on the basis of this report, that is something not to be considered at all. So reflect.

Both victories took place during the reign of Khosrow Parviz. In Rawdat al-Safa, he says, in a translation of it: "When fourteen years of Khosrow's reign had passed, the Romans betrayed their king and killed him together with his son Bunatus. His other son fled to Khosrow, who equipped him with three commanders of high rank along with a great army. They entered the lands of Syria, Palestine, and Jerusalem, and took captive those there of bishops and others. They sent to Khosrow the Cross that had been buried among them in a golden coffer. Likewise, they seized Alexandria and the lands of Nubia until they reached the regions of Constantinople. They caused much destruction and strove to make the Romans obey the son of Caesar, but did not succeed. It is said that the Romans appointed over them a ruler named Heraclius (Hiraql), who was a just sultan fearing God, exalted is He. When he saw that the destruction of Persia had spread through the lands of the Romans in plunder and killing, he humbled himself, wept, and asked God, exalted is He, to deliver the Romans. His supplication met the target of response. In several nights he saw in his dream that Khosrow had been brought to him with a chain on his neck, and it was said to him: 'Hasten to fight Parviz, for victory and triumph will be yours.' So Heraclius gathered his army because of that vision and set out from Constantinople to Nisibis. Khosrow heard of this and equipped twelve thousand men under one of his commanders. Heraclius met them and defeated them, and killed nine thousand of them along with their leaders."

In some narrations: they tied their horses at al-Mada'in. I saw in some books that the cause of the Romans' victory over Persia was that Kisra sent to his commander Shahrayar, who was the one he had appointed to fight the Romans: "Kill your brother Farkhan for a statement he made, namely: 'I saw myself sitting on the throne of Kisra.'" But he did not kill him. So he (Kisra) sent to Persia: "I have dismissed Shahrayar and appointed his brother Farkhan." Farkhan became aware of the true situation, and returned the kingdom to his brother. Shahrayar wrote to Caesar, king of the Romans, and they cooperated against Kisra. The Romans defeated Persia, and the news came, and the Muslims rejoiced. That was among the clear and dazzling signs testifying to the truth of prophethood and that the Qur'an is from God, mighty and majestic, because it contains information about the unseen which none knows but God, the All-Knowing, the All-Aware. It is well established that many people embraced Islam at that time.

Ali, may God honor his face, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, al-Hasan, and Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah read ﴿Ghulibat al-Rum﴾ (the Romans have been overcome) in the active voice, and ﴿sa-yughlabun﴾ (they will be overcome) in the passive voice. The meaning, as it is said, is: the Romans prevailed over the outskirts of Syria, and the Muslims will overcome them. The Muslims attacked them in the ninth year after the revelation of the verse, and conquered some of their lands. The construction of ghalab (victory) with 'alayhi (over it) is an idafah of the verbal noun to the agent. The two readings were reconciled by saying that the verse was revealed twice: once in Makkah according to the reading of the majority, and once on the day of Badr, as al-Tirmidhi related and graded as good, from Abu Sa'id, according to this reading.

Some eminent scholars said: the correct view is that its revelation remains on its apparent sense, and by the Muslims' victory over them is meant what occurred at the Battle of Mu'tah, which took place in Jumada al-Ula in the eighth year. That is close to the date they mentioned for the first revelation of the verse, and there is no need for multiple revelations, since it is permissible for the meanings of the two readings to differ as long as they do not contradict each other, and for one group to be victorious and another defeated in two different times is not contradictory. So reflect. End of quotation.

It is not hidden from anyone who has examined the biographies (siyar) that this is hardly possible, because the Muslims did not defeat the Romans in that expedition. Rather, they withdrew from them after Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn Harithah, Abd Allah ibn Rawahah, Abbad ibn Qays, and others of the Companions, may God be pleased with them all, were struck, and they retreated as the vanquished do. Indeed, Ibn Hisham mentioned that when they [the army] reached Madinah, "the people began to throw dust on the army and say: 'O deserters! You fled in the way of God!' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'They are not deserters, but they are the returners, God willing.'"

It is related that "Umm Salamah said to the wife of Salamah ibn Hisham ibn al-As ibn al-Mughirah: 'What is the matter with me? I do not see Salamah attending the prayer with the Messenger of God ﷺ and with the Muslims?' She said: 'By God, he cannot go out. Whenever he goes out, the people shout at him: "O deserter! You fled in the way of God!" until he sat in his house and did not go out.'" She also mentioned verses of Qays al-Ya'muri in which he excuses what he did that day and what the people did. As it has been said, it contains a clarification that the people had retreated and hated death, and that Khalid ibn al-Walid withdrew with those who were with him. However, what has been mentioned is that it is the correct view upon further investigation. So perhaps the first explanation, in reconciling the two readings if this reading is authentic, is what was mentioned first. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 4 (part 2 of 2):

Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit): Our teacher, the master Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, used to relate from Abu al-Hakam ibn Barrajan that he had derived, from the Almighty's words ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ – to – ﴿for some years﴾, the conquest of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) by the Muslims, specifying its time and its day. At that time Bayt al-Maqdis was under Christian control. Ibn Barrajan died before the time he had specified for the conquest, and some time after his death the Muslims conquered it at the time Abu al-Hakam had specified. Abu Ja'far believed of this Abu al-Hakam that he would perceive some of the unseen matters, which he derived from the Book of God Most High. End of quotation. The deriving of unseen matters from the Glorious Qur'an by some of the gnostics (ʿarifun), such as Muhyi al-Din (may his secret be sanctified), al-Iraqi, and others, is a well-known matter. It is based on numerical calculations (qawaʿid hisabiyya) and letter-based procedures (aʿmal harfiyya), none of which has been reported from the earlier generations of the Community. Yet there is no restriction upon the bounty of God, Mighty and Majestic, and the Book of God Most High is beyond what occurs to human beings. ʿAli, may God honour his face, was asked: "Did the Messenger of God (ﷺ) confide to you anything that he concealed from others?" He said: "No, except that God gives a servant understanding of His Book."

This, and we ask God, glory be to Him, to enable us to understand the secrets of His Book, for the sake of the sanctity of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions.

﴿To God belongs the command, before and after﴾: that is, before this state and after it. This is the sum of what has been said, namely: before their being victorious, which is the time of their being defeated, and after their being defeated, which is the time of their being victorious. The fronting of the predicate (taqdim al-khabar) serves restriction (takhsis). The meaning is that each of their being defeated first and victorious last is only by the command of God Most High, His glorified decree, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿And these days We alternate among the people﴾ [Al ʿImran: 140].

Abu al-Simal and al-Jahdari, on the authority of al-Uqayli, read "min qablin wa min baʿdin" with a kasra and with tanwin (nunation, the "n" sound added to the end of a noun) on both. According to the well-known view, there is then no genitive noun (mudaf ilayh) implied at all. It is as if it were said: "To God belongs the command, before and after," meaning in an earlier time and in a later time. Some omitted the qualified noun. Al-Sakkaki mentioned that the genitive noun is also implied in such a case, and the tanwin is a substitute for it. Al-Farra' permitted the kasra without tanwin. Al-Zajjaj said that this is an error, because either the annexation (idafa) is not implied, in which case it takes tanwin, or it is implied, in which case it is indeclinable and built on a damma. As for implying its wording by analogy with the poet's words "between the two forelegs and the forehead of the lion," that is an analogy with a difference, since mention of the implied element there is remote, whereas our case is not like that. Al-Nahhas said to al-Farra' in his book: "There are many errors in what he says about the Qur'an. Among them is his claim that it is permissible to read 'min qabli wa min baʿdi' with kasra without tanwin. What is permissible is only 'min qablin wa min baʿdin', taking both as indefinite, that is, from something earlier and from something later." Ibn Hisham, in some of his books, followed the view of al-Farra'. And al-Kisa'i reported from some of the Banu Asad: "Li-llahi al-amru min qablin wa min baʿdu", with the first being genitive and tanwinned, and the second being damma-ended without tanwin.

﴿And on that day﴾, that is, on the day when the Romans defeat the Persians, ﴿the believers will rejoice﴾ ﴿in the victory of God﴾ and in His giving victory to those who have a Book over those who have no Book.

And the enemies who gloated over them among the disbelievers of Makkah will be enraged. That this is something to be taken as an omen (yutafaʾalu bihi), because the believers would prevail over the disbelievers, is also possible. It has been said: God Most High made the truthfulness of the believers manifest in what they told the polytheists about the Romans' defeating the Persians. It has also been said: the victory of God, Mighty and Majestic, is that He set some of the wrongdoers over others and caused division among their word until they contradicted one another and fought, and each of them weakened the strength of the other. It is reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that this coincided with the Battle of Badr, and in it there is, of the mighty victory of God Most High for the believers and their joy at it, what is not hidden. The first view is more fitting to His saying, Most High:

**﴿He grants victory to whomever He wills﴾**: that is, to whomever He wills among His servants to be granted victory over his enemy, and whom He causes to prevail over him. This is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that stands on its own) confirming the content of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs the command before and after﴾. The apparent reading is that (يَوْمَ, *yawma*, "on the day") is connected to يَفْرَحُ (*yafrahu*, "rejoice"), and likewise to نَصْرِ (*nasr*, "victory"). It has also been permitted to connect يَوْمَ to نَصْرِ, and likewise to connect بِنَصْرِ to الْمُؤْمِنِينَ (*al-mu'minin*, "the believers"). It has been said that يَوْمَئِذٍ (*yawma'idhin*, "on that day") is coordinated with قَبْلُ (*qablu*, "before") or بَعْدُ (*ba'du*, "after"), as if He had encompassed the three tenses, the past, the future and the present, and then began to report the rejoicing of the believers.

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾: the one who is intensely mighty and dominant, so that no one whom He wills to grant victory over another, whoever he may be, can frustrate Him. ﴿The Merciful﴾: the one who is intensely merciful, so He grants victory to whomever He wills, whichever group it may be. The mercy intended here is worldly mercy. As for the well-known reading, this is evident, because neither of the two groups deserves the mercy of the Hereafter. As for the last reading, it is because although the Muslims are deserving of it, what is intended here is their victory, which is one of the effects of worldly mercy. The mention of the attribute ﴿the Mighty﴾ first is because it comes first in consideration.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 6:

﴿Wa'da Allah﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing the content of the preceding sentence, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will be overcome﴾, and His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿The believers will rejoice﴾. It is also called the emphasizer of itself (al-mu'akkid li-nafsihi), because that (sentence) carries the sense of a promise. Its governing verb is obligatorily omitted, as if it were said: "Allah, Exalted is He, promised that a promise." ﴿Allah does not break His promise﴾, whatever promise it may be, whether it concerns this world or the Hereafter, because of the deficiency in His creation, which is impossible for Him, Mighty and Majestic is He. The placing of the noble Name in the position of the pronoun serves to indicate the judgment's causation (ta'lil hukmi) and to magnify it. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming the meaning of the verbal noun. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from it, in which case it would be like a described verbal noun, as if He, Glorified is He, were saying: "Allah, Exalted is He, promised a promise that will not be broken." ﴿But most of mankind do not know﴾ that He, Exalted is He, does not break His promise, due to their ignorance of His affairs, Mighty and Majestic is He, and their failure to reflect on what is necessary for Him, Majestic is He, and what is impossible for Him, Glorified is He. Or, they do not know what has preceded of His affairs, Majestic and Exalted is He. It has also been said: they know nothing, or they are not among the people of knowledge, so that they could know that.

﴿They know an outward appearance of the worldly life﴾: this is what they perceive of its adornments and pleasures, and of its other conditions that accord with their desires, suit their whims, and prompt them to immerse themselves in it and cling to it.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "They know its benefits and harms, when to plant and when to harvest, how to gather and how to build," meaning and the like, of things that will have no effect for them in the Hereafter. Something similar was narrated from Qatadah and Ikrimah.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan that he said concerning the verse: "So skilled is one of them in the affairs of his worldly life that he turns a dirham over on his fingernail and tells you its weight, yet he does not know how to pray properly." Al-Kirmani said: "Whatever is known by initial reflection (al-ruwiyyah, first thought) is the outward, and whatever is known by the proof of reason is the inward." It was also said that here it means enjoying its adornments and luxuriating in its pleasures, but this was objected to on the grounds that these two are not among the things they know of it, rather they are among the actions that follow from their knowledge. From Ibn Jubayr: the outward is what they know from the soothsayers, of what the devils steal by eavesdropping, but this is nothing, as is evident.

In any case, the apparent meaning is that "the outward" is the opposite of "the inward," and it serves to belittle and disparage. That is, they know an outward aspect that is base and contemptible. It was also said that it means "that which passes away and goes," as in the words of the Hudhali poet:

*The censorious ones reproached her, saying I love her, and that is a complaint whose shame has passed away from you.*

That is, they know a matter that is passing, having no permanence and no outcome, from the worldly life. ﴿And they, of the Hereafter﴾, which is the ultimate goal and the highest aim, ﴿they are heedless﴾, it never occurs to their minds, so how would they reflect upon it, or upon what leads to knowing it, from the world and its conditions? The sentence is conjoined to "they know" (يَعْلَمُونَ). Its being stated as a nominal sentence indicates the continuity and lasting of their heedlessness. The second "they" (هُمُ) is a repetition of the first and a verbal emphasis of it, to repel the notion of metaphor and of non-inclusiveness. The separation by the complement of the predicate, although contrary to the apparent usage, is made acceptable by the occurrence of the separation in pronunciation and by the emphasis on the Hereafter. Or "they" is the subject, and "heedless" (غافِلُونَ) is its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of the first "they." And the sentence "they know" etc. is a substitute (badal, apposition) for the sentence "they do not know," according to what the author of al-Kashshaf held. The one who does not know that Allah does not break His promise, or does not know His prior affairs, and does not reflect upon that, is the one whose vision is confined to the outward of the worldly life. What justifies the substitution is the unity of what both refer to, and the point that gives it preference is making their knowledge and their ignorance equal, in outward terms. The sentence ﴿and they, of the Hereafter﴾ etc. announces the firmness of their heedlessness of the Hereafter, which establishes what the preceding sentence requires, confirming their ignorance and likening them to beasts whose perception is restricted to the base outward aspects of the world, rather than its conditions which are the starting points of knowledge of the matters of the Hereafter.

Al-'Allamah al-Tibi chose that the sentence "they know" etc. is a resumptive sentence (isti'nafiyyah) explaining the cause of their ignorance: that Allah's promise is true, that to Allah belongs the command before and after, and that He, glorified is He, grants victory to the believers over the disbelievers. And perhaps this is the most evident.

[p. 22]

**Page 23 is not part of the commentary, so the translation begins with the text of the commentary.**

﴿Have they not reflected within themselves?﴾ This is a rebuke and a condemnation of their limiting their outlook to the outward life of this world that was mentioned, while being heedless of the Hereafter. The particle *wa* (and) is coordinating with an implied clause that the context requires. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿within themselves﴾, is an adverbial complement of "reflection." He mentioned it even though reflection occurs only within the self, in order to confirm the matter and to heighten the depiction of the state of those who reflect, as in your saying: "Believe it in your heart and see it with your eye." His, mighty and majestic is He, saying: ﴿God did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾ is connected either to the knowledge that reflection leads to and indicates, or to the statement that follows from it, as in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And they reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain"﴾ [Al-Imran: 191]. That is, either: "Know only the outward life of this world," or: "Restrict your outlook to that," and they did not produce reflection in their hearts, so that they would know that He, exalted is He, did not create the heavens, the earth, and what is between them of created beings, of which they themselves are part, except as entwined with truth in every matter. Or they would say this statement while acknowledging its content after having come to know it. By "truth" is meant that which is established and which deserves to be established necessarily, because it is founded upon profound wisdoms, among which is the witness that the responsible beings (*mukallafun*, those bound by religious obligation) bear, through its essence, its attributes, and its states, to the existence of its Maker, His oneness, His knowledge, His power, and His exclusive right to worship; and to the truth of His reports, among which is their being brought back to life after extinction in an everlasting life, and their being recompensed according to their deeds, by which the good-doer is distinguished from the evildoer, and the ranks of the individuals of each of the two groups are differentiated according to the differentiation of the levels of their knowledge and of their beliefs, which are determined by their examination of the signs, proofs, indications, and tokens placed in created things. This is as His saying, exalted is He, expresses: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [Al-Mulk: 2]. For deed is not restricted to the deeds of the limbs, and for this reason, upon him be prayers and peace, interpreted it by his saying: "Which of you is best in intellect, most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of God, Exalted, and swiftest in obedience to God, Mighty and Majestic."

His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿and for a specified term﴾ is coordinated with "truth." That is: and with a determined term that God, exalted is He, decreed for their continuance, which they must necessarily reach, and it is the time of the Hour's establishment, and the changing of the earth into another earth, and of the heavens. This is one view. It is also permitted that His, exalted is He, saying: "within themselves" be connected with "they reflect," and be an indirect object of purpose, in the sense: "Have they not reflected upon their own essences and selves, which are the nearest of created things to them, and they are more knowledgeable about their affairs and better informed about their states than about the states of anything else? Then they would contemplate what God, exalted is He, has deposited in them, outwardly and inwardly, of wondrous wisdoms indicating a providence that does not neglect, and that there must be an end for them at a time when the Wise One who arranged their affair will recompense the good with good and the evil with its like, so that at that time they would know that all other creatures likewise have their affair proceeding according to wisdom and providence, and that they must reach an end at that time." 

This has been objected to, on the ground that the affair of human return and recompense for what they did of evil and good is the matter intended in itself and the one that requires proof, so making it a means to proving the return of other things, while it is far from being a part of them, is an inversion of the matter. So consider this carefully. Abu Hayyan permitted that "what God created" and what follows be the object of "they reflect," with the negation suspending its action. You know that suspending the verb in such a construction is either impermissible or rare.

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And indeed, many of the people are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ is a concluding remark (*tadhyil*, an appended sentence that closes a passage with a general truth) that confirms what precedes it, by explaining that most of them do not stop at the heedlessness about the affairs of the Hereafter that was mentioned, nor at their turning away from reflecting on what would guide them to knowing it, namely the creation of the heavens and the earth and the created things between them. Rather, they are deniers and rejecters of the meeting with His reckoning and His recompense, mighty and majestic is He, through the resurrection. They are those who hold that this world is eternal, like the philosophers according to the well-known view.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 9:

﴿Have they not travelled through the earth?﴾ This is a rebuke for them for not taking warning from witnessing the conditions of those like them, which point to their outcome and their final end. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for rebuking denial, or for nullifying. Since it has entered upon a negation, and denying a negation is an affirmation, it has been said that it is for affirming the negated matter. The waw is for conjunction with an implied element required by the context, meaning: "Let them sit in their places, and have they not travelled through the earth?" His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and see﴾ is a conjunction with "travel," falling under its ruling. The meaning is that they have indeed travelled through the regions of the earth and witnessed ﴿how was the end of those before them﴾ from the destroyed nations, such as 'Ad and Thamud. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they were greater than them in strength﴾ and so on, is an explanation of the origin of their conditions and their outcome, meaning that they were more capable of enjoying the life of this world, since they were stronger than them. ﴿And they cultivated the earth﴾, i.e., they turned it over for tilling and farming, as al-Farra' said. It has been said: for extracting water, extracting minerals, and other things.

Abu Ja'far recited "wa-athāruū" (وآثارُوا) with a madd after the hamza. Ibn Mujahid said: "It is nothing." Abu al-Fath explained it as an elongation (ishba'), like the saying of the poet:

"And whoever blames the time for separation..."

and he mentioned that this is a necessity of poetry and does not occur in the Qur'an. Abu Haywa recited "wa-atharū" (وأثَرُوا) from al-atharah, which is exclusive control over a thing; and "ātharū al-arḍ" means they left traces in it. ﴿And they built it up﴾, i.e., those who were before them populated it with various kinds of construction, from farming, planting, building and others. It has been said: i.e., they dwelt in it. One says: "I populated the place of such-and-such," and "I populated it," meaning I dwelt in it. ﴿More than those had built it up﴾, i.e., a building more than the building of these people of it. The apparent meaning is that the greater quantity is considered relative to you. Some generalized it, saying: more in quantity, quality and duration. If "building" is taken in the sense of dwelling, the meaning is that they dwelt there for a longer duration than these people dwelt there. The use of the comparative form (af'al) carries a mocking of them, since there is no comparison between the unbelievers of Makkah and those destroyed nations. Those nations were known for their extreme strength and abundant construction, whereas the people of Makkah are weak, dependent on a valley without vegetation, fearing that people will snatch them away. Something similar is said when construction is taken as dwelling, for those peoples were famed for exceedingly long lifespans, while the lifespans of the people of Makkah are short, such that there is no notable comparison between them and the deeds of those destroyed.

﴿And their messengers came to them with the clear proofs﴾
Meaning: with the miracles, or the manifest signs. ﴿So Allah was not one to wrong them﴾, i.e., they denied them and so He destroyed them. So Allah, exalted is His glory, was not one to destroy them without a crime that calls for it on their part. Expressing this as "wronging" displays the perfection of His freedom from it. Otherwise, the People of the Sunnah have said that His destroying without a crime is not wronging at all, because He, mighty and majestic, is the Owner, and the Owner does with His possession as He wills. The dispute on this question is well known. ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾, in that they committed, by their own choice, sins which by the requirement of wisdom necessitated that. The placement of ﴿themselves﴾ before ﴿were wronging﴾ is for the sake of the verse-ending (fasila). It is also permissible that it is for restriction, relative to the messengers who called them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 10:

﴿Then the end of those who did evil [was the worst]﴾. That is, those who committed evil deeds (al-sayyi'at). He placed the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in the place of their pronoun in order to brand them with evil and to indicate the reason for the ruling. ("Then," thumma) is for real temporal sequence (li-l-tarakhi al-haqiqi), or for remoteness and difference in rank (li-l-istib'ad wa-l-tafawut fi al-rutba). ﴿al-su'a﴾, that is, the worst punishment (al-'uqubah al-su'a), which is punishment by the Fire. It is the feminine of al-asw'a (the worst), just as al-husna is the feminine of al-ahsan (the best). Or it is a verbal noun (masdar), like al-bushra, and the punishment is described by it as an intensification, as if it were the very essence of evil. It is in the nominative because it is the subject of kana (the verb "was"), and its predicate is ("end," 'aqibah). Ibn Kathir's companions... [note: this is not in source; omit]

Ibn Kathir... (omitted)

Al-Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Abu 'Amr read ("end") in the nominative (raf'), as the subject of kana, and ("the worst") in the accusative (nasb), as the predicate. Al-A'mash and al-Hasan read ("al-su-ya") by replacing the hamza with a waw and assimilating the waw into it. Ibn Mas'ud read ("al-su'a") with masculine gender.

﴿because they denied the signs of Allah﴾: this is the cause of the stated ruling, meaning "because" (li-anna) or "because that" (bi-anna) they denied. In reality it clarifies what the placing of the relative pronoun in the place of the pronoun implied, since that is general (mujmal).

Allah's words, ﴿and they used to ridicule them﴾, are a conjunction (ataf) upon ("they denied"), included with it in the same causal ruling. The use of ridicule (al-istihza') in the present tense indicates its continuity and renewal. It is also permitted that ("the worst") be an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of ("they did evil") without its own root, or an object of cause (maf'ul bihi lahu), because ("they did evil") means "they committed and acquired," and ("the worst") means "the sin," since it is a description, or its verbal noun is interpreted as such. That it is an attribute of the verbal noun of ("they did evil") from its own root, meaning "the worst evil," is far-fetched in wording and unnecessary in meaning. ("That they denied") is the subject of kana. That denial is their end, although they were never free of it, is explained either by considering its continuity, or by considering it as an expression for the seal (al-tab') upon the heart.

It is also permitted that ("that they denied") be a substitute (badal) for ("the worst") which functions as the subject of kana, or an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to it, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is that they denied." Also permitted is that ("that") be explanatory (tafsiriyya), meaning ("that," ay), and the thing explained is either ("they did evil") or ("the worst"). Evil may be verbal as well as practical, so before it there is an implied meaning of speech without its letters, and this implication becomes clear through the explanation. If Allah's words ﴿And the chiefs among them went forth, saying: "Walk on"﴾ (Sad 38:6) are permitted, then this is even more permissible. So this interpretation is not forced, contrary to Abu Hayyan.

It is also permitted, in the reading of the two Haramayn and Abu 'Amr, that ("the worst") be the relative clause of the verb, with ("that they denied") following it, or the predicate of an omitted subject, or on the assumption of the causal particle and an omitted predicate of kana, whose estimate is ("ruinous") or the like. Al-Bahr criticized this, saying: "It is a non-Arab understanding, because the sentence is complete and extremely beautiful without any deletion, and an omitted element with no indication has been imposed on it." Our companions do not permit the omission of the predicate of kana.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 11:

﴿Allah originates creation﴾, i.e., brings it into being.

ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) and Talhah read «yubdi'u» with a dammah on the yaʾ and a kasrah on the dal. The discussion of this has already been given earlier, so recall it, for "there is no lapse of time since the covenant" (i.e., it is not far in the past, so remember it).

﴿Then He will bring it back﴾ by resurrection, ﴿then to Him you will be returned﴾ for recompense. The fronting of the object (ilayhi, "to Him") before the verb is for restriction (al-takhsis). The apparent form would have been "yarji'una" with the third-person yaʾ, but it departs from this to the address to the polytheists (al-mushrikin), in order to confront them with the threat, face them with the warning, and give the impression that this applies specifically to them. This is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person) for the sake of emphasis in warning and frightening. Abu ʿAmr and Rawh read «yarji'una» with the third-person yaʾ, as is the apparent form.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 12:

Page 25
﴿And on the Day the Hour is established﴾, which is the time of the re-creation of creation and their return to Him, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿the criminals will be struck dumb (yublisu al-mujrimun)﴾, meaning they will fall silent and their argument will be cut off. Al-Raghib said: al-iblas (dejection) is a sorrow that befalls a person from intense despair, and from it, it is said, Iblis (Satan) was derived. Since the one struck with iblas often has to remain silent and forgets what concerns him, it is said: "Fulan ablasa" when he fell silent and his argument was cut off. And "ablasati al-naqatu" (the she-camel was struck dumb) means she is mibla., when she does not make a sound out of intense ill-temper. Ibn Thabit said: "Ablasa al-rajulu" is said when a man despairs of every good. And in the hadith: "I am their bringer of good news when they despair (ablasu)."

By "the criminals," according to what al-Tibi stated, is meant those who committed evil deeds (al-su'a), but he placed the apparent noun in the position of their pronoun in order to brand them with this abominable description and to indicate the reason for the ruling.

Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and al-Sulami read "yablasu" with a fathah on the lam. It was interpreted as the verb from ablasahu, meaning "he silenced him," and its apparent meaning is that it is transitive. Abu al-Baqa, al-Samin, and others denied this, to the point that they strained themselves and said: its original form is "yublisu iblasa al-mujrimin," with the verbal noun placed in the position of the subject, then they deleted it and put the genitive noun in its place. al-Khafaji, may Allah have mercy on him, criticized this, saying: It is not hidden that this is not correct, because "iblasa al-mujrimin" is a verbal noun annexed to its agent, and its agent is the very subject of the verb, so how can it be the deputy subject? So reflect.

You know that whenever the reading is sound, the claim that the usage of ablasa as transitive is not heard cannot be accepted.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 13:

﴿And there will not be for them, of their associates,﴾ those who were associated by them with Allah, glorified is He, in worship; and for this reason they were attributed to them (lit. "were added to them"). It has also been said: the attribution is due to their associating them with Allah, exalted is He, in their wealth. What is meant by them is the idols. Muqatil said: the angels, peace be upon them. It has been said: the devils. It has been said: their chiefs. ﴿intercessors﴾ who would protect them from the punishment of Allah, exalted is He, as they used to claim. The imperfect is used in negation with lam, which turns it into the past tense, to affirm its certainty. The plural form is used because it occurs in opposition to a plural; that is, there was not for any one of them any intercessor at all.

Kharijah on Nafi', Ibn Sinan on Abu Ja'far, and al-Antaki on Shaybah read "wa-lam takun" with the feminine ta' (التاء الفوقية).

﴿And they will be, in their associates,﴾ that is, in their divinity and their partnership, as the shift from "and they will be in them" indicates, ﴿disbelievers﴾, since they despaired of them and recognised the reality of their situation. ("And they were") is used to indicate continuity, not for the sake of preserving the ends of verses (ru'us al-fawasil), as it has been wrongly imagined.

It has been said: it is in the past tense, as is apparent, and the ba' in ("in their associates") is causal; that is, they were disbelievers in Allah, exalted is He, in the world because of them. Some of the eminent scholars did not accept this, since there is no worthwhile benefit in reporting it, and because what is evident is that ("on the day the Hour is established") is an adverbial complement of "they will be dumbfounded" and what is conjoined to it. For this reason it has been said that the appropriate reading of the waw is as a circumstantial (ha'liyyah), so that the meaning is that they did not intercede for them although they were the cause of their disbelief in the world. This is better than taking it as conjoined to the whole sentence together with the adverbial complement; and, moreover, on that reading it would be appropriate to make a full stop for caution. Yet it may be said that it was left out, relying on the rational indication, though this is contrary to the apparent sense.

"Shufa'wa'" is written in the Mushaf with a waw followed by an alif, which is contrary to analogy. The analogy would be to omit the waw or to place it after the alif, but the first is better, as has been mentioned in the discussion of the orthography (al-rasm). Likewise, analogy was departed from in writing "al-su'a" (السوأى), where it is written with an alif before the ya', whereas the analogy, as in al-Kashf, is deletion, because the hamza is written according to the form in which it is softened.

[Page 26]

"And on the Day the Hour arises" is repeated to magnify it and to emphasise the awfulness of what occurs in it. It is an adverbial of time (*zarf*) governing the verb after it. The phrase "that Day" (﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾), according to what al-Tabarsi mentioned, is a substitute (*badal*) for it.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan), the nunation (*tanwin*) in «يَوْمَئِذٍ» is the nunation of compensation (*tanwin 'iwad*) for an omitted clause. That is, the meaning is: "And on the Day the Hour arises, on that Day the criminals will be struck dumb, [and] they will separate (﴿يَتَفَرَّقُونَ﴾)." Its apparent sense is that «يَوْمَئِذٍ» is an adverbial of time governing (*li-taqumu*, "arises"). The objection to making the clause that the nunation compensates for be this is evident, as is the consideration he raised.

In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim (by Abu al-Su'ud), the statement of God Most High, ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ يَتَفَرَّقُونَ﴾ ("On that Day they will separate"), is a further magnification of the Day of the Establishment of the Hour, following another magnification. In it there is an allusion (*ramz*) to the fact that the separation occurs in part of that Day. The manner of the allusion through what has been mentioned is obscure. The pronoun in ﴿يَتَفَرَّقُونَ﴾ refers to the believers and the disbelievers, indicated by what precedes concerning the generality of creation and what follows concerning the detail. This view was taken by al-Zamakhshari and a group of others.

Abu al-Su'ud said: it refers to all of creation, indicated by what has preceded concerning their origin, their return, and their resurrection, not to the criminals alone. Abu Hayyan said: it appears that it refers to the creation mentioned before it, which is the subject of God Most High's statement, ﴿اللَّهُ يَبْدَأُ الخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ﴾ ("God originates the creation, then repeats it"). The intended meaning of their separation is their differing in places and states, as the detail indicates. This is not by consideration of each individual but by consideration of each group. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan that he said concerning this: "These are in 'Illiyyin, and these are in the lowest of the low" (*asfal safilin*). The detail also indicates this. This separation is after the completion of the reckoning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 15:

﴿فَأمّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ فَهم في رَوْضَةٍ يُحْبَرُونَ﴾ ﴿Then as for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a garden, delighted.﴾ *al-rawda* is land with plants and water. In the proverb "better than an egg in a meadow" (أحْسَنُ مِن بَيْضَةٍ في رَوْضَةٍ), they mean the egg of an ostrich. With regard to the water, it is said: "the land of the valley" (أرْضُ الوادِي). *Istarada* means its water became abundant. *Aradahum* means he gave them some irrigation (*ri*), from *arada al-hawd*, when he poured into the basin water that covers its floor. It is also said: "They drank until they were satisfied" (شَرِبُوا حَتّى أراضُوا), meaning they drank in small sips after heavy drinking. It is also said that the meaning of *aradu* is that they poured milk upon milk. The apparent view of the extensive commentary regarding *rawda* is that both plants and water are considered in it. I think Ibn Qutayba explicitly stated that land with plants but without water is not called *rawda*.

It is also said that it is a fine garden (بُسْتان), and it is said that it is a place of greenery. Al-Khafaji said: *al-rawda* is a garden, and its restriction to what has rivers is based on common usage. In any case, the tanwin on it here is for magnification, and what is meant by it is Paradise. *Al-habar* is joy. It is said: *habarahu yahburuhu* (with a *damma*), *habaran*, *habaratan*, and *hubuwran*, when he delighted him with a joy by which his face brightened and its effect appeared on it. In the proverb: "Their houses were filled with joy, so they are waiting for the consequence" (امْتَلَأتْ بُيُوتُهم حَبَرَةٌ فَهم يَنْتَظِرُونَ العِبْرَةَ). Al-Kisai related: *habartuhu* means I honored him and gave him comfort. It is also said: *al-habara* is every fine blessing, and *al-tahbir* is beautification. It is said: "So-and-so has good *habar* and *sabar*" (فُلانٌ حَسَنُ الحَبَرِ والسَّبَرِ), with a *fatha* on the *ba'*, when he is handsome and of good appearance.

The opinions differed regarding its interpretation here. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak, that both said: *yuhbarun* means *yukramun* (they will be honored).

A group related from Mujahid: *(yuhbarun)* means *yunaʿʿamun* (they will be given comfort and luxury). Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash said: they will be crowned upon their heads.

Ibn Kaysan said: they will be adorned with jewelry. Al-Awza'i, Waki', and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir said: they will listen to songs.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd related from the last-mentioned (Yahya ibn Abi Kathir) that he said: "It was said: O Messenger of God, what is *al-habar*? So the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, said: 'Pleasure and listening.'"

Some have mentioned that the apparent meaning is *yusarrun* (they will be made happy), and did not mention what they will be made happy with, to indicate the abundance of joys. What came in the report is by way of restricting to a part. Perhaps the questioner loved listening, so the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, mentioned it to him for that reason. The use of the present tense (*yuhbarun*) indicates the renewal of joy for them: every hour there comes to them what makes them happy, from renewed delights and their various kinds.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 30, verse 16:

﴿As for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs﴾, which include the clear verses concerning what has been detailed, ﴿and the meeting of the Hereafter﴾, meaning they denied the resurrection (al-ba'th). He mentioned this explicitly, although it is already included in the denial of the signs, because of the importance given to it. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then those﴾

is a demonstrative referring to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in view of its being described by what is in the scope of the relative clause (al-silah) of disbelief and denial of His signs, and of the meeting of the Hereafter. The effect of the difference between the state of the two groups, the believers who do righteous deeds and the disbelievers who deny the signs, and what each has of reward and punishment: He, glory be to Him, guided to what saves from the second and leads to the first. The first is placed before the second because *takhliyah* (clearing away, negation) precedes *tahliyah* (adornment), although the first is also what is addressed first to those who disbelieved, mentioned before, without any interval. The *fa'* (فَ) is for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes. The apparent sense of their speech is that *Subhan* (سُبْحانَ) here is in the accusative by a deleted imperative verb, as if it were said: "When you know that, or when the state of the two groups and their outcome has become sound and clear, then glorify God, *subhan Allah* etc.," that is, declare Him far above, with the glorification befitting Him, Mighty and Majestic, at these times. In *al-Kashf* (the commentary of al-Taybi) it says: "There is a difficulty here, because *subhana Allah* always keeps one fixed form, which an imperative verb does not govern, since it is *inshā'* (performative speech) of another kind. Likewise, it is for the *inshā'* of His glorification at these times, fleeing from the harm of His punishment and seeking His abundant reward. In the margins of Shaykh Zadah it is stated that an imperative, or indeed an *inshā'i* sentence in general, cannot validly be conditioned by a condition, because *inshā'* is bringing the meaning into existence through an utterance that accompanies it, and if it could be conditioned it would follow that it is delayed from the time of utterance, which is impermissible. What is conditioned is only the report about the *inshā'* of wishing, hoping, praising, blaming, questioning and the like. So when you say, "If I do such-and-such, may God forgive you," or "how excellent what you did," the meaning is: "You have done what makes you deserve that God forgive you, or that you be praised because of it." Except that the *inshā'* sentence is put in its place for emphasis, to indicate deservingness. This is perhaps more evident than what is in *al-Kashf*. Indeed, what it claimed does not appear, namely that the condition and the answer are spoken by the servants.

The speech of some of them seems to imply that the statement is by an implied "say," where he said: "as if it were said: when the outcome of the obedient and the disobedient has become sound and clear, then say, 'We glorify, *subhan Allah* etc.,'" and the meaning is "so glorify Him with glorification at these times." What is in this is not hidden. It is as if I see you preventing that *Subhan* must always be one form, the one mentioned first, since it is permissible for the imperative verb to govern it when the context requires it and the speech indicates it. But it seems you lean toward regarding the sentence as declarative in wording but *inshā'i* in meaning, meaning a command, to match the sentence *lahu al-hamd* (لَهُ الحَمْدُ). For although it is declarative, the report of the establishment of praise for Him and its being obligatory upon the discerning among the people of the heavens and the earth, as its following the mention of promise and threat indicates, and its branching from it with *fa'* in the sense of a command to it, is in the most emphatic manner, as some eminent scholars have stated. So it is as if it were said: "So glorify God as is befitting for Him in these times, and praise Him."

The apparent speech of most scholars is that the sentence *lahu al-hamd* etc. is conjoined to the preceding sentence, and that *ashiyyan* (عَشِيًّا) is conjoined to *hina tumsun* (حِينَ تُمْسُونَ). Indeed, they stated this explicitly. According to what was mentioned, the sentence *lahu al-hamd* is then an interjection between the conjoined element and what it is conjoined to, and the verse in this case resembles the verse of ablution, according to the view of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah). In *al-Kashshaf*, *ashiyyan* is connected to God's saying *hina tumsun*.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 18:

The statement of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And to Him belongs praise﴾ and so on, is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) between them, and its meaning is that it is incumbent upon all the discerning ones (al-mumayyizin) among the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth to praise Him.

Perhaps those who do not permit this make the prepositional phrase attached to the sense of stability (al-thubut) that the predication requires. By "glorification" (al-tasbih) and "praise" (al-hamd) is meant their apparent sense, according to what a group of the eminent scholars held. It was also said that by "glorification" is meant the prayer (al-salah). 

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from Abu Razin, who said: Nafi' ibn al-Azraq came to Ibn Abbas and said: "Do you find the five prayers in the Qur'an?" Then he recited: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening﴾ is the Maghrib prayer, ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾ is the Subh prayer, ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾ is the 'Asr prayer, ﴿and when you enter the noon﴾ is the Zuhr prayer; and he recited: ﴿And after the prayer of 'isha'.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him that he said: This verse gathered the times of the prayer: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening﴾ is Maghrib and 'Isha', ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾ is Fajr, ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾ is 'Asr, ﴿and when you enter the noon﴾ is Zuhr. Al-Hasan also held this, to the extent that he held that the verse is Medinan, because he holds that the obligation of the five prayers was in Medina, and that what was obligatory in Mecca was two rak'ahs at whatever time the prayer occurred. Imam al-Razi chose to take the glorification as purification (tanzih), saying: "It is stronger, and turning to it is preferable, because it includes the prayer. That is because the purification commanded encompasses purification by the heart, which is firm belief; and by the tongue together with that, which is good remembrance; and by the limbs together with both of them, which is righteous action. The first is the root, the second is the fruit of the first, and the third is the fruit of the second. That is because when a person believes something, it appears from his heart upon his tongue, and when he speaks, the truthfulness of his speech appears in the states of his actions. The tongue is the interpreter of the heart, and the limbs are the proof of the tongue. But the prayer is the best of the actions of the limbs, and it includes remembrance by the tongue and intention by the heart; so it is purification in reality. When He, glorified be He, says 'Purify Me,' this is a kind of purification, and the absolute command is not restricted to one kind over another, so it must be taken to cover everything that is purification, and this becomes a command to prayer. Then, our statement is suitable to what came before it, because when Allah the Exalted made clear that the highest station and the complete reward are for those who believed and did righteous deeds, saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a garden, delighted﴾, He, glorified be He, said: when you know that this station is for those who believed and did righteous deeds, and belief is purification by the heart and monotheism by the tongue, and righteous action is the employment of the limbs, then all of them are purifications and praises. So ﴿Glorify Allah﴾, that is, bring that which is the means of arriving at delight in the gardens and presence at the Pool." End of quotation.

I, for my part, follow the Imam in the claim that the apparent sense is the preferable one, and I also choose that the statement of Allah the Exalted, ﴿To Him belongs praise﴾, is an emphatic parenthesis between the conjoined and the conjoined-to in every case. Its meaning, as you have heard from al-Kashshaf, is that it is incumbent upon all the discerning ones to praise Him. If the glorification is taken as prayer, then this is a statement emphasizing the obligation, because praise is used figuratively for prayer just as glorification is. The point of the emphasis is its indication that this is a command encompassing all the accountable beings among the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. If it is taken in its apparent sense, then its manner is that this operates as a supplement (istidrak) to the command to glorify; and since both belong to one category, each of them emphasizes the other, and so it indicates the continuing obligation of praise at all times and the obligation of glorification upon the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. As for the indication of obligation, it comes from the following of "Glorify Allah" and so on; the promise and the threat are mentioned with the particle fa', for it conveys that this is determined as the path to deliverance from the lower ranks and to attaining the higher ranks, and whatever is determined as the path to something is obligatory; so stated in al-Kashf.

The Imam mentioned that in this parenthesis there is a subtle point: when Allah the Exalted commanded the servants to glorify Him, it is as if He had said, Glorified be He: Make clear to them that their glorifying Allah the Exalted is for their own benefit, not for a benefit that returns to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. So it is incumbent upon them to praise Allah the Exalted when they glorify Him, Glorified is His affair. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They think they have done you a favor by accepting Islam. Say: Do not consider your Islam a favor to me. Rather, Allah has done you a favor by guiding you to faith﴾ [al-Hujurat: 17].

Some have permitted that "'ashiyyan" (in the evening) be conjoined to His saying, "in the heavens" (fi al-samawat), but this was rejected on the ground that a temporal adverb is not conjoined to a spatial one, nor the reverse. It was said that it may be conjoined to an implied element, that is: "And to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth, always and in the evening," so that it is a specification after a generalization, and the sentence is parenthetical or circumstantial; but this, as you see, is weak. The mention of the specified times is for the manifestation in them of the traces of power, majesty, and mercy. He placed the evening (imsa') before the morning (isbah) because of the precedence of night and darkness, and He placed the late afternoon ('ashiyy) before the time of manifestation (ithar) because it relates to the time of manifestation as the evening relates to the morning. In al-Bahr: the evening is paired with the imsa', and the manifestation with the isbah, because each of them is followed by its counterpart: the 'ashiyy is followed by the imsa', and the isbah is followed by the ithar. Abu al-Su'ud said: the placing of 'ashiyyan before "when you enter the noon" is for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil), but this is not so. The Imam mentioned that the imsa' is placed before the isbah here, and is placed after it in His saying, ﴿And glorify Him morning and evening﴾ [al-Ahzab: 42], because the beginning of the discourse here is the mention of the gathering and the resurrection, and so is its end, and the evening is the last, so the last is mentioned first in order to recall the Hereafter. The change of wording in "'ashiyyan" is because it does not come from it a verb meaning entering into the evening, as with masa' (evening), sabah (morning), and zahirah (noon). Perhaps the secret in this, as it is said, is that it is not one of the times in which the states of people differ and change in a manifest way, justifying describing them as leaving what precedes it and entering what follows, as with the mentioned times, for each of these is a time in which states change manifestly. As for the evening and morning, this is evident. As for noon, it is a time in which one returns to removing outer garments for the midday rest, as was alluded to in Surat al-Nur. 

This is the case, and the excellence of glorification and praise is too evident to need proof, but the scholars have mentioned a number of reports concerning the merit of what the verse contains.
