﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who hear﴾ — that is, their condition is that they hear speech with the hearing of understanding and insight. In this there is an indication that the matter is so manifest that mere hearing suffices in it for one who has understanding and insight, and does not need observation, even though it is observed.

Al-Tibi said: "It was phrased this way because most people are sprawled out at night like the dead and wander about by day like beasts, not knowing for what purpose they are or why this is. But whoever gives ear while he is present (shahid) is alerted to the admonition of God, the Exalted, and listens to it, for the passing of nights and the recurrence of days call out in the tongue of state: 'Depart, depart, from the house of delusion to the house of abiding.' As God the Exalted said: ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day successive for whoever wishes to remember or wishes gratitude﴾ [al-Furqan: 62]." Al-Imam mentioned that among things, some require for their knowledge a standpoint on which one stands and a guide who directs to it, so that one understands when hearing from that guide. And since sleep and seeking may occur to many, and it may be thought that they are acts of servants, knowing that they are among His signs requires a guide who aids thought. It was said: ﴿for a people who hear﴾, as if it were said: "for a people who hear and direct their attention to the speech of the guide," end of quote. Perhaps the need for a guide who aids thought, regarding the fact that night and day are among the signs, based on what you have heard in explaining the reason for the middle placement, is more evident, so consider this carefully.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 24:

﴿And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning﴾. Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) held that it is construed with an implied *an* (the verbal *an*, *an al-maṣdariyya*), the original being *an yurikum*. The *an* was deleted and the verb was put in the nominative (*raf'*), which is the common usage after such deletion in cases like this. Its retention in the accusative after the deletion is rare (*shadhdh*), and both readings have been transmitted for the verse of Tarafa:

*Ala ayyuhadha al-zājiri uḥḍura al-waghā*
*wa-an ashhada al-ladhdhāti hal anta mukhlidi*

Page 33

"Ah, you who admonish me to attend the battle and to witness pleasures, will you grant me immortality?"

It is also permitted that the verb here is one that has been given the status of a verbal noun, so *an* is not implied. Rather, the verb is used for part of its meaning, namely the event, with regard to which time is disregarded, so it is a noun in the form of a verb. (*Fa-yurikum*) then means "seeing." On this basis the well-known saying is interpreted:

*Tasma' bi-l-Mu'aydiyyi khayrun min an tarāhu*

"Hearing of al-Mu'aydi is better than seeing him."

It is also permitted that *an* is deleted here, and this is supported by the transmission of *tasma'a* in the accusative. Some eminent scholars did not accept this, because the meaning is not about the future. As for *an tarāhu*, the futurity in it is relative to the hearing, so it does not contradict it. Similar to this is his saying:

*Fa-qālū mā tashā'u fa-qultu alhū*
*ilā al-iṣbāḥi āthira dhī athīr*

"They said, 'What do you wish?' I said, 'Let me amuse myself until morning, [with] the wine of the one who has been chosen [with] a vessel.'"

The construction of the verb as a verbal noun, indicating that it is like a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), is preferred, because of the concern for the intended meaning, as in his saying *āthira dhī athīr*. The justification that *mā tashā'u* is a question about what they wish at the present moment, while *an* denotes the future, is not valid, because the wish always relates to the future.

Al-Jami' al-Isfahani said: the estimated sense of the verse is: "And among His signs is a sign: He shows you the lightning," with *yurikum* being a qualifier (*ṣifa*), the qualified noun (*mawṣūf*) being deleted and the qualifier placed in its position, as in his saying:

*Wa-mā al-dahru illā tārataān fa-minhumā*
*amūtu wa-ukhrā abtaghī al-ʿayysha akdaḥu*

"Time is only two turns: in one of them I die, and in the other I seek life, toiling." That is, "one of them is a turn in which I die." It was said: then a returning pronoun (*rāji'*) is necessary, so it is estimated as *fīhā* or *bihā*. Al-Rummani specified the second, as in *al-Bahr*. Both, as in *al-Kashf*, fail to give the meaning.

It was said: the estimate is: "And among His signs is the lightning," then *yurikum al-barqa* is resumed as a new statement. It was also said: *min āyātihi* is a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the lightning, meaning: "He shows you the lightning while it is among His signs." Abu Hayyan permitted that it is connected to *yurikum*, with *min* denoting the starting point (*ibtida' al-ghāya*), but this contradicts its counterparts.

In *al-Kashf*: It seems most likely that *min āyātihi* is the predicate (*khabar*) of an deleted subject (*mubtada'*), meaning: "Among His signs is what is mentioned, or what is recited to you." Then it was said: *yurikum al-barqa* is an explanation of that. Then he said: this is the least forced of all of them. You know that the most likely reading is the one with which the verse agrees with its counterparts.

﴿Khawfan﴾, that is, from the thunderbolts, ﴿and ṭam'an﴾, in the rain. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥak. Qatada said: *khawfan* is for the traveller, because it is a sign of rain, which harms him because he has nothing to shelter him, and it gives him no benefit. *Ṭam'an* is for the resident. It was said: *khawfan* that it may be dry (*khalaban*, without rain), and *ṭam'an* that it may be rain-bearing. Ibn Sallam said: *khawfan* of the hail that destroys the crops, and *ṭam'an* in the rain.

Their accusative (*naṣb*) is as an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*, the reason or cause) according to al-Zajjaj. This is according to the view of those who do not require that the verbal noun of the object of purpose be the same as the verb it explains in terms of the agent, which is evident. As for the view of most scholars who require this, it has been said in its justification that this is by estimating a noun in the genitive (*muḍāf*), meaning "the will of fear and hope," or by interpreting fear and hope as causing fear and causing hope, either by taking their root meaning as such with the augments deleted, or by making them metaphors for their causes.

It was said: this is because their being shown entails their seeing, so the objects are in meaning the subjects, and it is as if it were said: "He made you seeing, in fear and in hope."

It was objected that fear and hope are neither the aim of seeing nor its motives. Rather they follow it. How then can they be a cause, on the assumption of sufficiency with the like of this according to those who require the condition? It was answered that by seeing is not meant merely the occurrence of sight, but intentional seeing with attention and noticing. It is like: "I sat out of the battle through cowardice." Abu Hayyan did not accept this either. Then he said: if it were said, according to the view of those who require the condition, that the estimate is "He shows you the lightning, so you see it in fear and in hope," with the operative deleted because it is indicated, it would be a valid construction.

It was said: perhaps the more evident view is that their accusative is as an object of purpose for the showing, because of the concurrence and the unity of the agent, since God Most High is the creator of fear and hope. As for the meaning of the grammarians' statement that the object of purpose must be the act of the agent, that it is necessary that it be characterized by it, as with *ikrām* in your saying "I came to you out of honour for you," if this is granted, then there is no obstacle to the accusative by analogy in the concurrence and unity mentioned.

It was objected that the meaning being as mentioned is not in doubt, and it has been mentioned by the author of *al-Intiṣāf* and others, since the linguistic agent is not the real agent. So hesitation about it, and the claim that there is no obstacle to the accusative by analogy, has no basis. I myself incline to not requiring unity of the agent, because of the frequency of the accusative with non-unity, as the investigation and reference to the commentary on *al-Kafiya* by al-Radi bears witness. Interpretation in the face of such frequency has no justification. It is also permitted that the accusative here is as an absolute object (*maṣdar*), meaning "you fear a fear, and you hope a hope," with the clause being a circumstantial state. Better than this is that they are accusative as circumstantial states, meaning "fearing and hoping."

﴿And He sends down water from the sky﴾. Several readers read it with the lighter pronunciation (*takhfīf*, *yunazzilu*). ﴿So He gives life thereby﴾, that is, by means of the water, ﴿to the earth﴾, by His bringing forth vegetation through it, ﴿after its death﴾, its dryness. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who use reason﴾, who employ their minds in deducing its causes and how it comes into being, so that the perfection of the power of the Maker, may His majesty be exalted, and the perfection of His wisdom, may He be glorified, become manifest to them.

Al-Tibi said: since what has been mentioned is an illustration of the reviving of people and the bringing forth of the dead, and since illustration serves to bring near what is imagined to what is rationally understood, and to present what is imagined in the form of what is established, it is fitting that the concluding phrase be *li-qawmin ya'qilūn* (for a people who reason).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 25:

﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command﴾, that is, by His saying, the Exalted: "Stand," or by His will, Mighty and Majestic is He. The expression of it as "command" serves to indicate the perfection of power and independence from principles and causes. The intended meaning of their standing is not their creation, because He has already explained that state by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, nor is it their standing without a visible supporter, as has been said. For that is among the completions of their creation, even though it is not explicitly stated, relying upon what was mentioned in another place in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He created the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾ [Luqman: 10], and so on. Rather, their standing and their remaining in the state they are in until their term, which was alluded to by His saying, the Exalted, before this: ﴿Allah did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth and for a specified term﴾ [al-Rum: 8].

And since the remaining is future with regard to its latter part and what follows the revelation of this verse, the word "an" (that), which is a marker of the future, has been made apparent here. The Imam (al-Razi) held that al-qiyam (standing) means standing still and not descending. Then he said, as one of them summarized it: "An" has been mentioned here and not in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And among His signs He shows you the lightning﴾, because standing, since it does not change, has the verb, with "bi-anna" (that), removed in the future, and has been made a verbal noun to indicate permanence, while the showing of lightning, since it is among the renewed matters, has been introduced with the future form and nothing has been mentioned with it that indicates the verbal noun. End of quote. ﴿Then when He calls you with one call from the earth, behold, you come out﴾: "Idha" (when) the first is conditional, and the second is sudden (fuja'iyyah), taking the place of the "fa" (then) of the response, because both share the sense of immediate sequence. It has been said that the conditional clause is coordinated with "an taqum" (that it stands) according to the interpretation of a singular noun, as if it were said: "And among His signs is the standing of the heaven and the earth by His command, then your coming out from your graves swiftly when He calls you." The author of al-Kashshaf says: it has been placed in the position of a singular in meaning, but as far as its form is concerned, it is a clause coordinated upon His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And among His signs that﴾, and this is in the style of ﴿the station of Abraham, and whoever enters it is safe﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], and its benefit is what you heard shortly before. The apparent statement of some of the eminent scholars is that the coordination upon it is apparent in not intending to count what was mentioned as a sign. Abu al-Su'ud, may Allah have mercy upon him, chose that the coordination is coordination of sentences, and that what is mentioned is not among the signs. He said: since the sign of the standing of the heaven and the earth by the command of Allah, the Exalted, is later than the rest of the enumerated signs, being connected to the resurrection in existence, it was delayed after them and was made connected to it in mention as well, so it was said: ﴿Then when He calls you﴾, etc. The speech is directed to inform of the occurrence of the resurrection, and its existence after the expiry of the term of their standing is consequent upon the multiplicity of His signs, the Exalted, that indicate it, not being included in their thread, as has been said. As if it were said: "And among His signs is the standing of the heaven and the earth in their state by the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, until a specified term which Allah, the Exalted, has determined for their standing. Then when He calls you," that is, after the expiry of the term, "from the earth, and you are in your graves, with one call," by His saying, Glorified is He: "O dead, come out!", "you suddenly come out from them." Perhaps what Sahib al-Kashf pointed to is more subtle and more far-reaching in meaning, so reflect. ("Min al-ard" [from the earth]) is connected to "da'a" (called), and ("min") is for the beginning of the limit. It suffices in that, if the caller is Allah, the Exalted, Himself, and not an angel by His command, Glorified is He, that the one called is in it. It is said: "I called him from the bottom of the valley, and he came up to me," not by a call. For when the River of Allah, Mighty and Exalted, comes, the River of Ma'qil is nullified. Yes, it has been permitted that this be an attribute of it (the call), and that it be a circumstantial clause from the object pronoun, and that "they do not come out" is not... because what follows "idha" does not act upon what precedes it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "min" in my opinion is for the end of the limit, and Sibawayh affirmed this. Abu Hayyan said: this is a rejected view according to our companions. The apparent meaning of the reports is that the dead are literally called to come out of the graves. It has been said: the intended meaning is to liken the sequence of the occurrence of the coming out upon the connection of His will, without delay, without any need to bear effort, to the swiftness with which the response of an obeyed caller follows his calling. So in the speech there is a metaphor, either dramatic (tamthiliyyah), imaginative (takhyiliyyah), and implicit (makniyyah), by likening the dead to a people who want to go to the place of a great king and are prepared for that, and the affirmation of the call for them, its indication being the context, or it is an explicit subordinate metaphor in His saying, the Exalted: ("called you") to its end. And "thumma" (then) is either for temporal delay or for delay of rank, and the intended meaning is the greatness of what is in the coordinated clause, the revival of the dead in itself, and in relation to what it is coordinated upon. This does not contradict His saying, the Exalted, that comes later: ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾.

That it is greater than the standing of the heaven and the earth is because it is the purpose of origination and creation, and by it the settling of the blessed and the wretched in the ranks and the depths is established, and it is the purpose of the creation of the earth and the heavens. Thus what Ibn al-Munir said is refuted, namely that the rank of what is coordinated upon here is the higher, together with the fact that the coordinated element being of higher rank in such a context is a majority and not a universal rule, as al-Tibi explicitly stated. So there is no obstacle to considering delay of rank if the coordinated element is not of higher rank. It is also permissible to interpret delay as general distance, encompassing the temporal and the ranked.

The Seven Readers, except Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, read "tukhrajun" with a dammah on the ta' and a fathah on the ra'. It is mentioned that this verse is among those recited over the afflicted. Ibn Abi Hatim reported, from al-Azhar ibn 'Abd Allah al-Jarazi, who said: "It is recited over the afflicted when he is seized: ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command, then when He calls you with one call from the earth, behold, you come out﴾." Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan mentioned, regarding the reason for the order of the verses and the concluding of each of them with what it was concluded with, a lengthy discussion, which you may return to if you need it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 26:

﴿Wa-lahu﴾ (And to Him) — He, exalted and majestic, alone, is the owner of ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, from among the angels and the two weighty creations (humans and jinn), in creation, dominion and disposal. None other than Him, glorified is He, has any partnership in that in any way whatsoever. ﴿Kullun lahu﴾ (All belong to Him) — not to anyone else, exalted is He and high — ﴿qanitun﴾ (are devoutly obedient): submissive to His action, not resisting Him, majestic is His glory, in any of their affairs, even if some of them do not submit to His command, glorified is He. Thus what is meant is obedience to His will, not obedience to the command to worship. This is the substance of what has been related from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan said: (qanitun) means standing as witnesses to His oneness, exalted is He, as the poet said:

"And in everything there is a sign for Him that indicates that He is One."

Page 36
Ibn Jubayr said: (qanitun) means sincere (in devotion). It has also been said: acknowledging servitude. According to these two interpretations, the generality is not on its apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 27:

﴿It is He who originates creation, then repeats it﴾ after death. The repetition serves to reinforce the affirmation, given the intensity of their denial of resurrection (ba'th), and to prepare for what follows in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾. The pronoun in "huwa" (it) refers to the restoration (i'adah). Its masculine form is for the sake of the predicate (khabar), or because it is interpreted as "an" and the verb, which has the status of a masculine verbal noun (masdar). Or it is because it is interpreted as resurrection (al-ba'th) or similar. As for the view that it refers to a verbal noun understood from "yu'idu-hu" (He repeats it), and that since it was not mentioned with the word i'adah it gives no benefit, as has been said, because the word is well known for it, so that when it is understood from it, the specific wording is taken into account, this is not persuasive. The pronoun in the genitive refers to God, exalted is His majesty. "Ahwan" (easier) is in the comparative form, meaning: restoration is easier for God, exalted is He, than origination. The ease is according to the method of analogy, in relation to what humans do that they are able to do, for restoring a thing from its original material is easier for them than producing it from the beginning. The purpose is to bring it closer to the minds of the ignorant who deny resurrection. Otherwise, all possibilities are equal in relation to His power, exalted and majestic. It is as if it were said: "And it is easier for Him" in relation to your capacity and by the measure of your own origins.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned another aspect of the comparative: that origination is among the category of grace (tafaddul), in which the agent has the choice between doing it and not doing it, whereas restoration is among the category of obligation (wajib), which must be done, because it is for the recompense of deeds, and its recompense is obligatory. Actions are either impossible (muhal), and the impossible is absolutely precluded and outside the realm of what is within power; or there is something that turns the Wise away from doing it, namely the ugly (qabih), which is the counterpart of the impossible, because the turning-away prevents the existence of the act just as impossibility prevents it; or it is grace, and grace is in an intermediate state for the agent, who may do it or not do it; or it is obligatory, which must be done and there is no way to neglect it. So the obligatory is the furthest of acts from non-existence and the closest of them to occurrence. Since restoration is in the category of the obligatory, it is the furthest of acts from non-existence, and when it is furthest from that, it is most amenable to attainment and facilitation, so it is easier than origination. End of quotation. In al-Taqrib it is said: "There is scrutiny in this, because it is based on rational obligation, and because obligation, when it is essential, negates power, as impossibility does; otherwise it would be possible, and then the two acts are equal, since they share the factor that makes them capable of being willed, namely possibility."

Al-Kashf commented on this, saying: "I say: it is not obligatory in itself, and it does not follow from it that it is equal to grace in ease of attainment. As for equality in the factor that makes it capable of being willed, it has no bearing on what we are discussing. The summary of it is that even if it is granted that the motive for doing it is stronger, there is no doubt that it is closer to existence than that for which the motive is not so. Yes, if the motive is pure for both categories, they become equal, but the discussion is not under that assumption." End of quotation.

The truth is what Abu al-Su'ud said: that what is meant by the comparative of an act is not its being closer to existence by reason of the great number of factors motivating the agent to produce it and the strength of their demand for its falling under His power, but rather its being easier to attain and to proceed from Him when His power is applied to its existence; and there is no difference in this whether that application is by way of necessity or by way of choice.

Al-Zajjaj narrated from Abu 'Ubaydah and many lexicographers that "ahwan" here means "hayyin" (easy). This was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Rabi', and it is likewise read in the codex of 'Abd Allah. This is like saying: "Allah is greatest" meaning "great"; "you are the one of people" meaning "the unique one among them"; and "I am indeed fearful" meaning "fearful." In al-Kashf, the verified view is that it is of the category of absolute excess, and it is said to mean "hayyin" only because it performs its function. It is also said that the comparative is on its own basis, and the pronoun "alayhi" refers to creation, in the sense that restoration is easier for the created, because origination involves gradual progression from stage to stage until one becomes a human being, whereas restoration does not require gradual stages; God simply calls, and it emerges.

As for the sense that restoration is easier for the created, that is, that they restore a thing and do it a second time after they have practised doing it and have come to know it at first, is easier than doing it first before practice. If this is the state of the created, then what of the Creator? It is not hidden that the apparent reading is that the pronoun refers to God, exalted is He. Then the prepositional phrase is the complement (silah) of "ahwan." The complement was placed first in His saying: ﴿He says: It is easy for Me﴾ [Maryam 19:9, 21], and it is placed last here, because there the emphasis of exclusivity was intended, and that is its essence, so it is said "it is easy for Me," even though it may seem difficult to you that a child be born to him (Zechariah) and a barren wife. As for here, there is no sense of exclusivity, especially since the matter is based on what they understand, namely that restoration is easier than initiation. Had the complement been placed first, the meaning would have changed.

When He, glorified is He, informed that restoration is easier for Him by way of analogy, He followed it with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And His is the highest description﴾, exalted is His majesty, exclusively, ﴿the description﴾, that is, the wondrous attribute, such as general power, perfect wisdom and all other attributes of perfection, ﴿the highest﴾, for which no other has anything approaching it, let alone equal to it. It is as if it were said: this is to make the limited minds understand, since His attributes are wondrous, His power, exalted is His majesty, is general, and His wisdom, glorified is He, is perfect. So everything, beginning, restoration, origination, and annihilation, is on an equal footing, and He has no like and no rival. It is narrated from Qatadah and Mujahid that "the highest description" is "there is no god but Allah." Perhaps they intended by this the oneness of His essence, exalted is He, and His attributes, glorified is He. The discourse on it is connected to what precedes it as well: it is as if it were said, "what has been mentioned is to make the limited minds understand, because none shares with Him, exalted is He, in His essence or His attributes, exalted and majestic." It is also said that it is connected to what follows, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has set forth for you a parable from yourselves﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "the parable" is His saying, exalted is He: "it is easier for Him," which Allah has set forth as a parable regarding what is easy and hard for you, and which is measured by your own standards. So the definite article in "al-mathal" is for prior reference and is taken in its literal sense, not as a metaphor for the wondrous attribute.

﴿In the heavens and the earth﴾ is connected to the content of the preceding clause, meaning that He, glorified is He, has been described by this and made known by it in both, on the tongues of creatures and the tongues of signs. It is said that it is connected to "the highest," and it is said to a omitted element that is a circumstantial (hal) qualifier of it, or of "the description," or of the pronoun in "the highest." It is also said that it is connected to what is connected to "His" (lahu), meaning: for Him in the heavens and the earth is the highest description. What is meant is that the indication of the creation of both upon great power is more complete than the indication of origination, so it is more indicative of the permissibility of restoration. For this reason it was made higher than origination. So reflect.

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, the Powerful who is not incapable of any possible beginning or its restoration, ﴿the Wise﴾, who directs actions according to the ways of wisdom and benefit.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 28:**

﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves﴾, by which the invalidity of association (shirk) becomes clear. "From yourselves" means drawn from your own circumstances, which are the matters nearest to you, the best known to you, and the clearest in indicating what has been mentioned of the invalidity of shirk, because they are by way of priority (awlawiyyah). "Min" (from) here denotes the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do you have﴾ to the end of the verse, is a depiction of the parable. The interrogation (istifham) is denunciatory, meaning negation. "Lakum" (for you) is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from what your right hands possess﴾, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿from partners﴾ comes afterwards, because it is a qualifier (na't) of an indefinite noun (nakirah) that has been placed before it, and the governing element in it, as in al-Bahr, is the governing element of the prepositional phrase that falls as a predicate. "Min" (of) here is partitive (li-l-tab'id), and "ma" (what) refers to the category. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from partners﴾, is a subject (mubtada'). "Min" is superfluous, for emphasis of the negation derived from the interrogation. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿in what We have provided you﴾, is connected to "partners", meaning: are there partners in what We have provided you of wealth and what is similar to it, in which you have disposal, being of the category that your right hands possess, of the kind of slaves and female slaves, who belong to you?

It has been permitted that "lakum" be connected to "partners", and that ﴿in what We have provided you﴾ be in the position of the predicate, as you say: "For Zayd in the city is one who hates [him]", so "for Zayd" is connected to "hates", which is the subject, and "in the city" is the predicate. The meaning is: are there partners for you who are of what your right hands possess, being in what We have provided you? His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so you are equal therein﴾, is a clause in the position of the answer to the denunciatory interrogation. "Fihi" (therein) is connected to "equal" (sawa'). In the speech there is an elided element conjoined to "antum" (you), meaning: "so you and they", that is, the owned ones are equal in it, with no difference between you and them in disposing of it. It has been said there is no elision, and "antum" (you) includes the owned ones by way of predominance (taghlib). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿you fear them﴾, is another predicate of "antum". Abu al-Baqa' said: it is a circumstantial clause from the subject pronoun of "antum" in "sawa'". His saying, exalted is He, ﴿as you fear one another﴾, is in the position of a qualifier of an elided verbal noun (masdar), meaning: you fear them that you would act independently in disposing of it without their opinion, a fear being like your fear of one who is of your own kind, i.e., the free partners with you. The intended meaning is the negation of the content detailed in the interrogative clause, that is: you do not accept that your owned ones share with you in what We have provided you of wealth and the like, while they are your equals in humanity, not created for you but for God, exalted is He. So how do you associate with Him, glorified is He, in worship, which is among His essential exclusive attributes, His creation, glorified is He, indeed the made thing of His creation, exalted is He, since you make it with your own hands, then you worship it.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited "anfusukum" with the nominative (raf'), on the basis that the verbal noun is annexed to the object, and "anfusukum" is its subject. Abu Hayyan said: this is a good reading, and there is no impropriety in annexing the verbal noun to the object when the subject is present.

﴿Thus﴾, that is, like that clear detailing, ﴿We detail the verses﴾, that is, We make them clear and explain them, not with a detailing less than this, for a parable is a depiction of intelligible meanings in the form of the perceptible, and a bringing forth of strange perceptions in the form of the familiar, so it is in the utmost degree of clarification and explanation.

﴿for a people who reason﴾, that is, who employ their intellects in reflecting upon parables. It has been said: in reflecting upon matters in general, and parables enter into that by primary entry. He singled them out for mention despite the general detailing of the verses for all, because they are the ones who benefit from them. Al-'Allamah al-Tibi mentioned that since the striking of parables is to bring the imagined near to the intelligible and to show the imagined in the form of the established, it was fitting that the closing phrase be ﴿for a people who reason﴾. This point is more evident here than in what preceded, so reflect.

'Abbas reported from Abu 'Amr the reading "yufassilu" with the third person (ya' al-ghaybah), in accordance with "daraba" (He coined), since it is attributed to what refers to the absent party. The reading of the majority is with the first person plural (nun), for consistency with "razaqnakum" (We have provided you).

Some scholars mentioned that in this verse there is evidence for the validity of the principle of partnership among created beings, because some of them need others. It is as if it were said: what is impossible and abhorrent is the partnership of slaves with their masters. As for the partnership of masters with one another, it is neither impossible nor abhorrent.

Rather, those who did wrong follow their own desires, [turning away] from addressing them, and from trying to guide them to the truth through the coining of parables, the detailed explanation of the signs, the use of sound and rational premises, and a demonstration of the impossibility of their following the truth. It is as if it were said: they did not understand anything of the detailed signs; rather, they followed their [own] deviant **desires** (ahwa', the plural of hawa). The relative pronoun (al-ladhina) was placed in the position of their pronoun in order to record against them that in that following they are wrongdoers, placing things in other than their proper place; or [it means] they are wrongdoers to themselves by exposing themselves to the everlasting punishment. ﴿Without knowledge﴾, i.e., ignorant of the falsehood of what they have embraced, bent upon it, with no barrier turning them away from it, unlike the way a knowing person turns away when he follows falsehood, since his knowledge of its falsehood [prevents him]. ﴿So who can guide one whom God has led astray﴾, i.e., whom God created misguidance in and made him an acquirer of it by his own choice. ﴿And they have not﴾, i.e., for whomever God Most High has led astray, and the plural is used in view of the meaning, ﴿any helpers﴾ who would rescue them from misguidance
page 39
and protect them from its consequences and calamities, meaning: none of them has a single helper, according to the well-known view regarding the contrast of plural with plural. (min) is superfluous, for emphasizing the negation. The statement is brought to console the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and as a preparation for his command, upon him be blessings and peace, by His saying, glorified is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 30:

﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth.﴾ The scholar al-Tibi said: After He enumerated the clear signs and the evidences indicating (God's) oneness, the negation of association (shirk), and the affirmation of the doctrine of the Return (ma'ad), and having struck the parable, glorified is He, and said: ﴿Thus do We detail the signs for a people who reason﴾, He, majestic is His affair, intended to console His beloved, may the blessings and peace of God Most High be upon him, and to prepare him to despair of their faith. So God Most High turned away from that and said, glorified is He: ﴿Rather, those who did wrong follow their own desires﴾. He made the cause of this that He, mighty and majestic, did not will their guidance, and that their hearts are sealed. For this reason He ordered upon it His saying, Most High: ﴿So who can guide one whom God has sent astray?﴾ as a rebuke and denunciation. Then He, glorified is He, concluded all of this with His saying, Most High: ﴿And for them there are no helpers.﴾ That is: if God Most High wills that for them, there is no deliverer for them from it, and no one will rescue them, neither you nor anyone else. So do not let your soul go to waste over them in regrets; concern yourself with the wellbeing of your own self and those who follow you, and set your face... etc. End quote. From this one learns the status of the fa' in His saying, Most High: (fa-man) and likewise in His saying, glorified is He: (fa-aqim). Al-Nisaburi estimated for the second: "When the truth becomes clear and oneness becomes manifest, then set (your face)..." etc. Yet what al-Tibi indicated is perhaps better. Furthermore, it appears from his words that there is a possibility that the relative pronoun (alladhina) stands in place of the pronoun of (alladhina zalamu); so reflect.

"Aqim" is from aqama al-ʿud (he set the stick upright), and it is also said qawwama al-ʿud, when he straightened it, and the intended meaning is the command to devote oneself to the religion of Islam, and to steadfastness and persistence upon it, and to attentiveness in arranging its causes. The speech is a figurative representation of this: whoever gives attention to a thing perceptible by sight fixes his glance upon it, directs his gaze toward it, and turns toward it with a face not turned away from it. It is as though it was said: "So straighten your face toward the religion and turn toward it with complete devotion, not turning right or left." Some eminent scholars said: setting the face toward something is a kinayah (metonymy) for complete attentiveness to it. Perhaps he meant by kinayah the majaz (figurative usage) branching from the kinayah, for it does not require the possibility of intending the literal meaning.

"Hanifan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in (aqim), or from (al-din). Abu Hayyan permitted it to be a state from (al-wajh). The origin of hanaf is inclining from error toward uprightness, and its opposite is janaf with a jim.

"Fitrata Allah" is in the accusative by way of incitement (al-ighra'), i.e., adhere to the fitrah of God Most High. Whoever permits the omission of verbal nouns (asma' al-af'al) permits that here one estimates "ʿalaykum" as a verbal noun. Makki said: it is accusative by an omitted verb, i.e., follow the fitrah of God, and His saying, Most High: (fa-aqim wajhaka lil-din) indicates it, because its meaning is "follow the religion." Al-Tibi preferred this and said: it is closer to the composition of the arrangement, because it agrees with His saying, Most High: ﴿Rather, those who did wrong follow their own desires﴾, and because His saying, Most High: (fa-aqim wajhaka) is ordered upon it by the fa'.

It is permitted that it be accusative by an omitted "a'ni" (I mean), and that it be an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of an omitted verb indicated by what follows, i.e., "He originated you with the fitrah of God," and the action of the verb "fatara" mentioned afterward cannot govern it, because it is from His attribute. And that it be accusative by what the preceding sentence indicates, as a verbal noun emphasizing itself. And that it be a substitute (badal) for "hanifan." What comes to mind most readily is the accusative by way of incitement, and the omission of the verb in the address to the plural, although what precedes is "fa-aqim," which is what al-Zamakhshari chose, so that it matches His saying, Most High:

[Page 40]

﴿Turning back to Him (munībīna ilayhi)﴾: it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the plural pronoun in the verb it is attached to, and the statement of the Exalted, ﴿Fear Him, establish the prayer, and do not be among the polytheists﴾, is taken as conjoined (ma'ṭūf) to that verb.

Al-Ṭībī said, after choosing the supposition (taqdīr) "follow" and preferring it for the reason you have heard: As for the statement of the Exalted, ﴿turning back﴾, it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "establish" (aqim). It is in the plural only because it is addressed in meaning, since the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is also an address to his community. So it is as if it were said: "Establish your faces, turning back."

Al-Farrā' said: That is, "Establish your face," and also those who follow you, like the Exalted's statement, ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded, and those who turn with you﴾ [Hud: 112]. Therefore He, glory be to Him, said ﴿turning back﴾. In al-Murshid it is stated that ﴿turning back﴾ is connected to an implied verb, meaning "be turning back," because of the Exalted's later statement, ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾. End of quote. The excellence of al-Zamakhsharī's statement is not hidden from the fair-minded. And what has been mentioned, that his address ﷺ is the address of the community, strengthens the indication, and that is upon this implied element, not that ﴿turning back﴾ may be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "establish." The apparent sense of al-Farrā's words requires that the circumstantial clause be from something both mentioned and omitted, and that is rare in speech. The implication of "be" (kūnū) together with the implication of a governing verb for ﴿the nature of Allah (fiṭrata Allāh)﴾ necessitates a great deal of implication, while implying it without implication, as some have said, necessitates departing from what is immediately evident there. The fiṭrah, according to what Ibn al-Athīr said, is a state, like the sitting (jilsah) and the kneeling (rukbah), from the root faṭr, meaning origination and invention. Many have interpreted it here as readiness for the truth and preparedness to perceive it. They said: its persistence means continuing to act in accordance with its requirement, and not violating it by following desire and the enticements of the devils of humankind and jinn. He described it with the Exalted's statement, ﴿which He originated for humankind﴾, to emphasize the obligation to obey the command. And it is reported from ʿIkrimah that its interpretation is the religion of Islam.

The report also indicates this. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ḥammād ibn ʿUmar al-Ṣaffār, who said: I asked Qatādah about the Exalted's statement, ﴿the nature of Allah which He originated for humankind﴾, and he said: Anas ibn Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, related to me that he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The nature of Allah, which He originated for humankind upon, is the religion of Allah."

By their origination upon the religion of Islam is meant that He created them ready to accept it, not turning away from it nor denying it, responsive to reason and in harmony with sound reflection, such that, were they left alone, they would not choose any other religion over it.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No child is born except upon the fiṭrah. Then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to a complete animal. Do you see in it any mutilation?"

By "humankind" in both interpretations is meant all of them.

Some claimed that by them, on the second interpretation, is meant the believers, but this is nothing. An objection was raised regarding the generality, that it was reported concerning the boy whom al-Khiḍr, peace be upon him, killed that he had been sealed upon disbelief. It was answered that the meaning of that is that it was decreed that if he lived he would become a disbeliever, either through others misleading him or through some human affliction. This, as has been said, is what is meant by the Prophet's statement, peace and blessings be upon him: "The wretched one is wretched in his mother's womb."

That does not contradict the origination upon the religion of Islam, in the sense of creating him prepared for it and disposed to accept it. So reflect. The matter still needs verification.

It has also been said: The nature of Allah is the covenant taken from the children of Adam. Its meaning, that He originated them upon it, is said to be: He created them with the knowledge of Him firmly implanted within them, as is indicated by the Exalted's statement, ﴿If you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [Luqmān: 25; al-Zumar: 38], and by His statement, glory be to Him, ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of Allah﴾, which is a justification for the command to adhere to His nature, or for the obligation to obey by it. So by "the creation of Allah" is meant His nature mentioned first. In this there is the placing of an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun without its earlier wording. The meaning is: there is no validity or soundness in altering the nature of Allah, the Exalted, by violating what it requires and by not carrying out its demands by following desire and accepting the whisperings of the devils.

It has also been said: The meaning is that no one is able to change the creation of Allah, glory be to Him, or His nature, mighty and majestic is He. So the alteration must be understood as the alteration of the nature itself by removing it entirely and putting another nature in its place that does not make one capable of accepting the truth or of being able to perceive it, for the alteration in the first sense is possible, indeed it certainly occurs. Thus the justification is then on the basis that the soundness of the nature is realized
[Page 41]
in every person, so it must persist by carrying out its requirements upon it, and not violating it by what has been mentioned of following desire and the whisperings of the devils.

The Imam said: It may be said that Allah created His creation for worship, and they are all His servants. There is no alteration in the creation of Allah, meaning that their being servants is not like the state of a slave belonging to a human being, who passes from him to another and leaves his possession through manumission. Rather, there is no departure for creation from worship and servitude. This is to demonstrate the falsity of the view of those who say: worship is for attaining perfection, and once a servant has attained perfection through it, no obligation remains upon him.

And the statement of the polytheists: "The deficient is not fit to worship Allah, and he worships only things like the stars," while they are servants of Allah, the Exalted. And the statement of the Christians: "Jesus, peace be upon him, attained perfection through Allah's indwelling in him, and became a god." End of quote. In it there is what there is. Among the strange things is what is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the meaning of ﴿there is no alteration in the creation of Allah﴾ is a prohibition against castrating male animals.

It has also been said: The statement relates to the disbelievers, as if it were said: "So establish your face for the religion as a ḥanīf, and adhere to the nature of Allah upon which He originated humankind, for these disbelievers are a creation of Allah, the Exalted, and disbelief belongs to them, and there is no alteration in the creation of Allah," meaning that they will not prosper. You know that it is not fitting to interpret the words of Allah, the Exalted, in this way.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the religion commanded to be turned toward, or to the obligation of adhering to the nature of Allah, the Exalted, understood from the urging, or to the fiṭrah, with the masculine demonstrative used according to the meaning of the predicate, or by interpreting the referent as masculine.

﴿The upright religion (al-dīn al-qayyim)﴾: the straight one, in which there is no crookedness and no deviation from the truth in any respect, as the intensive form indicates. Its origin is qayyūm on the pattern of fayʿil. The waw and the yāʾ came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukūn, so the waw was changed to yāʾ and the yāʾ was assimilated into it.

﴿But most people do not know﴾ that, so they turn away from it with aversion.

It has also been said: That is, they have no knowledge at all, and if they had knowledge they would know this. Here the verb is treated as intransitive.

﴿Turning back to Him (munībīna ilayhi)﴾: that is, returning to Him, the Exalted, in repentance and sincerity of deeds, from nāba, nawbatan and nawban, meaning he returned once after another. It is also from al-nawwāb, that is the bees, so named because they return to their dwelling place. It has also been said: That is, cutting themselves off to Him, the Exalted, from al-nāb, the tooth behind the four front teeth, because of the severance that occurs through it that does not occur through other teeth. This has been criticized as far-fetched, because al-nāb is from the yāʾ root and this is from the wāw root. Several views regarding the case of its accusative have already been mentioned, not far off, and al-Baḥr added to them the view that it is accusative as a circumstantial clause from ﴿humankind (al-nās)﴾ in the Exalted's statement ﴿He originated humankind﴾, and he preferred it over all other views. It is, as you see, not so.

Also already mentioned is what has been said about the conjunction of the Exalted's statement ﴿and fear Him﴾, that is, from opposing His command, the Exalted, ﴿and establish the prayer, and do not be among the polytheists﴾, those who alter the nature of Allah, glory be to Him, in any alteration. The apparent meaning is that by them is meant everyone who associates partners with Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and the prohibition is connected to the commands before it. It has also been said that it is connected to "establish the prayer," and the meaning is: "do not be among the polytheists by abandoning it." This view was taken by Muḥammad ibn Aslam al-Ṭūsī, and it is, as you see, not so.

وقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ فَرَّقُوا دِينَهُمْ﴾ بَدَلٌ (badal, substitution or apposition) مِنَ المُشْرِكِينَ بِإعادَةِ الجارِّ، وتَفْرِيقُهم لِدِينِهِمُ اخْتِلافُهم فِيما يَعْبُدُونَهُ عَلى اخْتِلافِ أهْوائِهِمْ، وقِيلَ: اخْتِلافُهم في اعْتِقاداتِهِمْ مَعَ اتِّحادِ مَعْبُودِهِمْ، وفائِدَةُ الإبْدالِ التَّحْذِيرُ عَنِ الِانْتِماءِ إلى حِزْبٍ مِن أحْزابِ المُشْرِكِينَ بِبَيانِ أنَّ الكُلَّ عَلى الضَّلالِ المُبِينِ.

وقَرَأ حَمْزَةُ، والكِسائِيُّ «فارَقُوا» أيْ تَرَكُوا دِينَهُمُ الَّذِي أُمِرُوا بِهِ، أوِ الَّذِي اقْتَضَتْهُ فِطْرَتُهم ﴿وكانُوا شِيَعًا﴾

[Page 42]

أيْ فَرِقًا تُشايِعُ كُلُّ فِرْقَةٍ إمامَها الَّذِي مَهَّدَ لَها دِينَها، وقَرَّرَهُ، ووَضَعَ أُصُولَهُ ﴿كُلُّ حِزْبٍ بِما لَدَيْهِمْ﴾ مِنَ الدِّينِ المُعْوَجِّ المُؤَسَّسِ عَلى الرَّأْيِ الزّائِغِ، والزَّعْمِ الباطِلِ ﴿فَرِحُونَ﴾ مَسْرُورُونَ ظَنًّا مِنهم أنَّهُ حَقٌّ. والجُمْلَةُ قِيلَ: اعْتِراضٌ مُقَرِّرٌ لِمَضْمُونِ ما قَبْلَهُ مِن تَفْرِيقِ دِينِهِمْ، وكَوْنِهِمْ شِيَعًا، وقِيلَ: في مَوْضِعِ نَصْبٍ عَلى أنَّها صِفَةُ (شِيَعًا) بِتَقْدِيرِ العائِدِ، أيْ كُلُّ حِزْبٍ مِنهُمْ، وزَعَمَ بَعْضُهم كَوْنَها حالًا. وجَوَّزَ أنْ يَكُونَ (فَرِحُونَ) صِفَةً لِكُلٍّ، كَقَوْلِ الشَّمّاخِ:

وكُلُّ خَلِيلٍ غَيْرُ هاضِمٍ نَفْسَهُ ∗∗∗ لِوَصْلِ خَلِيلٍ صارِمٍ أوْ مُعارِزِ

(And every friend, not suppressing his own self for the union of a friend who cuts off or shuns.)

والخَبَرُ هو الظَّرْفُ المُتَقَدِّمُ، أعْنِي قَوْلَهُ تَعالى: ﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ فَرَّقُوا دِينَهُمْ﴾ فَيَكُونُ مُنْقَطِعًا عَمّا قَبْلَهُ، وضُعِّفَ بِأنَّهُ يُوصَفُ المُضافُ إلَيْهِ في نَحْوِهِ، صَرَّحَ بِهِ الشَّيْخُ ابْنُ الحاجِبِ في قَوْلِهِ:

وكُلُّ أخٍ مُفارِقُهُ أخُوهُ ∗∗∗ لَعَمْرُ أبِيكَ إلّا الفَرْقَدانِ

(Every brother from whom his brother departs, by the life of your father, except the two Farqadan [stars].)

وفِي البَحْرِ: أنَّ وصْفَ المُضافِ إلَيْهِ في نَحْوِهِ هو الأكْثَرُ، وأنْشَدَ قَوْلَهُ:

جادَتْ عَلَيْهِ كُلُّ عَيْنٍ تِرَةً ∗∗∗ فَتَرَكْنَ كُلَّ حَدِيقَةٍ كالدِّرْهَمِ

(Every eye poured over him in blood-vengeance, so they left every garden like a dirham.)

وما قِيلَ: إنَّهُ إذا وُصِفَ بِهِ كُلٌّ، دَلَّ عَلى أنَّ الفَرَحَ شامِلٌ لِلْكُلِّ، وهو أبْلَغُ، لَيْسَ بِشَيْءٍ، بَلِ العَكْسُ أبْلَغُ لَوْ تُؤُمِّلَ أدْنى تَأمُّلٍ.

﴿And when harm touches people﴾, that is, hardship, ﴿they call upon their Lord, turning back to Him in repentance﴾, returning to Him, exalted is He, away from calling upon other than Him, the Mighty and Majestic, such as idols and others. ﴿Then when He lets them taste mercy from Him﴾, deliverance from that hardship, ﴿behold, a group of them associate partners with their Lord﴾, the One whom they had called upon, turning to Him in repentance. ﴿Associate partners﴾ means that a group of them suddenly commits shirk, by attributing their deliverance to other than Him, exalted is He, such as an idol, or a star, or something similar among created beings. The singling out of this act to some of them is because not all of them are like that. The indefiniteness of "ضُرٌّ" and "رَحْمَةً" is for the purpose of ta'lil (explaining the cause), indicating that, because of their lack of patience, they panic at the slightest calamity and become insolent at the slightest blessing. "Thumma" (ثُمَّ) indicates a sequence of ranking (tarakhi rutbi) or of time (tarakhi zamani).

The lam in ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾ is the lam of consequence (*lam al-'aqibah*), and the fact that it implies a delay is why it is also called *lam al-ma'al* (the lam of ultimate outcome). Shirk and kufr are close in meaning, with no delay between them, as some have said. That view has no basis. It has also been said that the lam is the lam of command (*lam al-amr*), used for threat, as one says in anger: "Disobey me as much as you can." This fits His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know﴾, since it is a threatening command. The possibility that it is a past-tense verb conjoined to (*yushrikun*) is not hidden from view in its state. The fa' is causal (*lil-sababiyyah*). Al-tamattu' means enjoyment and pleasure. In it there is a shift (*iltifat*) from the third person to the second person: ﴿then you will soon know﴾ the evil consequence of your enjoyment.

Abu al-'Aliyah read *fa-yumatta'u* with a yā' at the beginning and in the passive voice, and it is conjoined to (*yakfuru, fa-sawfa yan'alamun*), also with a yā'. Also from Abu al-'Aliyah: *fa-yatamatta'u* with a yā' before the tā', and it is likewise conjoined to (*yakfuru*). From Ibn Mas'ud: *wal-yatamatta'u* with a lam and a yā', and it is a conjunction to *li-yakfuru*.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 35:

﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority (sultan), so that it speaks of what they used to associate with Him?﴾ This is an iltifat (shift) from address (khitab) to the third person (ghaybah), signaling turning away from them and enumerating their offenses to others by way of indirect speech (al-mubathabbah). "Am" (or) here is munqati'ah (disjunctive). The sultan is the proof (hujjah), so the "sending down" is a metaphor for instruction or informing. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-huwa yatakallamu﴾ ("so it speaks"), means "so it indicates," which makes "speaking" a metaphor for indicating. You may also take into account here all the possibilities that they considered in their saying "the situation spoke" (nataqat al-hal). It is also permissible that "sultanan" be understood as "dha sultan," meaning a king with whom there is a proof, in which case there is no metaphor at either point.

The clause ﴿huwa yatakallamu﴾ ("it speaks") is the answer to the interrogative implied by "am," since the meaning is: "Rather, have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks..."
