﴿of what they used to associate﴾, that is, of their associating others with Allah, mighty and majestic is He. Its soundness holds if "ma" is a verbal-noun (masdariyyah) and the pronoun in "bihi" refers to Him, exalted is He; or with respect to the matter by which they associate and His divinity, if "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah) and the pronoun in "bihi" refers to it, with the "ba'" being causal (sababiyyah). The intended meaning is the negation that they have any support on which they may rely in their polytheism.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 36:

﴿And when We let the people taste mercy﴾, i.e., a blessing of health, abundance, and the like, ﴿they rejoice in it﴾ out of insolence and exultation. For this is the blameworthy joy, as opposed to joy that is praise and thanks, and this is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy, in that let them rejoice﴾. The Imam (al-Razi) said: The blameworthy is rejoicing in the mercy itself, and the praiseworthy is rejoicing in the mercy of Allah, exalted is He, insofar as it is attributed to Allah, exalted is He. ﴿And if an evil befalls them﴾, i.e., hardship, ﴿because of what their hands have put forward﴾, because of the ill-omen of their sins, ﴿behold, they despair﴾, i.e., they suddenly fall into despair of His mercy, mighty and majestic is He. The expression with "idha" (when/behold) at the beginning is for the certainty and abundance of mercy, not its counterpart. In attributing the mercy to Him, exalted is He, but not the evil, there is an instruction to the servants that evil should not be attributed to Him, glorified is He, and this is frequent, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the way of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have evoked anger﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7] (the words "an'amta" and "al-maghdubi" in al-Fatihah 7). The non-mention of the cause for the tasting of mercy, and the mention of the cause for the befalling of evil, is a hint that the first is bounty (tafaddul) and the second is justice ('adl). The use of the present tense in ﴿behold, they despair﴾ is for the sake of the rhyme (ra'ayat al-fasilah) and to indicate continuance in despair. The word "al-nas" (the people) may refer either to a group other than the first, with the definite article being for prior reference (al-'ahd) or for the genus (al-jins); or to the first group, but the first judgment is established for them in a state of bewilderment, like witnessing drowning, and this judgment applies to them in another state. So there is no contradiction between His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when harm touches the people, they call upon their Lord, turning to Him in repentance﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have put forward, behold, they despair﴾. Thus there is no need to strain at reconciling them by saying that the verbal supplication is customary and does not contradict the inner despair. That is why it was heard that some of those engaged in the blood of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, were supplicating during their circumambulation and saying: "O Allah, forgive me, though I do not think You will." Or the meaning is that they act as those who despair, such as preoccupation with gathering stores in times of scarcity. And it is not hidden that in the suddenness (al-mufaja'ah) there is a certain remoteness from this; so reflect.

And it was read "yaqnituna" with a kasra on the nun.

﴿Have they not seen﴾, i.e., have they not looked and not observed, ﴿that Allah extends provision for whom He wills﴾, that He, exalted is He, extends it for him, ﴿and restricts it﴾, i.e., constricts it for whom He wills to constrict it. This is either with regard to two persons, or with regard to one person at two different times. The intent is to deny their rejoicing and despair in the two states of ease and hardship, meaning: have they not seen that, so why do they not give thanks, and why do they not seek reward in ease and adversity as the believers do? ﴿Indeed in that﴾, the extending mentioned and its opposite, or everything that was mentioned, ﴿are signs for a people who believe﴾, who thereby infer the perfection of power and wisdom. And how right is the one who said:

The toil of the discerning and the ease of the ignorant
have both guided you to a perfect Wise One.

Al-Tibi said: The closing phrase was His saying ﴿for a people who believe﴾, as a notice that He, exalted is He, does this purely by His own will, glory be to Him. Wealth is not by the servant's act and effort, nor is poverty by his incapacity and idleness. None knows this except one who believes that it is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing, as he said:

How many a discerning man, whose heart understands,
perfect in intellect yet poor and destitute,

and how many a foolish man whose wealth is abundant:
that is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing.

[p. 44]

﴿So give the near of kin his right﴾, from kinship ties, charity, and all other acts of kindness; ﴿and the needy and the wayfarer﴾ what they deserve. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, with the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) being the primary intended addressee, and the other believers being included secondarily. Al-Hasan said: It is an address to every listener.

Some scholars have permitted that it be addressed to whoever has been granted abundant provision. The connection of this command with what precedes it, and its being joined by the particle *fa* (so), according to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, is that when Allah (Exalted is He) mentioned that the evil had befallen them because of what their hands had sent forth, He followed it with mention of what must be done and what must be avoided. The summary of this, according to *al-Kashf*, is that obeying Allah's commands (Exalted is He) brings about His pleasure, and a good life follows it, just as disobeying Him (glory be to Him) brings about His wrath, and drought and hardship accompany it. When this is established, then give, O Muhammad, and whoever follows him, or give, O you to whom provision has been extended, ﴿the near of kin his right﴾, etc.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) mentioned another aspect, based on the view that the command follows from the discussion of extending and restricting provision: when Allah (Exalted is He) explained that He extends and restricts, He commanded spending (Exalted is He), as an indication that a person should not hesitate in doing good, for when Allah extends provision it does not diminish by spending, and when He restricts it, it does not increase by withholding, as it has been said:

*When the world has been generous to you, then be generous with it to people, all of them, for it turns about.*
*Generosity does not exhaust it when it comes, and stinginess does not preserve it when it departs.*

The author of *al-Kashf*, may Allah sanctify his soul, said: What al-Zamakhshari mentioned is more fitting to the composition of this noble text, for His saying: ﴿Do they not see that Allah extends provision﴾ serves to complete the rebuke against one who rejoices in a blessing without thanking the Benefactor, and despairs when it departs from him. The apparent meaning, according to what al-Imam mentioned, is that the intended "right" is the financial right, and likewise what is intended in the case of the needy and the wayfarer. Some have understood this as referring to the obligatory zakat. It has been objected that the surah is Meccan, whereas zakat was only enjoined in Medina; the exception of this verse and the claim that it is Medinan require a sound transmission, and the precedence of revelation over the ruling is far-fetched. For this reason the remaining categories are not mentioned here.

It is related that Abu Hanifa derived from the verse the obligation of maintenance (nafaqah) for every maḥram relative, male or female, when they are poor or unable to earn. It was argued that (*ātī*, "give") is an imperative for obligation, and that the apparent meaning of "right", given the context of what precedes, is financial. If the intended meaning were zakat, the near of kin would not have been given precedence, for the apparent purpose of its precedence is distinction.

The Shafi'is rejected the obligation of maintenance for those mentioned, and said: there is no maintenance due by kinship except for children and parents, as explained in *fiqh* (jurisprudence). The "right" expressed regarding the near of kin means the maintenance of family ties in its various forms, and the "right" implied regarding the needy and the wayfarer is charity, which was obligatory before zakat was enjoined, or obligatory zakat itself. The verse is either Medinan or Meccan, and the revelation preceded the ruling.

This was objected to on the grounds that if the right of the last two is interpreted as zakat, then the right of the first must be interpreted as obligatory maintenance, lest the imperative form be used for both obligation and recommendation. This is why Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) used the verse as evidence for what was mentioned earlier. There is discussion in this.

One of the eminent Shafi'i scholars, responding to this argument, said: How can it hold given the possibility that the command refers to giving charity as well, as indicated by what follows? Moreover, (*dhā al-qurbā*, "the near of kin") is ambiguous according to the one who argues this, and from where does he derive that it is explained as the mahram relative? Likewise His saying (*ḥaqqahu*, "his right"). Then he said: The truth is that He commanded the full provision of his right of kinship ties, not specifically maintenance, and maintaining family ties is among the strongly emphasized obligations, end of quote. Truth is more worthy of being followed. Al-Imam's (may Allah have mercy on him) evidence is not this alone, as is not hidden from the scholars of his school.

Some restricted the address to the Prophet ﷺ alone and said: The intended meaning of "the near of kin" is the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib; the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to give them their share of the spoils (*ghanima*) and the *fay'* (property taken without battle). In *Majma' al-Bayan* by al-Tabarsi, from the Shi'a, the meaning is: And give, O Muhammad, your relatives their rights which Allah has assigned to them from the fifths.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and others narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) gave Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with her) Fadak and handed it over to her. This is also narrated from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah. End of quote.

In this there is an objection: this contradicts what is well known among both groups, that she (may Allah be pleased with her) claimed Fadak by way of inheritance. Some claimed that she claimed it by way of gift, and brought in support of this 'Ali, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with them) and Umm Ayman (may Allah be pleased with her), but it was not accepted from her because of the relationship of marriage and descent, and because one woman's testimony is not sufficient in this matter. So she claimed inheritance, and what happened, happened. This discussion is mentioned most completely in *al-Tuhfa*; if you want it, refer to it.

Some restricted (*ibn al-sabīl*, "the wayfarer") to the guest, and his right to be treated kindly until he departs. The well-known view is that he is the one cut off from his wealth. The two meanings overlap partially. The near of kin is mentioned first out of concern for his matter, and this is the reason for placing the second object before the conjunction, and for departing from saying: "give the near of kin and the needy and the wayfarer their rights." He expressed "near of kin" in all places, and did not express "needy" as "one of poverty," because kinship is established and does not renew itself, and the construction *dhū* plus a noun is generally used only for what is established. Do you not see that they say of one who repeatedly holds sound opinion: "So-and-so is one of sound opinion," and you hardly hear them say this of one who was right in his opinion only once? Similarly, such expressions as "So-and-so is one of standing," and "So-and-so is one of boldness." Since poverty is something that comes and goes, one does not say "one of poverty" regarding the needy. Thus said al-Imam.

﴿That﴾, i.e., the giving implied by the command, ﴿is better﴾ in itself, or better for those who seek it, ﴿for those who desire the Face of Allah﴾, i.e., His Essence (glory be to Him), meaning they intend Him (Mighty and Majestic) by their good deeds, sincerely; or His direction (Exalted is He), i.e., they intend the direction of drawing near to Him (glory be to Him), not any other direction. The two meanings, as in *al-Kashf*, are close, but the approach differs.

﴿And those are they who are the successful﴾, those characterized by giving, because by spending what perishes they have gained lasting bliss. The restriction is relative, according to what has been said: i.e., those are the successful, not those who were stingy with what they had and spent nothing from it.

It has also been said: It is absolute, on the basis that those characterized by the mentioned giving are those who believed, established prayer, turned to Him (Exalted is He), and feared Him (Mighty and Majestic). There is no contradiction between this restriction and the restriction mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, so reflect.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 39:**

﴿And what you give as *riba*﴾. The apparent meaning is that *riba* here refers to the well-known increase in transactions that the Lawgiver (al-Shari') prohibited. This is the view of al-Jubba'i (a Mu'tazilite theologian), and it is narrated from al-Hasan [al-Basri]. It is supported by what is narrated from al-Suddi, that the verse was revealed concerning the *riba* of Thaqif, who used to practise *riba*, and so did Quraysh. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Tawus, and others, that it refers to a gift (*'atiyya*) given in expectation of a greater return. According to this view, calling it *riba* is a metaphor (*majaz*), because it is a cause of increase. It has also been said that it is called *riba* because it is a favour that is not obligatory upon the giver.

It is narrated from al-Nakha'i that the verse was revealed concerning people who give to their relatives and brothers, intending to benefit them and make them wealthy, and to favour them, so that they might increase their own wealth by way of benefiting them. This is also a narration from Ibn 'Abbas. Thus the meaning of *riba* is the gift given to relatives in order to increase their wealth. The reason for calling it by what has been mentioned is clear from what we have stated. In any case, *fa-min* (in the phrase *fa-min*, "from") is explanatory (*bayan*) of *ma* (what), not causal (*li-l-ta'lil*).

Ibn Kathir read *ataytum* with a short vowel (*bi-l-qasr*), meaning *ji'tum* (you came with), i.e., "what you came with of gift of *riba*". According to the reading of the majority (*al-Jumhur*), its meaning is *a'taytum* (you gave). ﴿That it may increase in the wealth of people﴾, i.e., that this *riba* may increase and grow in the wealth of the people to whom you gave it.

Ibn al-Shaykh said: The meaning, according to the interpretation of *riba* as gift, is that this *riba* increases in attracting and bringing in the wealth of people. In the same sense it has been said: so that this may increase by means of the wealth of people, and that some of it may come to you through the gift. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Abu Raja', al-Sha'bi, Nafi', Ya'qub, and Abu Haywa that they read *li-tarbu* with a *ta'* on top (*ta' fawqiyya*), vowelled with a *damma*, and attributing the verb to them. This is the pattern of verbs that are transitive to one object by means of the causative *hamza* (*hamzat al-ta'diya*). The object is omitted, meaning: so that you cause it to increase and grow the wealth of people. Alternatively, it is like the phrase *yajrahu fi 'arāqībihā naṣlī* (his blade wounds her hamstrings), meaning: so that you increase and grow the wealth of people. It may also be that this is for *al-sayrura* (becoming), meaning: so that you become possessors of *riba* in the wealth of people.

Abu Malik read *li-turbūhā* with a feminine pronoun. The pronoun refers to *riba*, given that it is interpreted as gift or something similar.

﴿So it does not increase with Allah﴾, i.e., it is not blessed in His decree and His judgement, exalted and majestic is He.

﴿And what you give as *zakat*﴾, i.e., as *sadaqa* (charity), ﴿seeking the Face of Allah﴾, i.e., seeking by it His Face, exalted is He, purely.

﴿Those are the ones who receive multiplication﴾. That is, those who have multiples (*dhawu al-adh'af*), taking *mudh'if* as an active participle of *adh'afa* (to multiply), meaning he became one who has *di'f* (double/multiple), with a *kasra* and then a sukun, by his reward for what he gave being multiplied for him. It is like *aqwā* (he became strong) and *aysar* (he became wealthy) when one becomes possessed of strength and wealth. In this case the form indicates the subject's becoming what its root describes. It may also be that it comes from *ad'afa*, with the *hamza* being causative and the object omitted, meaning: those who had their reward and their wealth multiplied by the blessing of *zakat*.

The reading of Ubayy, *al-mud'afūn* (those who are multiplied), as a passive participle, supports this interpretation. The apparent expression would have been "so it increases with Allah" (*fa-huwa yarbū 'inda Allāh*), since that is what the contrast requires. However, the wording was changed, because it asserts something other than what came before it. In the arrangement of the text, earlier it used a verbal sentence, and here it uses a nominal sentence introduced by the demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*) together with the separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*), for the purpose of emphasis. Thus it affirmed for them the multiplication, which is more eloquent than mere increase, by way of emphasis through the nominal sentence and the pronoun. It restricted that multiplication to them by way of entitlement, along with what the demonstrative conveys of exaltation, since it indicates elevated rank. It left out what they gave, and mentioned the recipients for another purpose.

The shift from address (*iltifat*) occurs where it says ﴿those﴾ (*ulā'ika*) rather than ﴿you﴾ (*antum*), for exaltation. It is as if Allah, glory be to Him, addressed by this the angels, peace be upon them, and the elite of creation, to acquaint them with their state. It is also possible that the expression with what has been mentioned is for generalisation, by intending by "those" both these people and others. The return pronoun in the sentence refers to *ma* (what), which is omitted, whether *ma* is taken as a relative pronoun, or as a conditional particle according to the more correct view, since in every case it is a predicate. The meaning is: ﴿those are the ones who receive multiplication by it﴾, or: *fa-mu'tūhu* (those who give it), in the form of an active participle: ﴿those are the multipliers﴾. The omission is due to the indication in the speech of what points to it. On the assumption of the general *mu'tūhu* (what is given), there is no *iltifat* in the conventional sense. Considering it as *iltifat* is preferable. In the *Kashshaf* (of al-Zamakhshari) it is stated that the discourse on this basis is more full of benefit, and he explained this by saying that the speech is directed to praising those who give, as an incitement to action. And this, on the assumption of *iltifat*, is of several aspects:

First, the indication by *ulā'ika* (those) as exaltation of them. Second, the rebuke of the angels, peace be upon them, by praising them. Third, what is inherent in the *iltifat* itself of beauty. Fourth, what is in *ulā'ika* on this interpretation of the benefit established in such a verse as:

*"That is, that he perishes, and his praise is enough for me"*

In contrast, if it is taken as a description of those who give, then on that assumption it conveys the exaltation of the act, not of the agent. And even if it entails the agent by implication, this does not contradict what it conveys essentially. So reflect.

The verse, on the first meaning of *riba*, is in the sense of His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Allah deprives *riba* of blessing and gives increase to charities﴾ [al-Baqara: 276]. The sense is "like for like" (*sawā' bi-sawā'*). What Kathir's statements imply is that the verse indicates a prohibition of *riba* in that sense. But you know that if it indicated that, it would indicate the prohibition of *riba* in the sense of a gift expected to bring a greater return, on the assumption of interpreting *riba* as such. Yet they explicitly stated that this is not forbidden for others than the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and that it is forbidden to him, upon him be blessings and peace, on account of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not confer favour seeking to gain more﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 6]. Likewise they stated that what the giver takes from the recipient of that gift in excess of what he gave is not unlawful, and the one who pays it is not sinful. But he is not rewarded for paying the excess, because it is not an original gift, but rather in exchange for what was given first. There is no reward for what is paid as a return. Likewise there is no reward in giving that gift in the first place, because it is a hunting net. The meaning of the saying of some of the Successors (*tabi'un*): "The party who is richer is rewarded for his gift," is that when a stranger gives you a gift so that you will reciprocate and give him more, then repay him from his gift and give him more.

**[Page 47]**

The apparent reading is that the noble Name (*al-Ism al-Jalil*, "Allah") is the subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject in a nominal sentence), and "who" (*alladhi*) is its predicate (*khabar*). The interrogative is a denial (*istifham inkari*, a rhetorical question that denies). "Of your associates" (*min shurakaikum*) is a fronted predicate (*khabar muqaddam*), and "anyone" (*man*) is a delayed subject (*mubtada' mu'akhkhar*). The *min* in it is partitive (*lil-tab'id*, indicating a part of a whole). "Of those" (*min dhalikum*) is an adjectival modifier of "thing" (*shay'*) which was placed before it, so it is parsed as a circumstantial (*hal*). The *min* in it is also partitive. "Thing" (*shay'*) is the direct object of "does" (*yaf'alu*). The *min* that precedes it is an added particle (*za'ida*) for emphasising total comprehensiveness (*li-ta'kid al-istighraq*).

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the noble Name be the subject, with "who" (*alladhi*) as its attribute (*sifa*), and the predicate being ﴿*hal min shurakaikum*﴾ and so on. The link (*rabit*) is the demonstrative pronoun referring to His previously mentioned acts, the Exalted: "of those" (*min dhalikum*) meaning "of His acts." The sentence quoted serves as a predicate because it is in meaning a negated predicate, even though it is apparently interrogative. It is as if it were said: "Allah, the Creator, the Provider, the Causer of death, the Giver of life, has no partner from among those who do not perform these acts of His."

Some scholars made it a predicate by supposing an implied verb of saying (*taqdir al-qawl*), so that it is as if it were said: "Allah, who is described as Creator, Provider, Causer of death and Giver of life, is the one of whom it is said: Is there any of your associates who is described as being described by this?"

Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that a demonstrative cannot serve as a link unless it refers to the subject, and here it does not refer to it. However, it resembles what al-Farra' permitted regarding linking by meaning (*al-rabt bil-ma'na*), though the scholars disagreed with him. This is found in the words of the Exalted: ﴿*wa-alladhina yutawaffawna minkum wa-yadharuna azwajan yatarabbasna*﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234], where the implied meaning is "they await their wives," so the pronoun is supposed to be a noun attached to a pronoun referring to "those who" (*alladhina*), and the link is thereby achieved.

Likewise al-Zamakhshari supposed "of those" (*min dhalikum*) to mean "of His acts," attached to a pronoun referring to the subject. But it is not hidden that the attachment is not considered valid, and if it were considered, another noun would have to be supposed. It is also permitted that the first *min* be to clarify who does the act, with its complement omitted, and "anyone who does" (*man yaf'alu*) be the subject of an omitted verb, meaning: "Has there come about and been established anyone who does, being from among your associates?" Likewise it is permitted that the second *min* clarify the thing covered by the comprehensive term. It has been said that the first *min* and the second *min* are both added, like the third. This, as you see, is untenable.

According to what we have said first, the verse contains two sentences. The first establishes what is among the necessary attributes equivalent to divinity, namely creation, provision, causing death and giving life, to Him, Mighty and Majestic. The second, through an intermediary, conveys the converse of the universal negative (*'aks al-salbiyya al-kulliyya*), and negates these acts entirely from their associates whom they took as partners to Him, Glorified, from among idols and others, emphasised by denial. Reason judges that whatever is taken as a partner is like what was taken in the stated ruling, namely the negation of those acts from it. If you wish, you may make "your associates" (*shurakaukum*) include both categories.

From this it is understood that partnership is invalid, since it is not conceivable that something which is not a god should share in divinity, because the necessary attribute of divinity is not present in it, for the one who is God in divinity. To emphasise this, He, Glorified and Exalted, said: ﴿*subhanahu wa-ta'ala 'amma yushrikun*﴾, meaning: "Glorified is He, and exalted above their associating." The expression in the present tense (*al-mudari'*) is used because of the strangeness of association, or to indicate its continuity and renewal on their part.

Some scholars have pointed out that from these two sentences two premises may be drawn, one affirmative and one universal negative, arranged in the form of a syllogism of the second figure (*qiyas min al-shakl al-thani*). The words of the Exalted ﴿*subhanahu*﴾ and so on yield a universal negative, which is the conclusion of that syllogism. Thus the two sentences mentioned are in the position of a syllogism of the second figure, and the words of the Exalted ﴿*subhanahu*﴾ and so on are in the position of its conclusion. It is not hidden that this requires considerable strain, so reflect deeply on it.

Al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read ﴿*tushrikun*﴾ with the second person (*ta' al-khitab*), i.e., "you associate."

ظَهَرَ الفَسادُ في البَرِّ والبَحْرِ ﴾ "Corruption has appeared on land and sea," such as drought, plague, the frequency of burning and drowning, the failure of hunters and pearl-divers, the loss of blessings in everything, and a general scarcity of benefits with an abundance of harms. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the land became barren, and the supply of the sea was cut off. They said: when the rain ceases, the creatures of the sea go blind. Mujahid said: corruption appeared on land through the killing of Adam's son his brother, and at sea through the seizing of ships by force. In another report from Ibn 'Abbas: through the seizing by force of every ship by Julanda (a tyrant). Perhaps the intended meaning is an example, and the same is said about the killing of Adam's son his brother, which was the first act of disobedience to appear on land. Al-Dahhak said: the earth was green and lush, and no son of Adam came to a tree without finding fruit on it. The water of the sea was sweet, the lion did not prey on the cow, nor did the wolf prey on the sheep. When Qabil (Cain) killed Habil (Abel), everything on earth shuddered, the trees were stricken, the water of the sea became salty and deadly, and animals attacked one another.

It is mentioned that the first act of disobedience at sea was the seizing by Julanda of every ship that passed by him. Thus the mention of these two matters may be for that reason. Whatever the case, "land" and "sea" are to be taken in their literal sense. From Mujahid: "land" means the distant lands far from the sea, and "sea" means the coasts and the cities that are beside the sea and the rivers. Qatadah said: "land" means the deserts and the places of the tribes, and the people of the open country and the pasturelands; "sea" means the cities. The Arabs call the great cities "seas" because of their vastness. From this is the saying of Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah about 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul: "The people of this little sea, meaning Madinah, have certainly agreed to crown him."

Abu Hayyan said: this is supported by the reading of 'Ikrimah, "wa-l-buhur" (and the seas) in the plural, and it is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Al-Nahhas permitted that "sea" be taken in its literal sense, but that the speech contains an omitted modifier, meaning "the cities of the sea," so it is like ﴿وَاسْأَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ﴾ [Yusuf: 82] ("And ask the town"). It is also permitted that by "corruption" is meant acts of disobedience, such as highway robbery, oppression and others. The "al-" in "al-barr wa-l-bahr" (the land and the sea) is for the genus, and likewise in "al-fasad" (the corruption), meaning that the genus of corruption appeared, namely drought, plague and the like, in the genus of land and the genus of sea. ﴿بِمَا كَسَبَتْ أَيْدِي النَّاسِ﴾ ("because of what the hands of people have earned") means: because of what people have done of acts of disobedience and sins, and their evil consequence. This is like His saying: ﴿وَمَا أَصَابَكُم مِّن مُّصِيبَةٍ فَبِمَا كَسَبَتْ أَيْدِيكُمْ﴾ [al-Shura: 30] ("Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned"). On the first interpretation of "corruption" this is clear. As for its interpretation as acts of disobedience, the meaning is: acts of disobedience appeared on land and sea through people's earning and committing them. The meaning of His saying ﴿لِيُذِيقَهُم بَعْضَ الَّذِي عَمِلُوا لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ﴾ ("that He may make them taste some of what they have done, so that they may return") on the first interpretation is clear: that Allah has ruined the means of their worldly life and destroyed them, and the consequence of some of their deeds in this world before He punishes them with all of them in the Hereafter, so that they may return from what they are upon. As for the second interpretation, the "li-" (that) is figurative, in the sense that the appearance of disobedience through them is among the things for which they deserved that Allah make them taste the consequence of their deeds, in the hope that they would return. It is as if they only became corrupt and caused it because of the spread of disobedience on earth for that reason.

Al-Sulami, al-A'raj, Abu Haywah, Sallam, Sahl, Rawh, Ibn Hassan, and Qunbul (by the route of Ibn Mujahid), and Ibn al-Sabbah, Abu al-Fadl al-Wasiti from him, and Mahbub from Abu 'Amr read "li-nudhiqahum" (that We may make them taste) with the nun. The appearance of the aforementioned corruption, as Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah, was before the Prophet ﷺ was sent. When he was sent, whoever returned from among the people returned from misguidance and oppression. It was also said that it was at the beginning of the mission. That is because the disbelievers of Quraysh did what they did of acts of disobedience, persisted in polytheism, and harmed the Messenger ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ then invoked against them, and they suffered drought, and such calamity befell them as befell them. Allah, glorified is He, informed that this was because of their disobedience, ﴿لِيُذِيقَهُم بَعْضَ الَّذِي عَمِلُوا لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ﴾ ("that He may make them taste some of what they have done, so that they may return").

This speaker interpreted "the people" as the disbelievers of Quraysh. It was also said that it was in a time before the time of revelation, general in that it is either the period just before the mission or after it, or otherwise. The ruling of the verse is general to every corruption that appears until the Day of Resurrection. From here it is said: whoever commits a sin, all creatures, of humans, animals, beasts, birds and ants, will be his adversaries on the Day of Resurrection, because He, exalted is He, withholds rain because of the evil of disobedience, so the people of land and sea are all harmed by it. It is reported from Shaqiq al-Zahid that he said: whoever eats what is unlawful has betrayed all people. The connection of the verse with what precedes it is that it contains a censure of what encompasses polytheism and other acts of disobedience, while what precedes it censures polytheism, and it contains a warning to the polytheists of what it contains.

The Imam said regarding the connection: it is that polytheism is the cause of corruption, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿لَوْ كَانَ فِيهِمَا آلِهَةٌ إِلَّا اللَّهُ لَفَسَدَتَا﴾ ("Had there been in them gods besides Allah, they would have been ruined") [al-Anbiya: 22]. When polytheism is its cause, Allah, exalted is He, made their manifestation of polytheism a cause of the appearance of corruption. Had He dealt with them according to what their claim requires, the heavens and earth would have been ruined, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿تَكَادُ السَّمَاوَاتُ يَتَفَطَّرْنَ مِنْهُ وَتَنْشَقُّ الْأَرْضُ وَتَخِرُّ الْجِبَالُ هَدًّا﴾ ("The heavens are about to burst from it, and the earth split open, and the mountains collapse in ruin") [Maryam: 90]. To this Allah, mighty and majestic is He, alluded by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿لِيُذِيقَهُم بَعْضَ الَّذِي عَمِلُوا﴾ ("that He may make them taste some of what they have done"). End. So reflect, and be fair.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 42:

Allah's saying, ﴿Say: Travel through the earth and see what was the end of those before (you)﴾, is brought to emphasize that sins are a cause of the wrath of Allah (ghadab Allah) and His punishment (nakal), since they were commanded to travel, so that they might look and see how Allah destroyed the nations and made them taste the evil end (su' al-'aqibah) because of their sins, and so that they might verify the truth of what has preceded. And His saying, ﴿Most of them were polytheists﴾, is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) to indicate that polytheism alone was not the cause of the destruction of all of them; rather, it is the cause of destruction for most of them, while the other sins besides it are a cause of it for a few of them.

It is also permitted that it indicates that their evil end was due to the spread (fushuw) of polytheism among them and its dominance over them. In this case there is an emphasis on the gravity of the matter of polytheism, that it is a trial (fitnah) that does not afflict only those who did wrong specifically.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 43:**

﴿So set your face toward the upright religion﴾. That is, if the matter is as described, then set (your face). The complete discussion of what is here is known from what has preceded in this noble surah. ﴿Before there comes a Day that has no repelling from Allah﴾. It has been permitted that it be connected to *maradd* (ﻣَﺮَدّ), which is a verbal noun meaning *radd* (repelling). The meaning is: He, glorified is He, does not repel it after it has come, and there is no repelling of it from His side, mighty and majestic is He. This conveys the negation of any repelling of it by other than Him, exalted is He, by a demonstrative method. It was objected that if this were so, then *yawmun* (يَوْمٌ) would have to carry nunation (*tanwin*), because it resembles the annexed noun (*mudaf*).

It was answered that this is based on what Ibn Malik said in *al-Tashil* (*al-Tashil*, the book on grammar), that the one resembling the annexed noun (*shabih bi-l-mudaf*) may sometimes be treated as an annexed noun, so its nunation is dropped. On this interpretation is understood the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no preventer of what You give."

Its details are in his commentary on it. Some scholars made it connected to an omitted element indicated by *maradd*, meaning: it is not repelled from His side, i.e., He, mighty and majestic is He, does not repel it. It was also said that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the estimate is: "it," i.e., the negated repelling, is from Allah, exalted is He. The sentence is then a resumption (*istinaf*), answering an implied question: "From whom is that negated repelling?" It was also said that it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase which is the predicate of *la* (no). It was also said that it is connected to the negation or to what indicates it. It was also said that it is connected to an omitted element functioning as an attribute of *yawm* (the Day). Many scholars permitted its connection to *ya'ti* (comes), meaning: before there comes from Allah, exalted is He, a Day that no one can repel.

This has been criticized on the grounds that it contradicts what is apparent from the wording and the meaning, and that it is in any case of little benefit. Al-Tibi approved it and said: "This aspect is more eloquent, because it gives the repelling an absolute sense and magnifies the Day, and because its coming from the side of a great, capable one possessing overpowering authority." From this it is known that it is not of little benefit.

Yes, it contains the separation that causes ambiguity (*al-fasl al-mulbis*), but the situation of the other aspects is not hidden from anyone with discernment. ﴿On that Day﴾, that is, the Day when it comes, ﴿they will be separated﴾. Its original form is *yatasadda'una* (يَتَصَدَّعُونَ), then its *ta'* was changed into *sad* and assimilated (*idgham*). *Tasaddu'* (التَّصَدُّع), in its original sense, is the scattering of the parts of vessels, then it was used for any kind of dispersal. The meaning is that they will disperse: a group into Paradise, and a group into the Blaze.

It was also said: they will disperse as individuals are dispersed, according to His statement, exalted is He: ﴿The Day when people will be like scattered moths﴾ (101:4), not as two groups are separated. For the intensity of dispersal implied by *yassaddaʿūna* (يَصَّدَّعُونَ) suits the first interpretation. The second was preferred because it suits the context and the preceding discourse, since the speech concerns believers and disbelievers. Thus what is mentioned is an explanation of their difference in the two abodes, and the intensity of the great distance between the two stations, sensory and conceptual, is sufficient for the emphasis.

This is an interpretation transmitted by Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir, from Qatadah. It is also narrated from Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 44:

﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief.﴾ That is, the burden (wabal) of his disbelief, which is the everlasting Fire. In the speech there is an elided genitive (mudaf muqaddar), or "disbelief" is a metaphor for its recompense, or rather for all the harms beyond which there is no further harm. The pronoun is singular in accordance with the wording of "man" (whoever). In this there is an indication of how little they are regarded by God Most High and how contemptible they are, despite the known multitude of their number. And He made it plural in His saying, Most High: ﴿And whoever does righteousness, for themselves they prepare [the way]﴾ in accordance with its meaning. In this, together with observing the rhyme (fasila), there is an indication of the great worth and magnitude of these (believers) before God Most High.

(Yamhudun) is from "mahada firashahu," meaning he prepared and spread out his bed. That is, they prepare for themselves just as a man prepares his bed for himself, so that nothing in his resting place will harm him, disturb him, or spoil his sleep, such as a protrusion or pebbles, or some other thing that troubles the sleeper. It is as if the state of the responsible person with his righteous deed, and what he gains from it of reward and is freed from punishment, is likened to the state of one who prepares and spreads his bed so that he may rest upon it, and nothing in his resting place disturbs him. It is also permitted that the meaning be: "upon their own selves they have compassion," based on the people's proverb said of one who is compassionate: "Has she spread (the bed) and put him to sleep?" In that case the speech is an allusive metonymy (kinaya iymaʾiyya) for compassion and mercy. The first (interpretation) is more apparent. The apparent sense is that this preparation is for what follows death, such as the grave and other things. A group related from Mujahid that he said: "For themselves they prepare" means they make the resting places in the grave level; but that is not the right understanding.

The fronting of the adverbial phrase in both places serves to indicate exclusivity (ikhtisas); it was also said that it serves to express concern (ihtimam). The contrast of "whoever disbelieves" with "whoever does righteousness," rather than with "whoever believes," is either to highlight the importance of faith, on the basis that it is what is meant by righteous deed, or for greater attention to the status of the believing doer, on the basis that by righteous deed is meant what includes both the deed of the heart and the deed of the body. It also suggests that by "whoever does righteousness" is meant the believing person of knowledge, the saying of God Most High:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 45:

﴿That He may reward those who believe and do righteous deeds from His bounty.﴾ This is the reason ('illah, cause) for "they will be made to prepare [a resting place]" (*li-yamhadun*). The relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) is used here in place of a pronoun, to give the reason for the reward, because the relative pronoun has the sense of a derived noun (*al-mushtaqq*), and attaching the judgment to it indicates that the source of derivation is the cause. The phrase "from His bounty" is mentioned to show that the reward is pure grace (*tafaddul mahd*). Interpreting it as "gift" or "increase beyond what is deserved of reward" is a departure from the apparent meaning. It is also permitted that this is the reason for "they will be divided" (*li-yassadda'un*). Limiting the statement to the reward of the believers indicates that it is the primary intended purpose, and it relies on the implication of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers.﴾ The absence of love is a kinaya (metonymy) for hatred in common usage, and this requires that the requital corresponding to it be applied, so it is as if it were said: "and that He may punish the disbelievers."

In the Kashshaf: the repetition of "those who believe and do righteous deeds," and the avoidance of a pronoun in favour of the explicit noun, establishes that before Him, exalted is He, none succeeds except the believing righteous person. His words, exalted is He, "Indeed He..." etc., are a confirmation after a confirmation, by way of direct and reverse correspondence (*al-tard wa al-'aks*). By this he means every pair of statements in which the first confirms the second and vice versa, whether explicit, allusive, implicit or stated. An example is the verse of Ibn Hani:

"No generosity surpasses him, nor does it stand before him, but generosity goes wherever he goes."

Its explanation in our context is that His words, "That He may reward those who believe," indicate by their explicit meaning what has been established: their exclusive entitlement to the honouring reward, and by their implied meaning that they are the people of guardianship and nearness. His words, glorified is He, "Indeed He does not love the disbelievers," as a reason for the exclusivity, indicate by their explicit meaning that the absence of love requires their deprivation, and by their implied meaning that the reward for their opposites is complete. So He, may He be exalted and high, loves the believers.

Al-Allamah al-Tibi mentioned: The apparent meaning is that His words, exalted is He, "So set your face toward the upright religion," to the end of the verse, are like an introduction to the question, and the address is to every one of the responsible persons. His words, exalted is He, "Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief," to the end of the verse, come as a resumption containing the answer. It is as if it was said: "Establish yourselves upon the upright religion before a day comes on which they will be divided," so it was asked: "What is for those who uphold the religion, and what is for those who deviate from it, and how will they be divided?" So it was answered: "Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief," to the end of the verse. As for His words, glorified is He, "That He may reward those who believe," to the end of the verse, it should be a reason for the whole, to distinguish what results for them and against them. However, it is connected only to "they will be made to prepare" because of the strong concern for the matter of faith and righteous deeds, and the lack of concern for the deeds of the disbeliever. For this reason, "Indeed He does not love the disbelievers" was placed in its position. End of quotation. So do not be heedless.

In the verse there is a subtle point that the Imam, may his secret be sanctified, drew attention to: when God, mighty and majestic, attributed disbelief and belief to the servants, He placed the disbeliever first; and when He attributed the reward to Himself, He placed the believer first. This is because His words, "Whoever disbelieves," are a warning to the responsible person so that he refrains from what harms him, in order that He, glorified is He, may rescue him from evil. His words, "and whoever does righteous deeds," are an encouragement to him and an incitement toward good, to bring him to the reward. Rescue takes precedence with the Wise and the Merciful. As for the reward, He, whose majesty is exalted, began with kindness, to manifest generosity and mercy.

Then, having mentioned, glorified is He, the appearance of corruption and ruin because of sins, He mentioned the appearance of righteousness, and He did not state, mighty is He, that it was due to righteous deeds. This is because the Generous One mentions a cause for His punishment so that injustice is not imagined from it, but does not mention a cause for His kindness. So the Mighty One, the Lord of the Worlds, said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 46:

﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds﴾: the south wind (al-Janub) and its direction is from the rising of Suhayl (Canopus) to the rising of the Pleiades (al-Thurayya). The east wind (al-Saba) and its direction is from the rising of the Pleiades to Banat Na'sh (the Bier stars). The north wind (al-Shamal) and its direction is from Banat Na'sh to the setting place of the Flying Eagle (al-Nasr al-Ta'ir). These are winds of mercy. As for the west wind (al-Dabur), its direction is from the setting place of the Flying Eagle to the rising of Suhayl, and it is a wind of punishment. It is mentioned that the first three winds fertilize the rain-bearing clouds and gather them together, and therefore they are mercy.

From Abu 'Ubayda: among the Arabs, the north wind is for refreshment (al-rawh), the south wind is for rain and dew, the east wind is for the fertilization of trees, and the west wind is for calamity. The least of its harm is that it stirs up a violent dust that irritates the eye, and it is the least frequent of them in blowing.

Al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi, in his Sunan, related from Ibn 'Abbas, in a hadith in which he mentioned what the Prophet (ﷺ) used to do and say when a wind arose: "O Allah, make them winds (of mercy), and do not make them a wind (of punishment)."

This is based on the premise that "winds" (al-riyah) are for mercy and "wind" (al-rih) is for punishment. In al-Nihaya it is said: the Arabs say that clouds are not fertilized except by winds that differ from one another. So it is as if he (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, make them fertilizers for the clouds, and do not make them a punishment." Then he said: the verification of this is that the plural is used in the verses of mercy, and the singular in the stories of punishment, such as "the barren wind" and "a violent, freezing wind" (rihan sarsaran).

Some have said that this is because when the wind is single, it comes from one direction and strikes the bodies of animals and plants from one side, so it affects them with an effect greater than they need. It harms them, and the side opposite to its path is harmed, and it misses its share of the air, which leads to their corruption. By contrast, when they are "winds," they encompass all sides of the body, so each side takes its share, and balance results. You know that the wind may be mentioned singly where there is no punishment, as in His saying: ﴿And they sailed with them with a good wind﴾ [Yusuf: 22], and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And to Sulayman, the wind﴾ [al-Anbiya: 81].

The hadith is disputed. Al-Suyuti marked it as good (hasan). Al-Hafiz al-Haythami said: in its chain is Husayn ibn Qays, who is abandoned (matruk), and the rest of its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih. Ibn 'Adi related it in al-Kamil by this route and criticized it on account of the aforementioned Husayn. Its weakness is also reported from Ahmad and al-Nasa'i. Yes, al-Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) attributed it in al-Fath solely to Abu Ya'la, from Anas, as a marfu' report, and said: its chain is sahih. So let this be noted.

Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i, and al-A'mash read "al-rih" in the singular, intending the sense of the plural. Therefore He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿bearing good news﴾, that is, with rain. ﴿And that He may let you taste of His mercy﴾, meaning the benefits that accompany it, such as the scattering of grains (for pollination), the lessening of mustiness, the watering of trees, and other kindnesses and blessings. It is said: it means the fertility that follows the descent of rain caused by them, or the refreshment that accompanies their blowing. There is no basis for restricting it. The "wa" (and) is for conjunction, and the conjunction is upon a deleted cause indicated by "bearing good news," meaning: so that He may give you good news, and so that He may let you taste. Or it is conjoined to "bearing good news" by meaning, since a circumstantial clause (hal) may be intended to express causation, as in the example: "Insult Zayd, (as) one who has done wrong," meaning: because of his wrongdoing. So it is as if it were said: in order to give you good news, and to let you taste. To consider it a conjunction by mere semblance (min 'atf al-tawahhum) is itself a mere semblance. Or it is conjoined to "He sends" (yursila), with an implied causative verb, and the sense is: and He sends them so that He may let you taste. To take the sense as "and He makes the winds run so that He may let you taste" is far-fetched. It is said: or it is conjoined to the clause "And among His signs" etc., with the sense: "and so that He may let you taste, He sent them or did what He did." Some have not accepted this, because the intended meaning is that tasting is included among the signs. It is also said: the "wa" is superfluous.

﴿And that the ships may run﴾ on the sea when they blow by His command, mighty and majestic is He. This restriction was added because the wind may blow without being favorable, so the joining of His will and His command to the wind is necessary for the desired outcome to be achieved. It is also said: this is to indicate that their blowing favorably is one of the matters of His, exalted is He, which no one other than Him, mighty and majestic, can control.

﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾ through the commerce of the sea, ﴿and that you may be grateful﴾, that is, and that you may thank the blessing of Allah, exalted is He, for what has been mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 47:

﴿And We certainly sent messengers before you to their peoples.﴾ This is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) to console him ﷺ with regard to those before him, in a manner that includes a promise to him, upon him be prayer and peace, and a warning to whoever disobeyed him. In this there is also a warning against neglecting the obligations of gratitude.

By "their peoples" is meant their nations, and the singular (qawmihim) is used for brevity where there is no ambiguity. The meaning is: And We certainly sent messengers before you to their nations, just as We sent you to your people, ﴿and they brought them the clear proofs﴾, that is, each nation's messenger came with the clear proofs specific to him, just as you brought your people your clear proofs. ﴿Then We took vengeance on those who committed crime﴾. The fa' (then) is fasiha (explanatory), meaning: some believed and some denied, and so We took vengeance. It has also been said: meaning, they denied them, and so We took vengeance upon them. The relative pronoun (alladhina) is placed in the position of their pronoun (hum) to indicate the cause and to draw attention to the place of the omitted element. It is also permissible that this be a detailed explanation of the general term, in that among them there was a criminal who was subdued and a believer who was granted victory. ﴿And it was incumbent upon Us to aid the believers﴾. In this there is great honour and dignity for the believers, in that they are made to be those whom Allah the Exalted is bound to help, and an indication that the vengeance was for their sake. By "them" is meant what includes the messengers, upon them be prayer and peace. It is also permissible to restrict this to the messengers by making the definite article a reference to a known group. The apparent meaning of the verse is that this victory is in this world, but some reports indicate that it is not restricted to it, and that it is general for all believers, thus including the community after the messengers.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu al-Darda', who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "No Muslim man defends the honour of his brother except that it is a right incumbent upon Allah the Exalted to avert from him the Fire of Hell on the Day of Resurrection." Then he ﷺ recited: ﴿And it was incumbent upon Us to aid the believers.﴾

In this there is an indication that ﴿ḥaqqan﴾ (truly/incumbent) is the predicate of kana (was), and ﴿naṣru al-mu'minin﴾ (the aiding of the believers) is its subject, as is the apparent reading. The subject was postponed because what is attached to it serves as the closing word (fasila), and for the emphasis placed on the predicate, since it is the locus of the benefit, as stated in al-Bahr.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Some readers paused on ﴿ḥaqqan﴾, taking the subject of kana to be the pronoun referring to the vengeance, meaning: the vengeance was true and just, not unjust. Its reference to it is in the manner of ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 8], and ﴿upon Us is the aiding of the believers﴾ is a new independent clause. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, which is supported by the (usual) reading, although there is no objection to it from the standpoint of meaning.

﴿Allah is the One who sends the winds﴾: this is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) brought to explain what was left general in the preceding description of the states of the winds. ﴿So they stir up clouds﴾, moving them and spreading them out. ﴿Then He spreads it out﴾ in a complete and continuous spread at times ﴿in the sky﴾, meaning in its direction and not in the very substance of the sky in the sense that first comes to mind, ﴿as He wills﴾, moving along, standing still, covering the whole sky, or not covering it entirely but only on one side and not another, and so on. Thus the imperative clause is, by interpretation (taʾwil), a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). ﴿And He makes it fragments﴾, that is, pieces at other times.

Ibn ʿĀmir recited ﴿kisafan﴾ with a sukūn on the sīn, which is either a lightened form of the vowelled ﴿kisafan﴾, or the plural of ﴿kisfah﴾, meaning a piece, or a verbal noun like ʿilm, described by it for emphasis, or by taʾwīl with the meaning of the passive participle, or by supposing an elided ﴿dhā kisafin﴾ (possessing pieces). ﴿Then you see﴾, O you who are capable of sight, ﴿the rain﴾, that is, the rainfall ﴿coming out from its openings﴾, that is, its gaps, the plural of ﴿khalal﴾. In both states there is continuity and fragmentation. The pronoun refers to the cloud, which is a collective noun that may be treated as masculine or feminine. It has been permitted, on the reading ﴿kisfan﴾ with sukūn, that the pronoun refer to the rain, but this is not correct.

﴿Then when He makes it strike whomever He wills of His servants﴾, meaning their lands and their farmlands. The bāʾ in ﴿bihi﴾ is for transitivity (taʿdiyah). ﴿Behold, they rejoice﴾, that is, they suddenly feel joy at the arrival of fertility.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 49:

﴿And indeed they were, before it was sent down to them﴾ (the rain) ﴿before it﴾, i.e. before the sending down, ﴿despairing﴾, i.e. hopeless. The repetition is for emphasis. As Ibn 'Atiyya said, it conveys the informing of the swift turning of human hearts from despair to joy. That is because ﴿before it was sent down to them﴾ carries a sense of an interval in time, so ﴿before it﴾ comes to indicate continuity and to dispel that possibility. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is emphasised to show how long it had been since they had seen rain, so that their despair is understood to be deep-rooted. What Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned is closer, because what is immediately understood from "before" is continuity, and the emphasis indicates its intensity. Abu Hayyan rejected both shaykhs and said: what they mentioned as the benefit of the emphasis is not apparent; rather, in my view it is merely for emphasis, and it only serves to remove the metaphorical sense. Qutrub said: the pronoun in ﴿before it﴾ refers to the rain, so there is no emphasis. You know that the sense then becomes: "before the sending down of the rain, before the rain," and this is a construction that is not permissible in eloquent speech, let alone in the Qur'an. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the crops indicated by the rain, i.e. before the sending down of the rain, before they sowed. The objection to this is that ﴿before it was sent down﴾ is connected to ﴿despairing﴾, and ﴿before it﴾ cannot also be connected to it, because two prepositions with the same meaning cannot be connected to one governing word unless through a conjunction or by way of apposition, and there is no conjunction here, and apposition is not apparently valid. Some permitted here badal al-ishtimal (partial apposition), content with the fact that the crops arose from the sending down, so the sending down included them; but this, as you see, is not sound.

Al-Mubarrad said: the pronoun refers to the clouds, because when they saw the clouds they were hoping for rain, and the meaning is "before the sight of the clouds." This also requires a conjunction for the two prepositions to be validly connected to ﴿despairing﴾. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: the pronoun refers to the sending (of the winds). Al-Kirmani said: it refers to the joy (istibshar), because it is paired with despair and He bestowed it upon them. Against both of these is raised the same problem of connection without a conjunction that was raised against those before them. If they say the conjunction is elided, there is a disagreement over whether that is permissible in a place like this by analogy. Some chose that it refers to the joy, with ﴿min﴾ (from) connected to ﴿yunazzila﴾ (is sent down), and the first ﴿min﴾ connected to ﴿mublisin﴾ (despairing), because this conveys the swiftness of the turning of their hearts from despair to joy, by indicating the extreme closeness of the two times, through showing the connection of despair with the sending down, which is connected to joy, as witnessed by the particle ﴿idha﴾ (suddenly). So reflect. ﴿Wa-in﴾ is a lightened form of the heavy (inna), and the lam in ﴿lamublisin﴾ is the distinguishing lam. There is no implied pronoun of situation (damir al-sha'n) for ﴿in﴾, because it is only assumed for the open (anna) form; as for the kasra form, it must be left inoperative, as al-Ansari detailed in al-Mughni. Some eminent scholars did hold that it is assumed.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 50:**

﴿So look at the effects of Allah's mercy﴾, which result from the sending down of rain: the plants, the trees, and the various kinds of fruit. The *fa'* (so) indicates the speed with which these effects follow from it.

Al-Haramayn (the two sanctuaries, Makkah and Madinah), Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr read *athar* in the singular, with a fatḥah on the hamzah and on the thaʼ. Salam read *ithr* with a kasrah on the hamzah and a sukun on the thaʼ. As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿how He gives life﴾, meaning Allah Exalted, ﴿to the earth after its death﴾, it is in the position of the accusative after the removal of the preposition. *Kayfa* (how) is governed by *unzur* (look), meaning: look at Allah Exalted's wondrous giving of life to the earth after its death. Ibn Jinni said that it is in the circumstantial (*hal*) position by way of interpretation, meaning *muhyiyan* (giving life). Whichever is the case, the command to look is intended to draw attention to the greatness of His power, Exalted is He, and the vastness of His mercy, Mighty and Majestic is He, together with what it prepares for the matter of resurrection that follows.

Al-Jahdari, Ibn al-Sumayqa, and Abu Haywa read *tuhyi* with the feminine *ta'*, and the pronoun refers to the mercy. It was permitted, according to the reading of the two sanctuaries and those with them, for the pronoun to refer to *athar* (effect), on the basis that it acquired the feminine gender from its genitive noun. But this is not valid, as is not hidden.

﴿Indeed, that﴾ (the one of great status) ﴿is the One who gives life to the dead﴾, meaning able to give them life. For that is the bringing into existence of the like of what was in the substance of their bodies of animal faculties, just as the giving of life to the earth is the bringing into existence of the like of what was in it of vegetative faculties. It has been said: it is possible that the newly growing plant comes from parts of plants that had disintegrated, dispersed, and mixed with the soil in which their roots were in some previous years, so that it is like the very same giving of life, by restoring the substances and faculties and not merely the faculties. This is a weak and distant possibility, and we do not concede that the Muslim seeking guidance knows that it occurs.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and He is over all things Powerful﴾, are a concluding appended statement (*tadhyil*) confirming the content of what came before it, meaning: He is exceedingly capable over all things, among which is their being given life, since the relation of His power, Mighty and Majestic is He, to all things is equal.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 51:

﴿And if We send a wind and they see it turned yellow﴾ — i.e., the crops (al-nabat) understood from the context, as Abu Hayyan said; or the trace (al-athar) indicated by the traces; or the crops referred to by the pronoun, according to what some have said. Al-nabat (plant growth) is originally a verbal noun (masdar) applicable to both the few and the many, and then the term was applied to what grows (ma yanbut).

Ibn 'Isa said: the pronoun refers to the cloud, because when it is yellow it does not rain. It was also said that it refers to the wind, which may be treated as masculine or feminine. Both opinions are weak, as stated in al-Bahr.

Jannah ibn Hubaysh read "musfarran" (مُصْفارًّا) with an alif after the fa'. The lam in (la'in) is a lam of preparation (muwatti'ah) for an oath, entering upon the conditional particle. The fa' in (fa-ra'awhu) is a fa' of elucidation (fasihah). The lam in His words, ﴿they would remain﴾ (la-zalluu), is the lam of the answer to the oath, which takes the place of both answers. The past tense is used with the meaning of the future, as stated by Abu al-Baqa', Makki, Abu Hayyan and others, and this is explained by the fact that in meaning it is the answer to (in), which can only be in the future. The learned Yemeni (al-Fadil al-Yamani) said: they only estimated the past with the meaning of the future because when the past is fully inflected and used as the answer to an oath, it must have both qad and the lam together; so the restriction is to the lam, since it is future in meaning. There is room for scrutiny in this. They also estimated it as a present verb emphasized with the nun, meaning: and by God, if We send a wind, hot or cold, that strikes their crops with yellowing, and they see it yellow after its greenness and freshness, they would surely remain ﴿after it﴾ — i.e., after the sending, or after the yellowing of their crops. It was said: after being hopeful and glad ﴿they would disbelieve﴾ without hesitation the blessing of God Most High.

In what is mentioned of their blame, for their lack of steadfastness and their quick vacillation between the two extremes of excess and deficiency, there is what is not hidden, since it was obligatory upon them to put their trust in God, glorified be He, in every state, to turn to Him, mighty and majestic, with seeking forgiveness when the rain is withheld from them, not to despair of the mercy of God Most High, to hasten to thank Him through obedience when He, exalted be He, bestows His mercy upon them, not to be excessive in rejoicing, and to be patient under His trial, Most High, when a calamity befalls their crops, and not to disbelieve in His favours, exalted is His glory. But they reversed the matter, refused what would benefit them, and committed what would harm them. And there is no concealing the indication in the verses of preferring the side of mercy over the side of punishment, so do not be heedless.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾. This is a justification for what is understood from the preceding discourse, as if it were said: Do not grieve over their failure to be guided by your reminder, for indeed you [cannot make the dead hear]. In al-Kashshaf: Know that His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It is Allah who sends the winds﴾, is a passage that came before, confirming what was understood from His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿And We certainly sent before you messengers to their peoples﴾ [al-Rum: 47], the verse, because it indicates that He, mighty and majestic, takes vengeance upon those who deny the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and gives victory to those who follow him. So He mentioned in it clear signs that had been summarized there, which point to power, wisdom and mercy. He chose from among the proofs those that combine all three. In it is also what guides to establishing both sides of faith, namely the origin (mabda') and the return (ma'ad). He explicitly mentioned their ingratitude for the blessing and their blaming in the three states, because this is something known to people of sound nature, and one forms their character accordingly. Within it is also embedded its indication of the return, through His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So look at the effects of Allah's mercy﴾. When he finished the discourse of their blaming, he built upon this embedded point, and upon what the context of the speech indicates of their persistence in misguidance despite such clear signs, which have no greater clarity in indication. So He, glorified be He, said: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make [the dead] hear﴾, up to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and they are submitting﴾. In it [is the implication] that they are, in that case, without doubt among those upon whom He will take vengeance, and that you and your partisans are among those given victory. And Allah knows best. So reflect upon it together with what we have mentioned.

The discussion of this sentence without the particle fa' has already been presented in Surat al-Naml, and likewise in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn their backs in retreat﴾, and ﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their misguidance. You can make hear only those who believe in Our signs, and they are submitting﴾. However, here we mention what the eminent scholars stated regarding the hearing of the dead, fulfilling what we promised there. So we say, and from Allah is success: It is reported from the scholar Ibn al-Humam that he said: Most of our shaykhs hold that the dead do not hear, citing as evidence His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ and similar verses, meaning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾ [Fatir: 22]. For this reason they did not hold the practice of instructing the dead at the grave (talqin al-qabr, the reciting of guidance to the deceased at the grave), and they said: If someone swears he will not speak to so-and-so, and then speaks to him when he is dead, he does not break his oath (yahnath). Al-Safarini, in al-Bahur al-Zakhira, relates that A'isha went to the view of negating the hearing of the dead, and a group of scholars agreed with her on this. Qadi Abu Ya'la, one of the great figures of our companions, meaning the Hanbalis, preferred this view in his book al-Jami' al-Kabir, and they argued with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ and similar verses. However, groups of scholars went to the view that they hear in general.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: Most scholars hold this view, and it is the preference of Ibn Jarir al-Tabari. Likewise Ibn Qutayba and others mentioned it. They argued with what is in the two Sahihs from Anas, from Abu Talha, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "When the day of Badr came and [the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)] prevailed over them, meaning the polytheists of Quraysh, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered about twenty-some men, and in another narration twenty-four men, from the chieftains of Quraysh, to be thrown into a well (tawī), meaning a well from the wells of Badr. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out to them: O Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, O Umayya ibn Khalaf, O Utba ibn Rabi'a, have you not found what your Lord promised to be true? Indeed I have found what my Lord promised to be true." Then Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: O Messenger of Allah, why do you speak to bodies that have no spirits? He said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, you are not more able to hear what I say than they are." In another narration by Muslim from Anas, there is an addition: "But they are unable to answer."

And with what Abu al-Shaykh narrated in a mursal report (one missing a companion in its chain) from Ubayd ibn Marzuq, who said: "A woman in Madina used to sweep the mosque, and she died. The Prophet (ﷺ) was not informed of her [death], and he passed by her grave. He said, peace be upon him: What is this grave? They said: Umm Mihjan. He said: The one who used to sweep the mosque? They said: Yes. So he arranged the people in rows and prayed over her. Then he (ﷺ) said: What deed did you find to be the best? They said: O Messenger of Allah, does she hear? He said: You are not more able to hear than she is. Then he, peace be upon him, mentioned that she had answered him: 'The sweeping of the mosque.'"

And with what al-Bayhaqi, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and others narrated from Abu Hurayra: "That the Prophet (ﷺ) stood over Mus'ab ibn Umayr and his companions when he returned from Uhud, and said: 'I bear witness that you are alive with Allah, the Exalted. So visit them and greet them, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, no one greets them except that they return the greeting until the Day of Resurrection.'"

And with what Ibn Abd al-Barr narrated, and Abd al-Haqq al-Ishbili said: its chain is sound, from Ibn Abbas, raised [to the Prophet (ﷺ)]: "There is no one who passes by the grave of his believing brother, whom he knew in this world, and greets him, except that he recognizes him and returns the greeting to him."

And with what Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, who said: "The spirit is in the hand of an angel who walks with it alongside the funeral procession, saying to it: Do you hear what is being said to you? When it reaches its grave, he buries it with him."

And with what is in the two Sahihs of his (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed, when the servant is placed in his grave and his companions turn away from him, he indeed hears the sound of their sandals."

Those who held the other view answered regarding the verse. Al-Suhayli said: It is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Can you then make the deaf hear, or guide the blind?﴾ meaning: Indeed Allah, the Exalted, is the One who makes hear and guides.

Some eminent scholars said: Its meaning is: You cannot make them hear except if Allah, the Exalted, wills, or: You cannot make them hear a hearing that benefits them. A thing may be negated because its benefit and fruit are absent, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see﴾ [al-A'raf: 179], the verse. This interpretation (ta'wil, reading a text away from its apparent sense) may be considered in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear﴾, and the reason for shifting from "Indeed, you cannot make the dead or the deaf hear" to what is in the sublime wording is the concern with negating hearing. It may also be that it is not considered in it, and the speech remains on its apparent meaning, and the reason for the shift is to indicate that "cannot make hear" carries the same meaning in each of the two sentences.

Those who held that they do not hear said: The original principle is not to resort to ta'wil, and to adhere to the apparent meaning until something is established that requires otherwise. They answered many of what the others had cited as evidence. Some of them said: What occurred in the hadith of Abu Talha, may Allah be pleased with him, may be a miracle (mu'jiza) for him (ﷺ), and this is the meaning of those who said it is among his special privileges (khususiyya), and such privileges are among the extraordinary events of custom (khawariq al-'ada), and the discussion is about its like, which is what was negated in the verse ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ and similar verses.

In his (ﷺ) saying: "You are not more able to hear what I say than they are," [the phrase] "than they are" rather than "than they are in what is said" and similar wording, is a confirmation of what is for this [the hearing of the dead]. The hadith of Abu al-Shaykh is a mursal report, and the ruling on using it as evidence is known; moreover, the possibility of a special privilege remains present in it as well. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Qatada said: Allah gave them life, meaning the people of the well, until He made them hear His (ﷺ) words as a rebuke, belittlement, vengeance, grief, and remorse. And it is supported by what al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stood over the well of Badr and said: Have you found what your Lord promised to be true? Then he, peace be upon him, said: Indeed they now hear what I say."

Here the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) restricted their hearing to "now." And if we say that the dead are questioned for seven days in their graves, whether they were believers, hypocrites or disbelievers, and that at the time of questioning their spirits are returned to them, then you could say: It is possible that the address to the people of the well occurred at the time their spirits were returned to their bodies for questioning, since, as in the hadith narrated by Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i, it was on the third day after their killing. And it is possible that his (ﷺ) address to Umm Mihjan occurred at the time of questioning, namely before seven days had passed over her. In that case, their hearing would not be part of the disputed matter, because when they heard they were alive, not dead. This is refuted by [the report] that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him, peace be upon him: "Do you speak to bodies that have no spirits?" and he (ﷺ) did not deny this from him; rather he said to him, peace be upon him: "You are not more able to hear what I say than they are."

Had the matter been as Qatada said, it would have been more apparent that he (ﷺ) would have said to him, may Allah be pleased with him: "The matter is not as you say; indeed Allah, mighty and majestic, has given them life for me," or something similar. And A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, rejected what occurred in the hadith of what was cited from it for the intended point.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Hisham, from his father, who said: "It was mentioned in the presence of A'isha that Ibn Umar narrated to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Indeed the dead person is punished by the weeping of his family over him.' She said:
