Ibn Umar made a mistake. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) only said: 'Indeed he is punished for his sin and his wrongdoing, and indeed his family are weeping over him now.' She said: That is like his saying that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood over the well in which were the slain of Badr from among the polytheists, and said to them what he said. [He said:] 'Indeed they hear what I say.' Rather he only said: 'Indeed they now know that what I used to tell them is true.' Then she recited: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ and ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾." Al-Suhayli followed up on this and said: A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, was not present at the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ), so others who were present are more knowledgeable of his exact words, peace be upon him.

And they said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, do you address a people who have already rotted? He said: You are not more able to hear what I say than they are."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verses 52–53 (part 2 of 2):

They said: "If it is possible that they were aware in that state, meaning as 'Aisha says, it is possible that they were hearing." End of quote. This is a strong statement. The fact that she was not present does not undermine her report, because it is a *mursal* (a report in which the Companion's source is omitted; *mursal al-sahabi*), and it is understood to mean that she heard it from someone who was present, or from the Prophet (ﷺ). If her absence were a flaw in her report, it would also be a flaw in the earlier report of Ibn 'Umar, since he was not present either. There is also no barrier to the Prophet (peace be upon him) having said both wordings, since, as is known from al-Suhayli's words, there is no contradiction between them. Some have said regarding what al-Bayhaqi, al-Hakim, and others transmitted, and which al-Hakim declared sound: "We do not accept its soundness, and al-Hakim's declaration of soundness is itself judged to be invalid. Even if we accept its soundness, we maintain that the dead who do not hear are those other than the martyrs. As for the martyrs, they do hear in general, due to their distinction over the rest of the dead through what has been reported about them, that they are alive with Allah, Mighty and Majestic." Regarding the hadith of Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, it was said that 'Abd al-Haqq, although he said its chain is sound, was countered by the hadith scholar Ibn Rajab, who said: "It is weak, rather it is *munkar* (a rejected report)." Regarding the hadith of Ibn Abi al-Dunya: even if its soundness is accepted, the claim is not established, because the address of the angel (peace be upon him) is to the spirit that is in his hand, and it is not dead. Regarding the hadith in the two Sahihs about the servant hearing the sound of his companions' sandals when they bury him and turn away from him: at that time his spirit returns to him for questioning, so he hears, while he is alive. The majority hold that the spirit returns to the body, or to part of it, at the time of questioning, in a manner that the people of this world do not perceive, except those whom Allah, Exalted, wills among them. Beyond this there are other opinions. The view of Ibn Jarir and a group of the Karramiyya is that the questioning in the grave is upon the body alone, and that Allah, Exalted, creates in it a perception by which it hears, knows, feels pleasure and pain. According to this view, one can say something similar to what was said regarding the first view. The view of Ibn Hazm and Ibn Maysara is that it is upon the spirit alone. The view of Abu al-Hudhayl and his followers is that the dead do not perceive anything at all except between the two blasts. The truth is that the dead hear in general, and this is in one of two respects. The first is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, creates in some part of the dead a power by which it hears, whenever Allah, Exalted, wills, the greeting and similar things that Allah, Glorified, wills for it to hear. Nothing prevents this from being the case because it lies beneath the layers of earth, even though that structure has dissolved from it and its joints have come apart. Whoever accepts that a blind man in China can see a gnat in Andalusia can hardly hesitate to accept this. The second is that this hearing belongs to the spirit without the mediation of any power in the body. There is nothing to prevent the spirit from hearing, or rather from sensing and perceiving in an absolute sense, after its separation from the body, without the mediation of powers within it. Since it has, according to the correct view, an attachment whose reality and manner none knows except Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to the whole body or to part of it after death, which is different from the attachment to the body that it had before, Allah, Glorified, has established His custom of enabling it to hear, and creates this for it at the time of visiting the grave, and likewise at the time of carrying the body to it, and at the time of washing it, for example. The existence of this attachment, and the claim that there is a power of hearing and similar faculties in the spirit itself, do not imply that it hears every thing that is heard, because hearing in general, and likewise all the other perceptions, are subject only to the will (of Allah). Whatever Allah, Exalted, wills, occurs, and whatever He does not will, does not occur. So one restricts oneself to saying that the dead hear what the revelation has reported them hearing, such as the greeting and similar things. This second view is the one that appears more correct to me. It does not require holding that the spirits of the dead are, absolutely, in the courtyards of the graves, because the basis of hearing in it is the will of Allah, Exalted, and the attachment whose manner and reality none knows except Him, Mighty and Majestic. So let the spirit be wherever it wills, or let it not be in any place, as is the view of those who hold that it is immaterial (*tajarrud*).

It is deduced from a statement mentioned by the gnostic Ibn Marjan in his commentary on the Most Beautiful Names of Allah that there is an investigation in another manner, namely that a person has a soul (*nafs*) purified from the innermost part from which the body was created, and this is the spirit of the body, and a spirit (*ruh*) that Allah, Blessed and Exalted, brought into existence from the innermost part from which He created the soul. The latter stands to the soul as the soul stands to the body. So the soul is its veil. After separation, in the case of the believing servant, the spiritual reality is made to dwell in the heights, from the lowest heaven to the seventh heaven, and indeed to wherever Allah, Exalted, wills among the heights, in joy and bliss. The psychic reality (*haqiqah nafsaniyyah*) is made to dwell in the lower regions, from his grave to wherever Allah, Exalted, wills in the atmosphere. For this reason, "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met Musa standing and praying in his grave, and Ibrahim (peace be upon him) under the tree before his ascent (peace be upon him) to the heaven, and he met both of them (peace be upon them) after the ascent in the high heavens." So those are their spirits, these are their souls, and their bodies are in their graves. The same is said of the disbeliever, except that his spiritual reality does not dwell in the heights, so the gates of heaven are not opened for them, rather it dwells in the abode of its wretchedness, and we seek refuge with Allah, Exalted. Between the two realities there is a connection, mediated by that, and by His will, Mighty and Majestic. He causes whoever greets him at his grave to hear the greeting. The hearing of the greeting is not confined to visiting on Friday night and its day, and early Saturday morning, or to Friday and a day before it and a day after it. Rather, it applies to the greeting at visiting in general. So the dead person hears, by Allah, Exalted, the greeting upon him from his visitor, at whatever time it is, and Allah, Glorified, empowers him to return the greeting, as has been stated in some reports.

As for what al-'Uqayli transmitted, that they hear the greeting but cannot return it, it is to be understood as negating the ability to return it in the familiar manner that the living hear. It was said: returning the greeting and not returning it varies according to the individuals. Perhaps a person is empowered by Allah, Exalted, to return it, but is not rewarded for it because the (opportunity for) deeds has ceased, and another person is not empowered by Him, Mighty and Majestic. In my view, the attachment also varies in strength and weakness according to the individuals, and even according to the times. By this, the varying reports and traditions can be reconciled.

As for the answer to the verse under discussion and similar verses that apparently indicate the negation of hearing, it is understood from what has preceded, so let it be understood. And Allah, Exalted, knows best.

In it [is the implication] that they are, in that case, without doubt among those upon whom He will take vengeance, and that you and your partisans are among those given victory. And Allah knows best. So reflect upon it together with what we have mentioned.

The discussion of this sentence without the particle fa' has already been presented in Surat al-Naml, and likewise in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn their backs in retreat﴾, and ﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their misguidance. You can make hear only those who believe in Our signs, and they are submitting﴾. However, here we mention what the eminent scholars stated regarding the hearing of the dead, fulfilling what we promised there. So we say, and from Allah is success: It is reported from the scholar Ibn al-Humam that he said: Most of our shaykhs hold that the dead do not hear, citing as evidence His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ and similar verses, meaning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾ [Fatir: 22]. For this reason they did not hold the practice of instructing the dead at the grave (talqin al-qabr, the reciting of guidance to the deceased at the grave), and they said: If someone swears he will not speak to so-and-so, and then speaks to him when he is dead, he does not break his oath (yahnath). Al-Safarini, in al-Bahur al-Zakhira, relates that A'isha went to the view of negating the hearing of the dead, and a group of scholars agreed with her on this. Qadi Abu Ya'la, one of the great figures of our companions, meaning the Hanbalis, preferred this view in his book al-Jami' al-Kabir, and they argued with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ and similar verses. However, groups of scholars went to the view that they hear in general.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: Most scholars hold this view, and it is the preference of Ibn Jarir al-Tabari. Likewise Ibn Qutayba and others mentioned it. They argued with what is in the two Sahihs from Anas, from Abu Talha, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "When the day of Badr came and [the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)] prevailed over them, meaning the polytheists of Quraysh, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered about twenty-some men, and in another narration twenty-four men, from the chieftains of Quraysh, to be thrown into a well (tawī), meaning a well from the wells of Badr. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out to them: O Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, O Umayya ibn Khalaf, O Utba ibn Rabi'a, have you not found what your Lord promised to be true? Indeed I have found what my Lord promised to be true." Then Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: O Messenger of Allah, why do you speak to bodies that have no spirits? He said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, you are not more able to hear what I say than they are." In another narration by Muslim from Anas, there is an addition: "But they are unable to answer."

And with what Abu al-Shaykh narrated in a mursal report (one missing a companion in its chain) from Ubayd ibn Marzuq, who said: "A woman in Madina used to sweep the mosque, and she died. The Prophet (ﷺ) was not informed of her [death], and he passed by her grave. He said, peace be upon him: What is this grave? They said: Umm Mihjan. He said: The one who used to sweep the mosque? They said: Yes. So he arranged the people in rows and prayed over her. Then he (ﷺ) said: What deed did you find to be the best? They said: O Messenger of Allah, does she hear? He said: You are not more able to hear than she is. Then he, peace be upon him, mentioned that she had answered him: 'The sweeping of the mosque.'"

And with what al-Bayhaqi, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and others narrated from Abu Hurayra: "That the Prophet (ﷺ) stood over Mus'ab ibn Umayr and his companions when he returned from Uhud, and said: 'I bear witness that you are alive with Allah, the Exalted. So visit them and greet them, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, no one greets them except that they return the greeting until the Day of Resurrection.'"

And with what Ibn Abd al-Barr narrated, and Abd al-Haqq al-Ishbili said: its chain is sound, from Ibn Abbas, raised [to the Prophet (ﷺ)]: "There is no one who passes by the grave of his believing brother, whom he knew in this world, and greets him, except that he recognizes him and returns the greeting to him."

And with what Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, who said: "The spirit is in the hand of an angel who walks with it alongside the funeral procession, saying to it: Do you hear what is being said to you? When it reaches its grave, he buries it with him."

And with what is in the two Sahihs of his (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed, when the servant is placed in his grave and his companions turn away from him, he indeed hears the sound of their sandals."

Those who held the other view answered regarding the verse. Al-Suhayli said: It is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Can you then make the deaf hear, or guide the blind?﴾ meaning: Indeed Allah, the Exalted, is the One who makes hear and guides.

Some eminent scholars said: Its meaning is: You cannot make them hear except if Allah, the Exalted, wills, or: You cannot make them hear a hearing that benefits them. A thing may be negated because its benefit and fruit are absent, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see﴾ [al-A'raf: 179], the verse. This interpretation (ta'wil, reading a text away from its apparent sense) may be considered in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear﴾, and the reason for shifting from "Indeed, you cannot make the dead or the deaf hear" to what is in the sublime wording is the concern with negating hearing. It may also be that it is not considered in it, and the speech remains on its apparent meaning, and the reason for the shift is to indicate that "cannot make hear" carries the same meaning in each of the two sentences.

Those who held that they do not hear said: The original principle is not to resort to ta'wil, and to adhere to the apparent meaning until something is established that requires otherwise. They answered many of what the others had cited as evidence. Some of them said: What occurred in the hadith of Abu Talha, may Allah be pleased with him, may be a miracle (mu'jiza) for him (ﷺ), and this is the meaning of those who said it is among his special privileges (khususiyya), and such privileges are among the extraordinary events of custom (khawariq al-'ada), and the discussion is about its like, which is what was negated in the verse ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ and similar verses.

In his (ﷺ) saying: "You are not more able to hear what I say than they are," [the phrase] "than they are" rather than "than they are in what is said" and similar wording, is a confirmation of what is for this [the hearing of the dead]. The hadith of Abu al-Shaykh is a mursal report, and the ruling on using it as evidence is known; moreover, the possibility of a special privilege remains present in it as well. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Qatada said: Allah gave them life, meaning the people of the well, until He made them hear His (ﷺ) words as a rebuke, belittlement, vengeance, grief, and remorse. And it is supported by what al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stood over the well of Badr and said: Have you found what your Lord promised to be true? Then he, peace be upon him, said: Indeed they now hear what I say."

Here the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) restricted their hearing to "now." And if we say that the dead are questioned for seven days in their graves, whether they were believers, hypocrites or disbelievers, and that at the time of questioning their spirits are returned to them, then you could say: It is possible that the address to the people of the well occurred at the time their spirits were returned to their bodies for questioning, since, as in the hadith narrated by Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i, it was on the third day after their killing. And it is possible that his (ﷺ) address to Umm Mihjan occurred at the time of questioning, namely before seven days had passed over her. In that case, their hearing would not be part of the disputed matter, because when they heard they were alive, not dead. This is refuted by [the report] that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him, peace be upon him: "Do you speak to bodies that have no spirits?" and he (ﷺ) did not deny this from him; rather he said to him, peace be upon him: "You are not more able to hear what I say than they are."

Had the matter been as Qatada said, it would have been more apparent that he (ﷺ) would have said to him, may Allah be pleased with him: "The matter is not as you say; indeed Allah, mighty and majestic, has given them life for me," or something similar. And A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, rejected what occurred in the hadith of what was cited from it for the intended point.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Hisham, from his father, who said: "It was mentioned in the presence of A'isha that Ibn Umar narrated to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Indeed the dead person is punished by the weeping of his family over him.' She said:

[Page 57]

Ibn Umar made a mistake. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) only said: 'Indeed he is punished for his sin and his wrongdoing, and indeed his family are weeping over him now.' She said: That is like his saying that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood over the well in which were the slain of Badr from among the polytheists, and said to them what he said. [He said:] 'Indeed they hear what I say.' Rather he only said: 'Indeed they now know that what I used to tell them is true.' Then she recited: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ and ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾." Al-Suhayli followed up on this and said: A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, was not present at the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ), so others who were present are more knowledgeable of his exact words, peace be upon him.

And they said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, do you address a people who have already rotted? He said: You are not more able to hear what I say than they are."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verses 52–53 (part 2 of 2):

They said: "If it is possible that they were aware in that state, meaning as 'Aisha says, it is possible that they were hearing." End of quote. This is a strong statement. The fact that she was not present does not undermine her report, because it is a *mursal* (a report in which the Companion's source is omitted; *mursal al-sahabi*), and it is understood to mean that she heard it from someone who was present, or from the Prophet (ﷺ). If her absence were a flaw in her report, it would also be a flaw in the earlier report of Ibn 'Umar, since he was not present either. There is also no barrier to the Prophet (peace be upon him) having said both wordings, since, as is known from al-Suhayli's words, there is no contradiction between them. Some have said regarding what al-Bayhaqi, al-Hakim, and others transmitted, and which al-Hakim declared sound: "We do not accept its soundness, and al-Hakim's declaration of soundness is itself judged to be invalid. Even if we accept its soundness, we maintain that the dead who do not hear are those other than the martyrs. As for the martyrs, they do hear in general, due to their distinction over the rest of the dead through what has been reported about them, that they are alive with Allah, Mighty and Majestic." Regarding the hadith of Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, it was said that 'Abd al-Haqq, although he said its chain is sound, was countered by the hadith scholar Ibn Rajab, who said: "It is weak, rather it is *munkar* (a rejected report)." Regarding the hadith of Ibn Abi al-Dunya: even if its soundness is accepted, the claim is not established, because the address of the angel (peace be upon him) is to the spirit that is in his hand, and it is not dead. Regarding the hadith in the two Sahihs about the servant hearing the sound of his companions' sandals when they bury him and turn away from him: at that time his spirit returns to him for questioning, so he hears, while he is alive. The majority hold that the spirit returns to the body, or to part of it, at the time of questioning, in a manner that the people of this world do not perceive, except those whom Allah, Exalted, wills among them. Beyond this there are other opinions. The view of Ibn Jarir and a group of the Karramiyya is that the questioning in the grave is upon the body alone, and that Allah, Exalted, creates in it a perception by which it hears, knows, feels pleasure and pain. According to this view, one can say something similar to what was said regarding the first view. The view of Ibn Hazm and Ibn Maysara is that it is upon the spirit alone. The view of Abu al-Hudhayl and his followers is that the dead do not perceive anything at all except between the two blasts. The truth is that the dead hear in general, and this is in one of two respects. The first is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, creates in some part of the dead a power by which it hears, whenever Allah, Exalted, wills, the greeting and similar things that Allah, Glorified, wills for it to hear. Nothing prevents this from being the case because it lies beneath the layers of earth, even though that structure has dissolved from it and its joints have come apart. Whoever accepts that a blind man in China can see a gnat in Andalusia can hardly hesitate to accept this. The second is that this hearing belongs to the spirit without the mediation of any power in the body. There is nothing to prevent the spirit from hearing, or rather from sensing and perceiving in an absolute sense, after its separation from the body, without the mediation of powers within it. Since it has, according to the correct view, an attachment whose reality and manner none knows except Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to the whole body or to part of it after death, which is different from the attachment to the body that it had before, Allah, Glorified, has established His custom of enabling it to hear, and creates this for it at the time of visiting the grave, and likewise at the time of carrying the body to it, and at the time of washing it, for example. The existence of this attachment, and the claim that there is a power of hearing and similar faculties in the spirit itself, do not imply that it hears every thing that is heard, because hearing in general, and likewise all the other perceptions, are subject only to the will (of Allah). Whatever Allah, Exalted, wills, occurs, and whatever He does not will, does not occur. So one restricts oneself to saying that the dead hear what the revelation has reported them hearing, such as the greeting and similar things. This second view is the one that appears more correct to me. It does not require holding that the spirits of the dead are, absolutely, in the courtyards of the graves, because the basis of hearing in it is the will of Allah, Exalted, and the attachment whose manner and reality none knows except Him, Mighty and Majestic. So let the spirit be wherever it wills, or let it not be in any place, as is the view of those who hold that it is immaterial (*tajarrud*).

It is deduced from a statement mentioned by the gnostic Ibn Marjan in his commentary on the Most Beautiful Names of Allah that there is an investigation in another manner, namely that a person has a soul (*nafs*) purified from the innermost part from which the body was created, and this is the spirit of the body, and a spirit (*ruh*) that Allah, Blessed and Exalted, brought into existence from the innermost part from which He created the soul. The latter stands to the soul as the soul stands to the body. So the soul is its veil. After separation, in the case of the believing servant, the spiritual reality is made to dwell in the heights, from the lowest heaven to the seventh heaven, and indeed to wherever Allah, Exalted, wills among the heights, in joy and bliss. The psychic reality (*haqiqah nafsaniyyah*) is made to dwell in the lower regions, from his grave to wherever Allah, Exalted, wills in the atmosphere. For this reason, "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met Musa standing and praying in his grave, and Ibrahim (peace be upon him) under the tree before his ascent (peace be upon him) to the heaven, and he met both of them (peace be upon them) after the ascent in the high heavens." So those are their spirits, these are their souls, and their bodies are in their graves. The same is said of the disbeliever, except that his spiritual reality does not dwell in the heights, so the gates of heaven are not opened for them, rather it dwells in the abode of its wretchedness, and we seek refuge with Allah, Exalted. Between the two realities there is a connection, mediated by that, and by His will, Mighty and Majestic. He causes whoever greets him at his grave to hear the greeting. The hearing of the greeting is not confined to visiting on Friday night and its day, and early Saturday morning, or to Friday and a day before it and a day after it. Rather, it applies to the greeting at visiting in general. So the dead person hears, by Allah, Exalted, the greeting upon him from his visitor, at whatever time it is, and Allah, Glorified, empowers him to return the greeting, as has been stated in some reports.

As for what al-'Uqayli transmitted, that they hear the greeting but cannot return it, it is to be understood as negating the ability to return it in the familiar manner that the living hear. It was said: returning the greeting and not returning it varies according to the individuals. Perhaps a person is empowered by Allah, Exalted, to return it, but is not rewarded for it because the (opportunity for) deeds has ceased, and another person is not empowered by Him, Mighty and Majestic. In my view, the attachment also varies in strength and weakness according to the individuals, and even according to the times. By this, the varying reports and traditions can be reconciled.

As for the answer to the verse under discussion and similar verses that apparently indicate the negation of hearing, it is understood from what has preceded, so let it be understood. And Allah, Exalted, knows best.

[Page 58]

**[Page 59]**

﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾: this is a subject and predicate construction. The meaning is that He originated you in a state of weakness, and made weakness the foundation of your condition, as in His words: ﴿And man was created weak﴾ [an-Nisa 4:28]. Here *min* (مِن) is *ibtida'iyyah* (indicating the starting point). In the word "weakness" there is an *isti'arah makniyyah* (implicit metaphor), in which weakness is likened to a foundation and a substance. The attachment of *min* to it contains *takhyil* (imaginative evocation). It is also permissible that by "weakness" is meant "the weak one," using the verbal noun as a description for emphasis, or by interpreting it as such. Or it may mean "one who has weakness," and what is meant by this is the drop of semen (*nutfah*): that is, Allah the Exalted, who originated your creation from a weak origin, which is the drop of semen, as in His words: ﴿from a despised fluid﴾ [as-Sajdah 32:8; al-Mursalat 77:20]. Although this interpretation is related from Qatadah, the first is more preferable and more fitting with His words: ﴿Then He made after weakness strength﴾, which refers to the time of your reaching puberty, or the attachment of the soul to your bodies. ﴿Then He made after strength weakness and gray hair﴾, when old age overtakes you. The weakness meant here is its beginning, and for this reason He placed gray hair after it. Or, in the more general sense, His words "gray hair" are for explanation, or to combine the change of your powers and your outward appearances.

 Asim and Hamzah read the *dad* (ض) of "ḍaʿf" in the first instance with a fatḥah (ضَعْفٍ), and this is the reading of ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) and Abu Rajaʾ.

[Page 59]

The majority read it with a ḍammah on it. The ḍammah and the fatḥah are two dialectal forms for this word, as in *al-faqr* and *al-fuqr* (poverty). The fatḥah is the dialect of Tamim, and the ḍammah is the dialect of Quraysh. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) chose the reading with ḍammah, as there is a hadith narrated by Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi (who graded it *hasan*), Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir, at-Tabarani, ad-Daraqutni, and others, from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: "I recited to the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾" — meaning with a fatḥah — "so he said: 'From ḍuʿf (with ḍammah), O my son'" — meaning with a ḍammah.

This is because it was the dialect of his people, peace be upon him. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not intend by this to reject the other reading, because it is also established by revelation, like the reading which he chose. It is also related from Asim that he read it with a ḍammah, and also from him that he read the first two with a ḍammah and the last with a fatḥah. It is related from Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, al-Jahdari, and al-Dahhak that they read the first with a ḍammah and what follows with a fatḥah.

Isa (ʿIsa) read the *ḍad* and the *ʿayn* both with a ḍammah (ضُعْفٍ), and this is also a dialect for it. It is related from many philologists that *ḍuʿf* with a ḍammah is what is in the body, and *ḍaʿf* with a fatḥah is what is in the intellect. Apparently, there is no difference between the ḍammah and the fatḥah in this, and both may be used to describe the body and the intellect. The weakness meant in the second instance is the same as the first, and it was made indefinite for harmony with "strength" (*quwwah*). The weakness meant in the last instance is other than the first, for it is the weakness of old age, while the first is the weakness of childhood. The strength meant in the second instance is the same as the first, and it was made indefinite for harmony with "weakness" (*ḍaʿfan*). The indefinite noun, when it is repeated, is not necessarily the same; some scholars have strained to establish a difference in what was made indefinite and repeated in the verse, so reflect on this.

﴿He creates what He wills﴾: He creates His creation from among things, of which are those mentioned: weakness, strength, and gray hair. Their creation may mean either the creation of their causes or their loci, or it may mean the bringing into existence of these things themselves, which is the apparent meaning, and there is no need for interpretation, for they are not a state of pure nonexistence.

﴿And He is the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful﴾: the one who is exceedingly perfect in knowledge and power. The alternation among the different states mentioned, while other possibilities exist, is among the clearest indications of knowledge and power.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 55:

﴿And on the day the Hour (al-sa'ah) is established﴾ — i.e., the Resurrection (al-qiyamah). It is called so because it is established (taqum) at the very end of the hours of the world, or because it comes suddenly (baghtah). It became its proper name by dominance (bi'l-ghalabah), like "the star" (al-najm) for the Pleiades (al-Thurayya) and "the planet" (al-kawkab) for Venus (al-Zuhrah). By its "establishment" is meant its existence, or the standing of creatures in it. ﴿The criminals will swear that they had tarried﴾ — i.e., that they had remained in the graves, as narrated from al-Kalbi and Muqatil; and what is meant is that they remained after death. ﴿but an hour﴾ — i.e., a small portion of time. Many narrators related from Qatadah that they meant: they had tarried in this world in the same way. It was also said: they mean they tarried in the interval between the end of the world and the resurrection, which is the interval between the two blasts (al-nafkhatayn).

In the authentic hadith, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "What is between the two blasts is forty." It was said: "Forty days, O Abu Hurayrah?" He said: "I refuse (abaytu)." It was said: "Forty months?" He said: "I refuse." It was said: "Forty years?" He said: "I refuse."

By his words, may Allah be pleased with him, "abaytu" (I refuse), he meant: I refrained from explaining that to you, or: I refused to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) about that. On account of this hadith it has been said: it is not known whether it is forty years or forty thousand years. Al-Saffarini, in al-Buhur al-Zakhirah, related from some scholars a claim of consensus among the narrations that what is between the two blasts is forty years. I say: the truth is that no one knows it except Allah the Exalted, and the claim of consensus has not been established for me by any evidence.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that this is a period in which their punishment ceases, and that they regarded the duration of their stay as trivial, either by lying, as narrated from al-Kalbi, or by forgetting the terror of the scene of the Gathering, as it has been said. It is also permissible that their regarding that period as small is in comparison with the duration of their punishment on that day. It is not far-fetched that they knew its length, whether this statement was made at the beginning of the time of the Gathering, or during it, or after entering the Fire. It is also permissible that they counted the period of their stay in the world as an hour because they did not benefit from it; and much without benefit is little, just as little with benefit is much.

﴿Thus they were deluded﴾ — i.e., the statement is one of regret and grief over their squandering the days of their lives. Between (al-sa'ah) and (sa'ah) there is a perfect homonymic pun (jinas tam mumathil), as the eloquent have agreed, except for one who is not counted. The difference in the case-vowel does not harm it, nor does the presence of (al) in one of the two words, since it adds to the word. Likewise, the unity of their meanings in origin does not harm it, because the definite form in this sense is like the indefinite, meaning a portion of time, owing to the transfer (naql) in the definite form and its becoming a proper name for the Resurrection, like the other transferred proper names. Deriving one from the other does not harm it either, as is clarified by what they have established concerning the derivative pun (jinas al-ishtiqaq).

Some thought that "the Hour" in the sense of the Resurrection is metaphorical, and therefore the pun was denied here, since this type of pun does not occur between a literal and a metaphorical sense. Thus there is no pun in such a phrase as: "I rode a donkey (himar) and met a donkey (himar)," meaning a dull man. It is well known that this type of pun does not occur in the noble Qur'an except in this place. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Hajar, may Allah have mercy on him, deduced another place, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sight﴾ and ﴿Allah alternates the night and the day; indeed in that is a lesson for those of insight (ulu al-absar)﴾ [al-Nur: 43, 44], because the first "absar" is the plural of "basar" (sight), and the second "absar" is intended to be the plural of "basirah" (insight). It was objected that although the second "absar" is intended as the plural of "basirah," it is not a matter of literal usage but of metaphor and figurative extension, because "basirah" is not pluralized as "absar" but as "basa'ir." The grammarians of Arabic said: the pattern af'al is one of the plurals of paucity, which applies regularly only to a triliteral noun with an open first letter like basar/absar, or a kasra-initial one like 'inab/a'nab, or a damma-initial one like rutab/artab, with a quiescent middle letter like thawb/athwab, or with a vowelled middle letter as already mentioned, and like 'adud/a'dad and fakhidh/afkhadh. The pattern fa'a'il is one of the plurals of abundance, which applies regularly only to a quadriliteral feminine noun ending in ta' marbutah, or one whose third letter is a long vowel in meaning, like sahabah/sahaib, basirah/basa'ir, halubah/halaib, shimal/shama'il, 'ajuz/'aja'iz, and Sa'id as a woman's name/sa'a'id. Thus "absar" is borrowed for "basa'ir" on the basis of the common element between them, namely perception and discernment. I have heard that this type of pun does not occur between a literal and a metaphorical sense, so let it be noted.

﴿Thus⦆ — i.e., like that deception, ﴿they used to be﴾ — i.e., in the world, ﴿turned away (yu'fakun)﴾ — i.e., diverted from truth and verification. The purpose of bringing this verse is to emphasize the description of the criminals in their persistence in denial and their insistence on falsehood. Or: like that deception they used to be deluded in being deceived by what has now become clear to them, that it was only an hour. So the discourse is in wonder at their being deceived by the glittering of the mirage. The aim is to make small in their eyes the enjoyments and adornments of the world, so that they might cease their obstinacy and return to the path of right guidance. It is as if it were said: like that wondrous deception they used to be deluded in the world, deceived by what they counted as an hour, reckoning it as brief. The one who diverts them is Allah the Exalted, or Satan, or desire; whichever it is, that is only due to the evil of their choice and the corruption of their disposition. And in this verse, according to one of the opinions, there is evidence that the disbelievers lie in the Hereafter.

Some have used it as evidence for denying the punishment of the grave, but this is nothing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 56:

﴿And those who were given knowledge and faith will say﴾ in the world, whether from among the angels, mankind, or both together, ﴿"You have indeed remained within the Book of God"﴾ that is, within His knowledge and decree, or what He has written and determined, glory be to Him, or the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or the Qur'an, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And before them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100]. In any case, the prepositional phrase is connected to what precedes it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, and there is in it what there is of remoteness, that the speech is in inverted order (taqdim and ta'khir), and the original is: "Those who were given knowledge and faith will say: 'You have indeed remained in the Book of God' ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾." The speech is a refutation of what they said, emphasized with an oath, or a rebuke, exposure, and mockery of them, so reflect. ﴿So this is the Day of Resurrection﴾ which you used to be promised in the world. The fa' (so) is explanatory (fasihah), as if it were said: "If you were denying the Resurrection, then this is its day," that is, "So We inform you that the falsity of your denial has become clear."
Page 61
It is also permitted that it be a conjunctive fa' (ataf), with the sequence being mentioned (dhikra), or causal (ta'liliyyah). ﴿But you used not to know﴾ that it is true, due to your negligence in reflection, so you hastened toward it mockingly. It was also said: you did not know the Resurrection and did not acknowledge it, and therefore your destination became the Fire.

Al-Hasan recited "al-Ba'atha" with a fatha on the ain in both places, and it was also read with a kasra on both. The first is a noun (ism) and the fathah form is a verbal noun (masdar). In the verse there is an indication of the virtue of scholars that is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 57:**

﴿Then on that Day﴾ means: when that occurs, namely the oaths of the disbelievers and the statement of those possessed of knowledge to them, ﴿the excuse of those who wronged will not benefit them﴾, that is, their excuse.

Most readers recite *tanfa'* (will benefit) with a *ta'* (تنفع), in keeping with the apparent form of the word, even though a separator intervenes between them. ﴿Nor will they be asked to make amends﴾. *Al-isti'tab* (seeking to remove displeasure) means seeking *al-'utba*, which is the noun of *al-i'tab* (appeasement), meaning the removal of displeasure, like *al-'ata'* (giving) and *al-isti'ta'* (asking for a gift). That is, it is not sought from them to remove the displeasure of God Most High, meaning His anger toward them, through repentance and obedience, for the punishment has already become binding upon them. If you wish, you may say: that is, it is not said to them, "Make your Lord content through repentance and obedience," as was said to them in this world. It has also been said: that is, they will not be given the chance to retract, so that they would be granted a return (to the world) by being sent back to the world.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is information about the terror of the Day of Resurrection and the severity of its circumstances for the disbelievers, that excuse-making will not benefit them, and they will not be given *'utba*, which is contentment. ﴿Yustata'tabun﴾ has the meaning of *ya'tibun* (they are appeased), just as you say *yamliku* and *yastamliku* (he owns / he takes ownership). The principle with the form *istaf'ala* is that it denotes seeking a thing, but this is not of that kind, because the meaning becomes corrupt if what is understood from it is that they are not sought to be appeased. End of quote. Thus he treated *istaf'ala* as having the meaning of *fa'ala*.

The resulting meaning according to al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan), as he states, is: they are in a state of neglect and of not being regarded, like one who is not deemed fit to be reproached. It has also been said:

The meaning according to this view is: they will not be reproached for their misdeeds, but rather they will be punished. What we mentioned first is what should be relied upon. But how strange it is that Ibn 'Atiyya claimed corruption in the meaning when what is understood from it is that they are not sought to be appeased, as you have heard.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 58:

﴿And We have certainly struck for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example.﴾ That is: by Allah the Exalted, We have certainly described for the people every attribute which is, in its strangeness, like an example (mathal), and We have related to them every attribute of wondrous matter, such as the attribute of those raised on the Day of Resurrection, what they say and what is said to them, and what of their excuses does not benefit them and what of their pleas for reconsideration is not heeded. So "darb al-mathal" (striking an example) means taking it and fashioning it, from the striking of the seal (khatam) and of the brick (labin).

The mathal is a metaphor for the strange attribute. What is meant by "this Qur'an" is either this glorious surah or the whole collection, and the latter is the apparent meaning. "Min" (from) is partitive (tab'idiyyah), though its being extra (ziyadah) has been permitted. It has also been said that the meaning is: by Allah the Exalted, We have certainly made clear to the people every example that informs them about tawhid (divine unity), resurrection, and the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace be upon him. Thus "darraba" here means "bayyana" (made clear), and "mathal" retains its original sense. It has also been said that mathal means a wondrous proof, and "al-Qur'an" means the collection.

﴿And if you bring them a sign﴾ That is: despite Our striking for them every example in this glorious Qur'an, if you bring them a sign from its signs, ﴿those who disbelieve will surely say﴾ out of their extreme obstinacy, their stubbornness, and the hardness of their hearts, addressing you and the believers, ﴿"You are nothing but falsifiers (mubtilun)."﴾ That is: fabricators (muzawwirun). It has also been permitted to understand the verse as referring to a miracle (mu'jizah): that is, if you bring them a miracle of those miracles which they have proposed, those who disbelieve will say, etc. The use of the relative pronoun (al-ladhina) rather than a pronoun indicates the reason that prompts the said statement. And if by "the people" is meant all people, including the disbelievers and others, then the reason for the explicit noun is clear. The singular address in "ji'tahum" (you brought them) is in accordance with what the apparent sense requires. As for the plural in their saying "in antum" (you are), it is so that, in their assumption, he (peace be upon him) would not have a witness from among the believers, since they made them all claimants.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: In the singular address in "jitahum" and the plural in "antum" there is a subtle point, which is that God the Exalted said: if you bring them every sign with which the messengers, peace be upon them, came, and it is possible that it be brought to them, they would say: "You all, O claimants to prophethood, are falsifiers." End of quote. But it is not hidden that what we have mentioned is better and more refined.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 59:

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that abominable sealing. It is also permissible that the meaning is "like that statement." ﴿Allah seals﴾, i.e., sets a seal (yakhtimu), ﴿upon the hearts of those who do not know﴾, He whose greatness is exalted and whose power is magnified, ﴿upon the hearts of those who do not know﴾, i.e., who do not seek knowledge and do not strive after the truth, but persist in superstitions they have adopted and absurdities they have invented. For compound ignorance (al-jahl al-murakkab) prevents the perception of truth and makes one deny the one who speaks the truth. From this they said: "It is worse than simple ignorance (al-jahl al-basit)." And how subtle is what was said:

The donkey of the sage Thoma said: "If they were just to me, I would be the one riding."

Because I am simply ignorant, ∗∗∗ while my companion is compoundly ignorant.

The use of the word "knowledge" for "seeking" is a metaphor, since seeking is customarily associated with it. It has also been said that the meaning is: Allah, exalted is He, seals the hearts of those who are not among the people of knowledge, but this is not the case. The intended meaning of ﴿those who do not know﴾ may be "those who disbelieved," in which case the relative pronoun has been placed in the position of their pronoun, with what is in its relative clause. It may also be general, and those (disbelievers) enter into it as a primary inclusion.

The apparent sense of the words of some of the eminent scholars leans toward the first possibility. The discussion of His sealing and stamping upon the heart, Mighty and Majestic is He, has already been presented earlier.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 30, verse 60:

﴿So be patient﴾, i.e., once you know their state, and God Most High has sealed their hearts, be patient with their displeasures of false speech and evil deeds. ﴿Indeed, the promise of God is true﴾, and He, Mighty and Majestic, has promised you victory, the manifestation of the religion, and the elevation of the word of truth. It is necessary that it be fulfilled and carried out without doubt. ﴿And let not those who have no certainty make you impatient﴾, i.e., let them not move you to haste and anxiety, ﴿those who do not have certainty﴾ regarding what you recite to them of clear verses, by denying them and harming you with their falsehoods, among which is their saying: ﴿You are but liars﴾. For they are doubters and astray, and such things from them are not to be wondered at. It has been said: i.e., they do not have certainty that God's promise is true. This is as you see, and although the admonition is addressed to someone other than the Prophet (ﷺ), the prohibition refers to him (peace be upon him). So it is of the type of "Let me not see you here", which has been previously verified. It is as if it were said: do not be lightened toward them out of distress. In the verse there is guidance from God to His Prophet (ﷺ), and His teaching him, Glorified is He, how to receive displeasures with a broad breast, which is not hidden.

Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub recited: ﴿wa-la yastahiqqannaka﴾ with an unpointed ḥāʾ and a qāf, from al-istiḥqāq (deserving). The meaning: let not those who have no certainty tempt you, and be more deserving of you than the believers. This is a metaphor for that, because whoever tempts someone wins him over to himself until he becomes more deserving of him than others. The prohibition in this reading refers to his community (peace be upon him) and not to him (ﷺ), because of his infallibility. Similar examples have been mentioned before, and what the scholars have said about them.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read with the doubling of the nūn (tashdid), and Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Ya'qub read it without doubling. Among the subtle things that are narrated is what Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from ʿAli, may God honor his face: that a man from the Khawarij called out to him while he was in the dawn prayer, saying: ﴿And it has been revealed to you and to those before you: If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely be lost, and you will surely be among the losers﴾. He, may God honor his face, answered him while in prayer: ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of God is true, and let not those who have no certainty make you impatient﴾.

There is no wonder in this answer, from the gate of "the city of knowledge" and the brother of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Furthermore, among the allusions in the verses: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. The Romans have been defeated, in the nearest land; but after their defeat they will overcome, within a few years﴾ to the end. It has been said: the alif is an allusion to the affection of the nature of the believers, the lam to the baseness of the nature of the disbelievers, and the mim to the forgiveness of the Lord of the worlds, exalted is His majesty. The Romans are an allusion to the heart, and Persia, the referent of the pronoun standing in for the subject, is an allusion to the soul, and the believers are an allusion to the spirit, the secret, and the intellect. So in the verse there is an allusion that the state of the people of seeking changes with the changing of times: the Persia of the soul sometimes overcomes the Rome of the heart, and at other times the Rome of the heart overcomes the Persia of the soul, by the support and victory of God Most High. This occurs over a few years, the days of seeking, and on that day the believers, the spirit, the secret, and the intellect, rejoice. Following this same method, al-Nisaburi proceeded with: ﴿They know an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾. In it there is an allusion to the state of the veiled and their standing at the outward appearances of things. There is nothing except that it has an outward aspect, which is what the outward senses perceive of it, and an inward aspect, which is what the intellect perceives by one of the ways of perception, from the aspects of wisdom in it. Among it is what lies beyond the level of the intellect, which is what is attained through the Divine overflow and the most perfect refinement of the soul. And although it is not among the deductions of the intellect, the intellect accepts it. The meaning of its being beyond the level of the intellect is not that the intellect rejects it and does not accept it, as is imagined. From what we have mentioned it is known that the inward need not be reached through the outward; rather, it may be attained without its mediation, and that is higher in rank than attaining it through it. So the saying of one who says that the inward cannot be reached except by crossing the outward is not free from scrutiny. ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, made joyful﴾, i.e., they will be gladdened by hearing in the meadow of witnessing, and that is the nourishment of their spirits and their bliss. The highest kinds of hearing in this life, according to the Sufi masters, are those that come from the Divine Presence to the holy spirits and the angelic ears. These ears have not been separated from the hearing of ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. Hearing among them is well known in listening to beautiful voices, and listening to things that stir what overcomes them of states: fear, hope, love, and reverence. Such is the hearing of the Qur'an, of admonition, of the drum, the shabbaba (flute), the strings, the mizmar (reed pipe), the chanting, the nashid (anthem), and in this there is the praiseworthy and the blameworthy. In the great Qawa'id of ʿIzz al-Din ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn ʿAbd al-Salam, a full detailed discussion of this is found in the most complete manner, and we shall, God willing, soon mention what relates to this. God Most High is the One who grants success to what is right. ﴿So glorify God when you enter the evening﴾ etc. In it there is an allusion that it is fitting to occupy the times in glorifying God, Glorified is He, and praising Him, exalted is He, with what He is worthy of. For that is the meadow of this life. And in a report: "The circles of remembrance are the gardens of Paradise." ﴿He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living﴾. In it there is an allusion that the branch does not necessarily have to be like its root:

"The rose comes only from the thorn, and the narcissus grows only from an onion."

﴿And among His signs is that He created for you mates from yourselves that you may find tranquility in them﴾. In it there is an allusion that sharing in kind is among the causes of affection, for birds of a feather flock together. ﴿Every party, in what they have, rejoices﴾. In it there is an allusion that He, Mighty and Majestic, has not compelled anyone to what they are upon, whether true or false; rather, the mutual passion among souls occurs according to their readiness and what they are. So God, Glorified is He, mighty in power, gives every lover the beloved whom the heart of his readiness has become infatuated with, and whose love has filled his heart. This is the secret of joy. How delicate is what Qays ibn Dhurayh said:

My spirit became attached to her spirit before our creation, and before we were drops in the cradle.

So it grew as we grew, and became ever-increasing, and when we die it is not a broken necklace.

But it remains constant through every event, and our visitor in the darkness of the grave and the tomb.

﴿And when harm touches people﴾, the verse. In it there is an allusion that human nature is mixed from the guidance of the spirit and its obedience, and from the misguidance of the soul and its disobedience. So when people are overshadowed by trial, afflicted by temptation, touched by calamity, their souls are broken, their impulses are stilled, and their spirits are freed from the captivity of the darkness of their desires, their spirits return to the Presence, and the souls agree with them against their natures. So they call upon their Lord, turning penitently to Him. Then when He, Glorified, graciously removes what has afflicted them, and Mighty and Majestic looks upon them with kindness, some of them rebel and return to their blameworthy habit and their wretched, despicable nature. ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea﴾, etc. In it there is an allusion that evils are not desired for their own sake; rather, they are like lancing a wound or cutting off a finger that has gangrene. ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of God is true, and let not those who have no certainty make you impatient﴾. In it there is an allusion for the people of the Muhammadan inheritance, the people of guidance, that they should be patient with the displeasures of the deniers, the veiled, who have no certainty regarding the truthfulness of their states. For this reason they make light of them, look upon them with contempt, reproach them, and object to what they say and do. We ask God Most High to make us among those who have certainty, and to protect us, our children, and our brothers from the illnesses of the heart and of the body, by the sanctity of His trustworthy Prophet (ﷺ), and upon his family and all his companions.
